Two practical rules follow.

Set the multiplicity correctly. Line 2 of every .xyz file in this lab is “charge multiplicity”. A triplet O atom run as a singlet gives a perfectly converged, perfectly wrong energy, too high by tens of kcal/mol, and every reaction that uses it is wrong.
Use an unrestricted calculation (UNRESTRICTED = TRUE in Q-Chem) for open shells, so that α and β electrons can have different orbitals. The generated inputs do this for you.

Open-shell atoms are hard for approximate functionals for additional reasons. The functional must describe spin polarization (different α and β densities) correctly. The p-shell of O and S is partly filled, and an approximate functional may give different energies for different ways of occupying the p orbitals, or break the spherical symmetry of the atom. The molecule, by contrast, is closed-shell. The errors in the two kinds of systems are different and do not cancel.






TipWorked example: an atomization energy from total energies



Suppose a calculation gives these total energies (illustrative numbers, not from any experiment in this course): E(H₂O) = −76.40000 Eh, E(O, triplet) = −75.05000 Eh, E(H, doublet) = −0.50000 Eh. For H₂O → O + 2 H, with ν(H₂O) = −1, ν(O) = +1 and ν(H) = +2:
\[
\Delta E = (+1)(-75.05000) + (+2)(-0.50000) + (-1)(-76.40000) = -76.05000 + 76.40000 = 0.35000\ E_\text{h}.
\]
In kcal/mol: 0.35000 × 627.5095 = 219.63 kcal/mol. Note the sign: atomization is endothermic, so ΔE > 0. If the O atom had been run as a singlet, its energy would be too high, and the atomization energy would come out too large.

title: Lecture 9 · Why some reactions are hard for DFT
text:
2.4 Absolute and relative errors
Reaction 5c, the atomization of sulfuric acid, has a reference value of 602.18 kcal/mol, by far the largest number in the course. A method that is “only” 1% off is wrong by about 6 kcal/mol. Is that good or bad?

In relative terms (the relative error defined in Lecture 7), 1% looks excellent, much better than a 0.3 kcal/mol error on a 1 kcal/mol rotational barrier (30%).
In absolute terms, 6 kcal/mol is six times chemical accuracy. It would change an equilibrium constant by a factor of about \(e^{6/0.5925} \approx 2.5\times 10^4\) at room temperature.

Chemistry is decided by absolute energies. Relative errors are useful to compare the difficulty of very different quantities, but they must never be used to excuse a large absolute error. Experiment 5 has a chart that shows the same errors in both ways.

title: Lecture 9 · Why some reactions are hard for DFT
text:
2.5 Training sets and fitted functionals
Many functionals contain parameters fitted to data (Lecture 6). B3LYP has 3; the Minnesota functionals have several dozen. The data used for the fit are the training set. A fitted functional reproduces its training set well by construction, so a good result on a training-set molecule is expected, not impressive. What matters for a user is how the functional performs on systems it was not fitted to.
Reaction 5b (CaO → Ca + O) belongs to the MR-MGM-BE4 subset of Minnesota Database 2015B (Yu and Truhlar 2015), and MN15 was parametrized on that database (Yu et al. 2016). Experiment 5 has a spotlight chart for this reaction. When you look at it, ask: is this result a test of MN15, or a check that the fit worked? The same caution applies to any benchmark: before you use a dataset to judge a functional, check whether it was part of the functional’s training set.






WarningCommon mistakes in hard cases




Running open-shell atoms as singlets, or with restricted orbitals.
Using the wrong coefficient for the atoms: in 5c there are 4 O atoms and 2 H atoms (ν = +4 and +2).
Expecting -D4 to fix everything. Dispersion corrections fix dispersion, not self-interaction or static correlation.
Judging a functional by a single good result, especially on its own training data.

title: Lecture 9 · Why some reactions are hard for DFT
text:
3.3 What to watch out for

Multiplicities. O, S and O₂ are triplets, H is a doublet, Ca and all the closed-shell molecules are singlets (Table 1). The generated inputs already set the multiplicity and UNRESTRICTED = TRUE. If you build an input by hand, check line 2 of the .xyz file.
Coefficients. In 5c, ν = −1 for H₂SO₄, +1 for S, +4 for O and +2 for H. In 5d, ν = −2 for O₃ and +3 for O₂.
SCF convergence. Open-shell atoms and ozone can take more SCF cycles. Check that every job converged before using its energy.
The charts. Besides the signed errors, you will see the relative-error chart, the CaO spotlight and the easy → hard chart, which combines your Experiments 3, 4 and 5 (from this browser) and shows how your functional-draft pick did.
Lock in your predictions on the experiment page first: how much larger will the errors be, which method will win, and will -D4 help?

title: Lecture 9 · Why some reactions are hard for DFT
text:
3.4 Key points

In Experiment 4 errors grew because reactants and products differ: bonds change in 4a, the number of close contacts in 4b and 4c.
-D4 and VV10 fix missing dispersion (4b, 4c) but not errors in bond formation (4a); hydrogen bonds (4d) depend mostly on electrostatics.
The self-interaction error is the spurious repulsion of an electron with itself; HF has none, approximate functionals do.
The delocalization error makes approximate functionals overstabilize spread-out electrons: stretched radical cations, transition states, charge transfer, conjugated systems. HF has the opposite (localization) error.
Static correlation arises when several configurations are nearly degenerate (stretched bonds, ozone, CaO); single-determinant methods struggle.
Atomization energies have no error cancellation. HF underestimates them badly because molecules have more correlation energy than their atoms.
Open-shell atoms need the right multiplicity (O, S triplet; H doublet; Ca singlet) and unrestricted orbitals.
Absolute errors decide chemistry; relative errors can hide large absolute errors.
A functional’s result on its own training data is not an independent test.

title: Lecture 9 · Why some reactions are hard for DFT
text:
3.5 Study questions

Why did -D4 help much more for 4c than for 4d? Answer in terms of the physical components of each interaction.
Give two reasons why the Diels–Alder reaction 4a is harder for DFT than the ethane rotation 3a.
Write Equation 3 in words. Why does Hartree–Fock satisfy it automatically?
Sketch E(N) between N₀ − 1 and N₀ + 1 for the exact functional, a GGA and HF. Use your sketch to explain why GGAs underestimate reaction barriers.
Why is a GGA’s dissociation curve for H₂⁺ too low at large distance?
Explain the difference between dynamic and static correlation, using H₂ at equilibrium and at a long bond length.
Why does Hartree–Fock underestimate atomization energies? Would you expect the error to grow or shrink for larger molecules?
Determine the ground-state multiplicity of N, C, F and Mg atoms. Which need an unrestricted calculation?
An atomization energy of 400 kcal/mol is computed with a 1.5% error. A conformational energy of 0.8 kcal/mol is computed with a 50% error. Which is the larger absolute error, and by how much?
A new functional reproduces a molecule’s bond energy within 0.1 kcal/mol, and that molecule was in its training set. What can you conclude? What would you check next?

title: Lecture 7 · How we test a functional
Lecture 7 · How we test a functional
text:
1.1 Experiment 1: the basis-set error
In Experiment 1 you computed the dissociation energy of the HCl dimer,
\[
\Delta E = 2\,E(\mathrm{HCl}) - E\big((\mathrm{HCl})_2\big),
\tag{1}\]
with four methods (HF, PBE, B3LYP, ωB97M-V) and six basis sets from two families (def2-SVP/TZVP/QZVP and cc-pVDZ/TZ/QZ). The reference value is 2.01 kcal/mol. Because the reaction is a dissociation, ΔE is positive, and a positive signed error ε = ΔEcomp − ΔEref means the dimer is bound too strongly.

1.1.1 What you probably saw for the density functionals
The chart How the error changes as the basis grows puts ζ (DZ, TZ, QZ) on the horizontal axis and |ε| on the vertical axis, one panel per family. For the three functionals the typical picture is:

the error is largest with the double-ζ basis sets, and the dimer is usually too strongly bound;
the error drops sharply from double-ζ to triple-ζ;
the change from triple-ζ to quadruple-ζ is small. The curve flattens out.

Two effects make the double-ζ number too large. The first is the basis-set incompleteness error (BSIE): a small basis cannot describe the orbitals well, and the error does not cancel between the dimer and the monomers. The second, and the dominant one for a weakly bound dimer, is the basis-set superposition error (BSSE). In the dimer, each HCl molecule can “borrow” the basis functions centered on its partner to improve its own description. The isolated monomers have no partner to borrow from. So the dimer is artificially stabilized, and the binding energy comes out too large. BSSE shrinks quickly as the basis grows, because a molecule that already has a nearly complete basis gains little from its neighbor’s functions. We return to BSSE and the counterpoise correction in Lecture 10.
When the curve flattens, you are close to the complete-basis-set (CBS) limit for that functional. What is left is the error of the functional itself. This is the most important lesson of Experiment 1: the basis-set error goes to zero as the basis grows, the functional error does not. With a quadruple-ζ basis, the remaining error tells you how good the method is. For (HCl)₂ the functional with built-in nonlocal dispersion (ωB97M-V) usually ends up closest to the reference. Functionals with no dispersion term can converge to a value that is slightly too small (underbinding), so their |ε| can go down and then up again as BSSE disappears and their real underbinding is revealed. That is why “no specific pattern” is a legitimate answer for some methods.


1.1.2 What you probably saw for Hartree–Fock
Hartree–Fock behaves very differently, and this is the first big surprise of the course. The HF error often does not decrease with the basis. It may even grow. The reason is physical. (HCl)₂ is held together by a mixture of dipole–dipole electrostatics and London dispersion. Hartree–Fock has no electron correlation at all, and dispersion is a correlation effect (Lecture 8 explains why). So at the CBS limit, HF underbinds the dimer. With a small basis, BSSE adds a spurious attraction that partly hides this missing physics. As the basis grows, the spurious attraction disappears and the true HF answer (too little binding) emerges.
In other words, HF/def2-SVP can look better than HF/def2-QZVP for the wrong reason. Keep this example in mind: a small basis can make a bad method look good. It is the theme of Experiment 6 and Lecture 10.






WarningCommon mistake: “the error got smaller, so the method got better”



A smaller error is not proof of a better description. Ask why it got smaller. If the improvement comes from an artifact (BSSE) that happens to compensate for missing physics (dispersion), it will not transfer to another molecule.




1.1.3 def2 or cc-pVnZ?
The two families were built for different purposes. The Dunning correlation-consistent sets, cc-pVnZ (Dunning 1989), were designed so that the correlation energy of wave-function methods (MP2, CCSD(T)) converges smoothly with n. Each step adds a full shell of polarization functions chosen for correlation. The Karlsruhe def2 sets (Weigend and Ahlrichs 2005) were optimized mostly at the Hartree–Fock and DFT level, with the goal of a balanced error across the whole periodic table. Head-Gordon and co-workers found the def2 family to be the most cost-effective for DFT (Witte et al. 2016).
What you probably saw is that, at the same ζ, the two families give errors of similar size, with def2 often a bit better for the functionals at double- and triple-ζ. The differences shrink at quadruple-ζ, where both are close to the CBS limit. Note also that “triple-ζ” does not mean “the same number of functions”: look at the number of basis functions you recorded for each set. Comparing basis sets by name alone is risky, and we will see this again in Experiment 6.


1.1.4 The cost: measured exponents
The second chart plots wall time against the number of basis functions N on a log–log scale. If the cost follows t = a Nn, then
\[
\log t = \log a + n \log N,
\tag{2}\]
and the slope of the straight line is the exponent n. In Lecture 2 you learned that the formal cost of HF and hybrid DFT grows as N⁴, because the number of two-electron integrals (μν|λσ) grows as N⁴. Most of you measured a smaller exponent, often between 2 and 3. Why?

Integral screening. Most of the N⁴ integrals are tiny because the Gaussians are far apart. Programs estimate integrals cheaply (Schwarz inequality) and skip the negligible ones. For large enough molecules the number of significant integrals grows closer to N².
Fixed overhead. Small jobs spend a large share of their time on start-up, reading the basis, building the grid and writing output. This cost does not depend much on N, and it flattens the curve at small N.
Other steps with different scaling. For functionals, the exchange–correlation integration on the grid scales roughly linearly with the size of the molecule. Linear algebra (diagonalization) scales as N³ but has a small prefactor.
A narrow range. Your N values span less than one decade. A fit over a short range is sensitive to noise and to the choice of points.

Figure 1 shows the effect of a fixed overhead on an ideal N⁴ law: at small N the curve is almost flat, and only at large N does it approach the true slope. Which of your points would you trust most? The largest ones.






Figure 1: Model cost curves on a log–log plot. Straight lines are ideal power laws t ∝ Nⁿ for n = 2, 3, 4. The dashed curve is an N⁴ law plus a constant overhead: at small N it is almost flat, so a fit over a short range of N gives an exponent well below 4. All curves are analytic models, not measured timings.





1.1.5 The best compromise
Putting accuracy and cost together, the usual conclusion is that triple-ζ is the sweet spot for DFT. Double-ζ is cheap but not converged (BSIE and BSSE are still large). Quadruple-ζ is close to the CBS limit but costs several times more than triple-ζ for a small gain. This is why Experiments 3–5 use def2-TZVP. If you checked the class results (when released), the heatmap shows the same picture for the whole class.

The most common mistakes were these:

Range separation is not the same as “hybrid”. M11-L is range separated, but both ranges use local (semilocal) exchange. It contains no HF exchange, so it is a meta-GGA. M11 and ωB97M-V, by contrast, use HF exchange at long range (and some at short range), so they are hybrid meta-GGAs.

Names that count parameters or exchange. The “3” in B3LYP and B3PW91 refers to three mixing parameters. The “2X” in M06-2X means twice the HF exchange of M06 (54% vs 27%). M06-HF has 100% HF exchange and is still a hybrid meta-GGA, because it also contains a meta-GGA part.

title: Lecture 7 · How we test a functional
text:
2.1 Why functionals must be tested
The exact exchange–correlation functional exists, but nobody knows its form. Every functional you use is an approximation, and unlike wave-function methods (HF → MP2 → CCSD → CCSD(T) → …), there is no systematic path that guarantees improvement. Climbing Jacob’s ladder usually helps, but a meta-GGA is not guaranteed to beat every GGA on every problem.
So we test. A functional is judged by how well it reproduces trusted reference values for many chemical problems. This is called benchmarking, and it is how the whole field decides which functionals to recommend (Goerigk et al. 2017; Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2017; Goerigk and Mehta 2019). In Experiments 3–5 you will do a small benchmark yourself.

title: Lecture 7 · How we test a functional
text:
2.2 Reference values
A benchmark is only as good as its reference values. There are two sources.

2.2.1 Experiment
Experimental thermochemistry (enthalpies of formation, bond energies, ionization potentials) has the advantage of being “real”. But experimental numbers cannot be compared directly with a single-point electronic energy:

experiments measure enthalpies or free energies at a finite temperature, which include zero-point vibrational energy and thermal corrections (see Lecture 13);
some experimental values have uncertainties of 1 kcal/mol or more;
many interesting quantities (a barrier height, the energy of an unstable conformer, a dimer at a fixed geometry) cannot be measured cleanly at all.

To compare with experiment you must back-correct the experimental value to an electronic energy difference, or add the corrections to the computed one. Both introduce extra uncertainty.


2.2.2 High-level theory: CCSD(T)/CBS
The alternative is to compute the reference with a method far more accurate than DFT, at the same geometries. The workhorse is CCSD(T), coupled cluster with single and double excitations and a perturbative estimate of triple excitations (Raghavachari et al. 1989). It is called the “gold standard” of quantum chemistry because, for molecules dominated by a single electron configuration, it reproduces experiment to a few tenths of a kcal/mol. Its cost scales as N⁷, so it is affordable only for small molecules.
CCSD(T) also needs a very large basis set, because the correlation energy converges slowly with the basis. The trick is to compute the energy with two or three basis sets of increasing cardinal number n (e.g., cc-pVTZ and cc-pVQZ) and extrapolate to the complete-basis-set (CBS) limit. A common form for the correlation energy is
\[
E_\text{corr}(n) = E_\text{corr}^\text{CBS} + \frac{A}{n^3},
\tag{3}\]
where A is fitted from two values of n (Helgaker et al. 1997). With two points, Equation 3 can be solved for the limit:
\[
E_\text{corr}^\text{CBS} = \frac{n^3 E_\text{corr}(n) - (n-1)^3 E_\text{corr}(n-1)}{n^3 - (n-1)^3}.
\tag{4}\]
The HF part converges much faster and is usually taken from the largest basis or extrapolated exponentially. The combination is written CCSD(T)/CBS. For the most demanding thermochemistry, composite protocols such as W4 add even higher excitations and small corrections, reaching uncertainties around 0.1–0.2 kcal/mol; the W4-17 database used for reaction 5d was built this way (Karton et al. 2017).






TipWorked example: a two-point CBS extrapolation



Suppose the CCSD(T) correlation energy of a small molecule is −0.27500 Eh with cc-pVTZ (n = 3) and −0.28500 Eh with cc-pVQZ (n = 4). These are made-up numbers for practice. Using Equation 4:
\[
E_\text{corr}^\text{CBS} = \frac{64(-0.28500) - 27(-0.27500)}{64 - 27} = \frac{-18.24000 + 7.42500}{37} = \frac{-10.81500}{37} = -0.29230\ E_\text{h}.
\]
The extrapolation adds −0.00730 Eh beyond the cc-pVQZ value, which is −0.00730 × 627.5095 = −4.58 kcal/mol. The basis-set error of the correlation energy is far from negligible even with a quadruple-ζ basis. For reaction energies much of it cancels, but not all.


The important point for you: the reference values in Experiments 3–5 come from CCSD(T)/CBS or better, computed at the same geometries you use. So the difference between your number and the reference is the error of your method (functional + basis set), with no thermal corrections or experimental uncertainty mixed in.

title: Lecture 7 · How we test a functional
text:
2.3 Benchmark databases
A single reaction says little about a functional. A benchmark database collects hundreds or thousands of reference values, grouped in subsets by chemical type. Three families of databases matter for this course.

2.3.1 GMTKN55
GMTKN55 (General Main-group Thermochemistry, Kinetics and Noncovalent interactions, 55 subsets) was published by Goerigk, Grimme and co-workers in 2017 (Goerigk et al. 2017). It contains about 1500 relative energies, organized in five categories:

basic properties and reaction energies of small systems (atomization energies, ionization potentials, proton affinities, …);
reaction energies of larger systems and isomerizations;
reaction barrier heights;
intermolecular noncovalent interactions;
intramolecular noncovalent interactions (conformers).

Reactions 3a and 3b come from its BHROT27 subset (rotational barriers), 3c from BUT14DIOL (butane-1,4-diol conformers), 3d from FH51 (reaction energies), and in Experiment 4 you will use DARC (Diels–Alder reactions) and ADIM6 (alkane dimers). The paper tested more than 200 functional/dispersion combinations, and it is one of the best places to look up how a functional performs.
Because the energies in GMTKN55 range from tenths of a kcal/mol (conformers) to hundreds (atomizations), a plain average would be dominated by the large ones. GMTKN55 therefore uses a weighted mean absolute deviation, WTMAD-2, in which the MAD of each subset i is scaled by the ratio between 56.84 kcal/mol (the average absolute reference energy over the whole database) and the average absolute reference energy of that subset, \(\overline{|\Delta E|}_i\):
\[
\text{WTMAD-2} = \frac{1}{\sum_i N_i}\sum_i N_i \,\frac{56.84\ \text{kcal/mol}}{\overline{|\Delta E|}_i}\,\text{MAD}_i .
\tag{5}\]
Take two subsets whose average reference energies are 1 kcal/mol (conformers) and 50 kcal/mol (reaction energies). An MAD of 0.5 kcal/mol in the first then weighs as much as an MAD of 25 kcal/mol in the second, because 0.5 × 56.84/1 = 25 × 56.84/50 = 28.4. A half-kcal/mol error on a 1 kcal/mol conformer energy really is as bad, chemically, as a 50% error on a larger reaction energy.


2.3.2 MGCDB84
MGCDB84 (Main-Group Chemistry DataBase, 84 subsets), assembled by Mardirossian and Head-Gordon (Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2017), contains close to 5000 data points. It grew out of the data used to develop the ωB97X-V, B97M-V and ωB97M-V functionals, and the same paper uses it to evaluate 200 functionals. Its categories distinguish “easy” from “difficult” problems: noncovalent dimers and clusters, isomerization energies, thermochemistry and barrier heights, each split into easy and difficult groups. The AlkIsomer11 and S66 subsets of Experiment 4 come from it.


2.3.3 The Minnesota databases
Truhlar’s group has built a long series of databases to develop and test the Minnesota functionals (M06, M11, MN15 and others). The latest, Minnesota Database 2015B, was used to parametrize MN15 (Yu et al. 2016; Peverati and Truhlar 2014). It includes many inorganic and transition-metal systems, and multireference cases. Reactions 5b (CaO) and 5c (H₂SO₄) come from it, and Experiment 1 came from its NCCE30 subset.


2.3.4 Training sets and test sets
Many modern functionals contain parameters fitted to a database. The data used for fitting form the training set. Data never used for fitting form the test set. A functional’s performance on its own training set is not an independent test: it is guaranteed to be good there, by construction. A fair benchmark looks at the test set, or at a database built by someone else. Keep this in mind for Lecture 9: one reaction in Experiment 5 belongs to the training set of one of your functionals.

title: Lecture 7 · How we test a functional
text:
2.4 Error statistics
You will compute these quantities in every experiment from now on. They are also defined in the units and errors guide.

2.4.1 The signed error
For one reaction k,
\[
\varepsilon_k = \Delta E_k^\text{comp} - \Delta E_k^\text{ref}.
\tag{6}\]
The sign carries meaning. If ε > 0, the computed reaction energy is more positive (less negative) than the reference. For an exothermic reaction (ΔE < 0), a positive ε means the method underestimates how favorable the reaction is. For a dissociation (ΔE > 0), a positive ε means the method overbinds. Always write down the direction of the reaction before interpreting the sign.


2.4.2 Statistics over a set of N reactions
\[
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\varepsilon_k, \qquad
\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}|\varepsilon_k|,
\tag{7}\]
\[
\text{RMSD} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\varepsilon_k^2}, \qquad
\text{MaxE} = \max_k |\varepsilon_k|.
\tag{8}\]

The mean signed error (MSE) measures systematic bias. A method with MSE ≈ 0 is not necessarily good: large positive and negative errors can cancel.
The mean absolute error (MAE, sometimes MAD or MUE) measures typical accuracy. It is the number most benchmark papers report.
The root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) weights large errors more heavily. RMSD ≥ MAE always; a RMSD much larger than the MAE warns you of outliers.
The maximum error tells you the worst case. If you design a drug or a catalyst, the worst case may matter more than the average.



2.4.3 The relative error
\[
\varepsilon_k^\text{rel} = \frac{\varepsilon_k}{|\Delta E_k^\text{ref}|}\times 100\%.
\tag{9}\]
The relative error puts reactions of very different size on the same footing. But chemistry is decided by absolute energies: an equilibrium constant depends on ΔG in kcal/mol, not on a percentage. A 1% error on an atomization energy of 600 kcal/mol is 6 kcal/mol, which changes a rate or an equilibrium by orders of magnitude. And a relative error is meaningless when the reference is close to zero. Experiment 5 has a chart for exactly this comparison.

WarningCommon mistakes with error statistics

Comparing MAEs computed over different sets of reactions.

title: Lecture 7 · How we test a functional
text:
2.5 Chemical accuracy
The traditional target for a computational method is chemical accuracy, an error of about 1 kcal/mol (4.2 kJ/mol). The number is not arbitrary. At 298 K, RT = 0.5925 kcal/mol, and an error δ in a free-energy difference changes an equilibrium constant (or a rate constant, through the barrier) by a factor exp(δ/RT):
\[
\frac{K_\text{comp}}{K_\text{true}} = e^{\delta/RT} = e^{1.000/0.5925} = e^{1.688} \approx 5.4 .
\tag{10}\]
So a 1 kcal/mol error means a factor of about 5 in K or in a rate. That is often good enough to tell which product dominates. A 3 kcal/mol error means a factor of e5.06 ≈ 160, which is often not.
For reference: on GMTKN55, the best hybrid and double-hybrid functionals reach a WTMAD-2 of a few kcal/mol, and the best functionals have MAEs well below 1 kcal/mol for easy noncovalent and conformational data, but several kcal/mol for difficult thermochemistry (Goerigk et al. 2017; Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2017). Chemical accuracy is not reached uniformly by any functional.

title: Lecture 7 · How we test a functional
section: 2.6 Why a single number never tells the whole story
text:
2.6 Why a single number never tells the whole story
Benchmark rankings are useful, but they must be read with care:

The composition of the database matters. A ranking depends on which reactions are included and how they are weighted. A functional that is excellent for organic chemistry may be mediocre for transition metals, and an overall average hides this.
Training sets. A functional fitted to a database will look good on that database (see above).
Error cancellation. A good number can come from a lucky cancellation between two errors (Experiment 1 already showed one). Lucky cancellations don’t transfer.
Outliers. A small MAE can coexist with a catastrophic failure on one system. Always look at the maximum error and at the distribution.
The reference itself. CCSD(T)/CBS is excellent for single-reference molecules, but less reliable for systems with strong static correlation (Lecture 9).

The practical advice: before using a functional for a new problem, look up its performance on the subsets most similar to your problem, not just its overall rank.

title: Lecture 7 · How we test a functional
text:
3.2 Methods and jobs
You will use the 16 methods of Table 1 with the def2-TZVP basis set. Eight molecules × 16 methods = 128 jobs. Each one is small and fast, but there are many, so submit them in batches (see working on a shared machine). For every job record the total energy, the number of SCF cycles and the wall time.

title: Lecture 7 · How we test a functional
text:
3.3 Why these reactions are “easy”
All four reactions compare two forms of the same molecule (two conformers, or a cis and a trans isomer). The atoms, the bonds and the number of electron pairs are the same on both sides. Only the arrangement in space changes. Most errors of an approximate functional are tied to specific features of the electron density: the core, the lone pairs, each type of bond. When the same features appear on both sides of the reaction, their errors largely cancel when you take products minus reactants.
This idea has a name in thermochemistry. An isodesmic reaction conserves the number and type of each bond, and a homodesmotic reaction also conserves the hybridization of the atoms. Chemists design such reactions on purpose, because they make the computed reaction energy much less sensitive to the method. Conformational changes are the extreme case: nothing changes but the geometry.
Error cancellation is not guaranteed, though. Ask yourself, for each reaction, what does change. In 3c an intramolecular hydrogen bond is broken. In 3a and 3b the barrier comes from a subtle balance of steric and hyperconjugative effects. How well does each rung describe a hydrogen bond? How does a method with no electron correlation at all (HF) do?

text:
3.5 What to watch out for

Read the reaction direction in the table: ΔE = E(product) − E(reactant). 3d is negative.
These reaction energies are small (1–3 kcal/mol). Keep every digit of the total energies.
Check that each job finished (“Thank you very much for using Q-Chem”) and that the SCF converged. Re-run any job that failed.
Lock in your predictions on the experiment page before you run anything, including the “functional draft”: the method you bet will win over Experiments 3, 4 and 5.

title: Lecture 7 · How we test a functional
text:
3.6 Key points

In Experiment 1 the basis-set error (BSIE + BSSE) of DFT shrinks quickly with ζ; what remains at quadruple-ζ is the error of the functional.
Hartree–Fock has no dispersion. Its apparent accuracy with small basis sets for (HCl)₂ comes from BSSE, an artifact that disappears as the basis grows.
Measured cost exponents are below the formal N⁴ because of integral screening, fixed overhead and the short range of N. Triple-ζ is the usual sweet spot for DFT.
The rung of a functional depends only on its ingredients. Range separation, “-V” and “-D4” are not rungs.
Functionals are judged by benchmarking against reference data, usually CCSD(T)/CBS, collected in databases such as GMTKN55, MGCDB84 and the Minnesota databases.
Signed error, MSE, MAE, RMSD, maximum error and relative error each answer a different question. Use more than one.
Chemical accuracy (1 kcal/mol) corresponds to a factor of about 5 in an equilibrium or rate constant at room temperature.
Performance on a functional’s own training set is not an independent test.

3.7 Study questions

In Experiment 1, the reaction is a dissociation. Explain in one sentence what a positive signed error means for the binding of (HCl)₂.
Why does BSSE make dimers too stable and not too unstable? Why does it shrink as the basis grows?
Explain why the HF error for (HCl)₂ can grow when going from def2-SVP to def2-QZVP. What does this tell you about judging a method by a single small-basis calculation?
A student measures time ∝ N2.3 for a hybrid functional. Give three reasons why the exponent is smaller than 4.
Classify M11-L, B97M-V, ωB97M-V and M06-HF on Jacob’s ladder, and explain the trap in each name.
Why are CCSD(T)/CBS values preferred over experimental values as references for benchmarking functionals? Give two reasons.
Using Equation 4, extrapolate correlation energies of −0.2000 Eh (n = 2) and −0.2300 Eh (n = 3). How large is the extrapolation correction, in kcal/mol?
A method has MSE = 0.0 kcal/mol and MAE = 3.0 kcal/mol on a set of reactions. Describe what its errors look like.
Show that an error of 2 kcal/mol in ΔG changes an equilibrium constant at 298 K by a factor of about 29.
Why might a functional rank first on one database and tenth on another?

title: Lecture 5 · Approximating the Hamiltonian II: density functional theory
Lecture 5 · Approximating the Hamiltonian II: density functional theory
section: 1 Why look beyond the wave function?
text:
1 Why look beyond the wave function?
The many-electron wave function \(\Psi(\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_N)\) depends on \(3N\) spatial coordinates (plus \(N\) spin coordinates). For benzene, with 42 electrons, that is a function of 126 variables. Suppose you wanted to store it on a coarse grid of only 10 points per coordinate: you would need \(10^{126}\) numbers, far more than the number of atoms in the observable universe. Walter Kohn called this growth the “exponential wall” of wave-function methods (Kohn 1999).
Correlated wave-function methods avoid storing \(\Psi\) on a grid, but they pay in a different currency: computer time. As you saw in Lecture 4, MP2 scales as \(N^5\) and CCSD(T) as \(N^7\) with system size. CCSD(T) on a molecule with 30 heavy atoms is a major undertaking, and on the 50–100 atoms of a typical catalyst or drug molecule it is out of reach for routine work.
Yet most questions in chemistry are about one simple function: where the electrons are. The electron density \(\rho(\mathbf{r})\) depends on only three coordinates, whatever the number of electrons. Density functional theory (DFT) is the theory that says this function is enough, in principle, to get the exact ground-state energy. In practice it is the method behind most of the quantum chemistry done today, and the method of almost every experiment in this course.

title: Lecture 5 · Approximating the Hamiltonian II: density functional theory
text:
2 The electron density

2.1 Definition and properties
The electron density is the probability of finding any electron at point \(\mathbf{r}\), with any spin, whatever the other electrons are doing:
\[
\rho(\mathbf{r}_1) = N \int \cdots \int \left|\Psi(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_N)\right|^2 d\omega_1\, d\mathbf{x}_2 \cdots d\mathbf{x}_N.
\tag{1}\]
We integrate \(|\Psi|^2\) over the spin of electron 1 and over all coordinates of the other \(N-1\) electrons. The factor \(N\) appears because the electrons are indistinguishable: any of them could be the one at \(\mathbf{r}_1\). Its main properties are:

It integrates to the number of electrons: \(\int \rho(\mathbf{r})\,d\mathbf{r} = N\).
It is positive everywhere and decays to zero far from the molecule. The decay is exponential, \(\rho \propto e^{-2\sqrt{2I}\,r}\), where \(I\) is the first ionization energy (in atomic units).
It has cusps at the nuclei. At each nucleus the density has a sharp peak whose slope is fixed by the nuclear charge (Kato’s cusp condition). So the density “knows” where the nuclei are and what their charges are.
It is an observable. X-ray diffraction measures the electron density of crystals, and electron-density maps are how crystallographers see molecules.
For a single determinant (Hartree–Fock or Kohn–Sham), it is simply the sum of the occupied orbital densities: \(\rho(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i}^{\mathrm{occ}}|\varphi_i(\mathbf{r})|^2\) (over spin orbitals).

For open-shell systems we also use the spin densities \(\rho_\alpha(\mathbf{r})\) and \(\rho_\beta(\mathbf{r})\), with \(\rho = \rho_\alpha + \rho_\beta\). Their difference, the spin density \(\rho_\alpha - \rho_\beta\), shows where the unpaired electrons are.


2.2 The cusp argument: a hint that the density is enough
Here is an informal argument, due to E. Bright Wilson, that the density should contain everything. From \(\rho\) you can read off \(N\) (integrate it), the positions of the nuclei (the cusps), and their charges (the slope at each cusp). But \(N\), the nuclear positions and the nuclear charges are all you need to write the electronic Hamiltonian (Lecture 1). With the Hamiltonian you can, in principle, solve for \(\Psi\) and everything else. So the ground-state density determines the ground-state wave function. The argument works only for Coulomb potentials. The general proof came in 1964.

title: Lecture 5 · Approximating the Hamiltonian II: density functional theory
text:
3 The Hohenberg–Kohn theorems
In the electronic Hamiltonian, the only part that depends on the molecule is the attraction to the nuclei. We collect it in the external potential \(v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r}) = -\sum_A Z_A/|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{R}_A|\). The kinetic energy \(\hat T\) and the electron–electron repulsion \(\hat V_{ee}\) are the same for every molecule with \(N\) electrons. In 1964 Pierre Hohenberg and Walter Kohn proved two theorems about this situation (Hohenberg and Kohn 1964).
First theorem (existence). The ground-state density determines the external potential, up to an additive constant. Since \(v_{\mathrm{ext}}\) and \(N\) fix the Hamiltonian, the density determines the Hamiltonian, and therefore the ground-state wave function, the energy, and every other ground-state property.
The proof is short. Suppose two different external potentials \(v\) and \(v'\) (with Hamiltonians \(\hat H\) and \(\hat H'\), and nondegenerate ground states \(\Psi\) and \(\Psi'\)) gave the same ground-state density \(\rho\). Use \(\Psi'\) as a trial function for \(\hat H\). By the variational principle,
\[
E_0 < \langle\Psi'|\hat H|\Psi'\rangle = \langle\Psi'|\hat H'|\Psi'\rangle + \langle\Psi'|\hat H - \hat H'|\Psi'\rangle = E_0' + \int \left[v(\mathbf{r}) - v'(\mathbf{r})\right]\rho(\mathbf{r})\,d\mathbf{r}.
\]
Swapping the roles of the two systems gives \(E_0' < E_0 + \int [v' - v]\rho\,d\mathbf{r}\). Adding the two inequalities gives \(E_0 + E_0' < E_0' + E_0\), which is impossible. So two different potentials cannot give the same ground-state density.
Second theorem (variational principle). The ground-state energy is a functional of the density,
\[
E_v[\rho] = F[\rho] + \int v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r})\,\rho(\mathbf{r})\,d\mathbf{r},
\tag{2}\]
and it is minimized by the exact ground-state density. For any trial density \(\tilde\rho\) that is positive and integrates to \(N\) (with some technical conditions), \(E_v[\tilde\rho] \ge E_0\).
A functional is a rule that takes a whole function and returns a number, just as \(E[\Psi] = \langle\Psi|\hat H|\Psi\rangle\) takes a wave function and returns an energy. We write functionals with square brackets.
The term \(F[\rho] = T[\rho] + V_{ee}[\rho]\) is the universal functional: the kinetic and electron–electron energy of the electrons. “Universal” means it is the same for every atom, molecule or solid. Only \(v_{\mathrm{ext}}\) changes from one system to another. Levy later gave a cleaner definition that removes most of the technical conditions: \(F[\rho]\) is the lowest value of \(\langle\Psi|\hat T + \hat V_{ee}|\Psi\rangle\) over all wave functions that give the density \(\rho\) (Levy 1979).






WarningWhat the theorems do not say



The Hohenberg–Kohn theorems are existence proofs. They say that \(F[\rho]\) exists, not what it is. Nobody knows the exact \(F[\rho]\), and it is very likely that nobody ever will, in a form that is cheap to evaluate. All of practical DFT is about approximating it. The theorems are about the ground state: excited states need extensions (time-dependent DFT), which we do not cover. And “DFT is exact” is true only for the exact functional. Every calculation you will run uses an approximation.

title: Lecture 5 · Approximating the Hamiltonian II: density functional theory
text:
4 A cautionary tale: Thomas–Fermi theory
The idea of using only the density is older than the theorems. In 1927, Thomas (Thomas 1927) and Fermi (Fermi 1927) wrote the energy of an atom as a functional of the density alone. They took the electrostatic terms exactly,
\[
E_{ne}[\rho] = \int v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r})\,\rho(\mathbf{r})\,d\mathbf{r}, \qquad J[\rho] = \frac{1}{2}\iint \frac{\rho(\mathbf{r})\,\rho(\mathbf{r}')}{|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|}\,d\mathbf{r}\,d\mathbf{r}',
\tag{3}\]
and approximated the kinetic energy by that of a uniform electron gas (electrons in a box with a uniform positive background) evaluated at the local density:
\[
T_{\mathrm{TF}}[\rho] = C_F \int \rho(\mathbf{r})^{5/3}\,d\mathbf{r}, \qquad C_F = \frac{3}{10}\left(3\pi^2\right)^{2/3} \approx 2.871.
\]
\(J[\rho]\) is the Hartree energy: the classical self-repulsion of the charge cloud \(\rho\). It is the same as \(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij}J_{ij}\) of Lecture 4, including the unphysical \(i = j\) terms. Dirac soon added an exchange term of the same local form (Dirac 1930), which we will meet again below.
Thomas–Fermi theory gives rough total energies of heavy atoms, but it fails for chemistry in a spectacular way: it has no shell structure (the density decreases smoothly from the nucleus, with no K, L, M shells), and Teller proved in 1962 that no molecule is bound in Thomas–Fermi theory (Teller 1962). Any molecule is always higher in energy than its separated atoms. The culprit is the kinetic energy. It is the largest energy term after the nuclear attraction, and the local formula above misses most of the subtle changes in kinetic energy that make chemical bonds. Orbital-free kinetic-energy functionals are still an active research topic, but they are not accurate enough for chemistry.
The lesson for what follows: do not approximate the kinetic energy with a simple density functional.

title: Lecture 5 · Approximating the Hamiltonian II: density functional theory
text:
5 The Kohn–Sham scheme

5.1 A fictitious system with the real density
In 1965, Kohn and Lu Jeu Sham found a way around the kinetic-energy problem (Kohn and Sham 1965). The idea is to bring orbitals back, but only as a tool.
Imagine a fictitious system of \(N\) non-interacting electrons moving in some effective local potential \(v_s(\mathbf{r})\), chosen so that the density of this fictitious system is exactly equal to the density of the real, interacting molecule (Figure 1). A system of non-interacting electrons is easy: its exact wave function is a single Slater determinant of orbitals \(\varphi_i\), each obeying a one-electron Schrödinger equation. And its kinetic energy can be computed exactly from the orbitals:
\[
T_s[\rho] = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\left\langle\varphi_i\left|-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^2\right|\varphi_i\right\rangle.
\tag{4}\]
\(T_s\) is not the true kinetic energy \(T\) of the interacting electrons, but it is close: typically it accounts for all but about 1% of it. It also contains the shell structure that Thomas–Fermi theory misses, because it is computed from orbitals.






Figure 1: The Kohn–Sham idea. The real, interacting molecule and a fictitious system of non-interacting electrons are linked by one requirement: they have the same electron density. The fictitious system is easy to solve (one Slater determinant). Everything it gets wrong compared with the real system is put into the exchange–correlation energy.





5.2 The Kohn–Sham energy decomposition
Kohn and Sham then rewrote the exact energy functional (Equation 2) by separating out the pieces we know how to compute:
\[
E[\rho] = T_s[\rho] + \int v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r})\,\rho(\mathbf{r})\,d\mathbf{r} + J[\rho] + E_{xc}[\rho].
\tag{5}\]
The four terms are:



Table 1: The Kohn–Sham energy decomposition. Only the last term must be approximated.











Term
Name
What it is
Known exactly?




\(T_s[\rho]\)
non-interacting kinetic energy
Equation 4, from the KS orbitals
yes


\(E_{ne}[\rho] = \int v_{\mathrm{ext}}\rho\)
electron–nuclear attraction
classical attraction of \(\rho\) to the nuclei
yes


\(J[\rho]\)
Hartree (Coulomb) energy
classical self-repulsion of \(\rho\) (Equation 3)
yes


\(E_{xc}[\rho]\)
exchange–correlation energy
everything else
no






The exchange–correlation energy is defined as whatever is needed to make Equation 5 exact. Comparing with \(F[\rho] = T[\rho] + V_{ee}[\rho]\):
\[
E_{xc}[\rho] = \Big(T[\rho] - T_s[\rho]\Big) + \Big(V_{ee}[\rho] - J[\rho]\Big).
\tag{6}\]
So \(E_{xc}\) collects three things:

Exchange: the Pauli-principle correction to the classical repulsion (the \(-K\) terms of Hartree–Fock), including the cancellation of the self-interaction contained in \(J[\rho]\).
Correlation: the extra lowering of the repulsion because electrons avoid each other dynamically.
The kinetic correlation energy \(T - T_s\): the difference between the true kinetic energy of interacting electrons and that of the non-interacting reference.

It is customary to split \(E_{xc} = E_x + E_c\). The exchange part is defined as the Hartree–Fock-like exchange energy evaluated with the Kohn–Sham orbitals; everything else is correlation. Exchange is by far the larger piece. For the helium atom, \(E_x \approx -1.03\) Eh and \(E_c \approx -0.042\) Eh. For the hydrogen atom, with a single electron, \(E_x = -J = -0.3125\) Eh and \(E_c = 0\) exactly. Although it is a modest fraction of the total energy (about 10% for the neon atom, and less for heavier atoms), \(E_{xc}\) is the “glue” that holds molecules together. Without it, as in Hartree’s original method, chemical bonding is very poorly described.


5.3 The Kohn–Sham equations
Minimizing Equation 5 with respect to the orbitals, under the constraint that they stay orthonormal, gives the Kohn–Sham equations:
\[
\left[-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^2 + v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r}) + v_J(\mathbf{r}) + v_{xc}(\mathbf{r})\right]\varphi_i(\mathbf{r}) = \varepsilon_i\,\varphi_i(\mathbf{r}).
\tag{7}\]
The operator in brackets is the Kohn–Sham operator. Its potential \(v_s = v_{\mathrm{ext}} + v_J + v_{xc}\) has three parts:

\(v_{\mathrm{ext}}\), the attraction to the nuclei;
the Hartree potential \(v_J(\mathbf{r}) = \int \rho(\mathbf{r}')/|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|\,d\mathbf{r}'\), the electrostatic potential of the whole electron cloud (the same as \(\sum_j \hat J_j\) in Hartree–Fock);
the exchange–correlation potential \(v_{xc}(\mathbf{r}) = \delta E_{xc}/\delta\rho(\mathbf{r})\), the functional derivative of \(E_{xc}\). For the approximations of this chapter, it is simply a function of \(\mathbf{r}\) computed from the density at (and near) that point.







NoteWhat is a functional derivative?



For an ordinary function \(f(x)\), the derivative tells you how much \(f\) changes when you change \(x\) a little. For a functional \(E[\rho]\), the functional derivative \(\delta E/\delta\rho(\mathbf{r})\) tells you how much \(E\) changes when you add a tiny bit of density at the point \(\mathbf{r}\). It is therefore itself a function of \(\mathbf{r}\): a potential. For a functional of the simple local form \(E[\rho] = \int g(\rho(\mathbf{r}))\,d\mathbf{r}\), the functional derivative is just the ordinary derivative of the integrand, \(\delta E/\delta\rho(\mathbf{r}) = g'(\rho(\mathbf{r}))\). For example, the LDA exchange energy introduced below, \(E_x = -C_x\int\rho^{4/3}\,d\mathbf{r}\), gives the exchange potential \(v_x(\mathbf{r}) = -\tfrac{4}{3}C_x\,\rho(\mathbf{r})^{1/3}\). The Hartree energy \(J[\rho]\) gives the Hartree potential \(v_J\) in the same way. This is how every term of the energy produces a term of the Kohn–Sham potential.


Compare Equation 7 with the Hartree–Fock equations of Lecture 4:



Table 2: Hartree–Fock and Kohn–Sham side by side.











Hartree–Fock
Kohn–Sham DFT

SCF loop

The two methods share almost all of their machinery. Kohn–Sham DFT expands the orbitals in the same basis sets, builds a Fock-like matrix, and solves the same generalized eigenvalue problem by the same SCF loop, with the same DIIS acceleration. That is why the SCF table of a DFT job in Q-Chem looks exactly like that of an HF job: cycle number, energy, DIIS error, and “Convergence criterion met” at the end. Everything you learned about convergence in Lecture 4 applies unchanged.






WarningCommon mistake: adding up orbital energies



As in Hartree–Fock, the Kohn–Sham total energy is not the sum of the occupied orbital energies. Each \(\varepsilon_i\) contains the full Hartree potential and the full exchange–correlation potential felt by electron \(i\). Summing them counts the electron–electron repulsion twice, and it uses \(\int v_{xc}\rho\) in place of \(E_{xc}\), which are different numbers. Programs therefore compute the energy from Equation 5 directly, with the density of the last SCF cycle. The number to use in your reaction energies is always the total energy printed at the end of the SCF (“Total energy in the final basis set”, see the guide on reading the output).








ImportantThe one sentence to remember



Kohn–Sham DFT is exact in principle: with the exact exchange–correlation functional, it would give the exact ground-state energy and density with the cost of a mean-field calculation. All the difficulty, and all the variety among the hundreds of functionals you will meet, is in approximating \(E_{xc}[\rho]\).








NoteWhat do the Kohn–Sham orbitals mean?



Strictly speaking, the KS orbitals and their energies belong to the fictitious non-interacting system. Only the density, and the total energy, are guaranteed to be physical. In practice, KS orbitals look very similar to Hartree–Fock orbitals, and chemists use them in the same way (MO diagrams, HOMO–LUMO pictures in IQmol). For the exact functional, \(-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HOMO}}\) equals the first ionization energy exactly. With the approximate functionals of this chapter and the next, \(-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HOMO}}\) is usually several eV smaller than the ionization energy, so Koopmans-style estimates work worse in DFT than in HF. The reason is the self-interaction error discussed in Section 8.

title: Lecture 5 · Approximating the Hamiltonian II: density functional theory
section: 6 The first approximation: the local spin-density approximation
text:
6 The first approximation: the local spin-density approximation

6.1 The uniform electron gas
To use Kohn–Sham DFT we need an approximate \(E_{xc}[\rho]\). The first and simplest approximation, already proposed by Kohn and Sham in 1965, uses the one system for which the exchange–correlation energy is accurately known: the uniform electron gas (also called jellium). It is an infinite system of electrons with constant density \(\rho\), neutralized by a uniform positive background. Its exchange–correlation energy per electron, \(\varepsilon_{xc}^{\mathrm{unif}}(\rho)\), depends only on the value of \(\rho\).
The local density approximation (LDA) treats every small volume element of a molecule as if it were a piece of uniform gas with the local density \(\rho(\mathbf{r})\), and adds up the contributions:
\[
E_{xc}^{\mathrm{LDA}}[\rho] = \int \rho(\mathbf{r})\,\varepsilon_{xc}^{\mathrm{unif}}\big(\rho(\mathbf{r})\big)\,d\mathbf{r}.
\tag{8}\]
For molecules we always use the spin-resolved version, the local spin-density approximation (LSDA), in which \(\varepsilon_{xc}^{\mathrm{unif}}\) depends on both spin densities \(\rho_\alpha\) and \(\rho_\beta\). LSDA is the first rung of Jacob’s ladder (Lecture 6).


6.2 LSDA exchange
For the uniform gas, the exchange energy can be computed analytically from plane-wave orbitals (Dirac, 1930 (Dirac 1930)). The result is
\[
E_x^{\mathrm{LDA}}[\rho] = -C_x\int\rho(\mathbf{r})^{4/3}\,d\mathbf{r}, \qquad C_x = \frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{3}{\pi}\right)^{1/3} \approx 0.7386.
\tag{9}\]
In spin-polarized form, exchange acts only between same-spin electrons, and each spin contributes separately:
\[
E_x^{\mathrm{LSDA}}[\rho_\alpha,\rho_\beta] = -\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{3}{4\pi}\right)^{1/3}\sum_{\sigma=\alpha,\beta}\int\rho_\sigma(\mathbf{r})^{4/3}\,d\mathbf{r}.
\tag{10}\]
For a closed shell (\(\rho_\alpha = \rho_\beta = \rho/2\)), Equation 10 reduces to Equation 9. Notice the power \(4/3\). You can check it by dimensional analysis: an energy in atomic units has dimension 1/length, a density 1/length³, and \(\rho^{4/3}\,d\mathbf{r}\) has dimension \((1/\text{length})^4 \times \text{length}^3 = 1/\text{length}\).
In 1951 Slater arrived at the same \(\rho^{4/3}\) form independently, by approximating the Hartree–Fock exchange potential (Slater 1951). His constant was \(3/2\) times larger. Programs later introduced the \(X\alpha\) method, with an adjustable prefactor \(\alpha\): Slater’s value is \(\alpha = 1\), and the uniform-gas (Kohn–Sham) value is \(\alpha = 2/3\). Today, “Slater exchange” in a functional name (the “S” in SVWN or SPW92) means Equation 10 with the uniform-gas constant.


6.3 LSDA correlation
The correlation energy of the uniform gas has no closed form. It is known analytically only in the limits of very high and very low density. In 1980, Ceperley and Alder computed it accurately at intermediate densities with quantum Monte Carlo simulations (Ceperley and Alder 1980). Others then fitted analytic formulas that reproduce the Monte Carlo numbers and the known limits, as functions of the Wigner–Seitz radius \(r_s = (3/4\pi\rho)^{1/3}\) (the radius of a sphere that contains, on average, one electron) and of the spin polarization \(\zeta = (\rho_\alpha - \rho_\beta)/\rho\). The two parametrizations you will see are:

VWN (Vosko, Wilk and Nusair, 1980) (Vosko et al. 1980), which comes in several variants (the paper gives more than one fit). Different programs use different VWN variants inside the same named functional, which is one reason why “the same” functional can give slightly different energies in different codes.
PW92 (Perdew and Wang, 1992) (Perdew and Wang 1992), a later and more careful fit.

In this course, LSDA means SPW92: Slater exchange plus PW92 correlation. Its close relative SVWN5 (Slater plus VWN correlation, form V) gives very similar results. Both are “pure” LSDA: they use nothing but the local spin densities.






NoteWorked example: LSDA for the hydrogen atom



The hydrogen atom is a good test because we know the exact answer. Its exact density is \(\rho(r) = e^{-2r}/\pi\), fully spin polarized (\(\rho_\alpha = \rho\), \(\rho_\beta = 0\)). The exact energy terms are \(T = 0.5\), \(E_{ne} = -1\) Eh and, since there is only one electron, \(V_{ee} = 0\). In Kohn–Sham language, \(J[\rho] = 5/16 = 0.3125\) Eh, so the exact \(E_{xc}\) must be \(-0.3125\) Eh: \(E_x = -0.3125\) Eh cancels the self-repulsion exactly, and \(E_c = 0\).
Evaluate the LSDA terms with the exact density (computed with the script in images/src/l04_l06_figures.py):




Exact

LSDA exchange recovers only 86% of the exchange energy needed to cancel the self-repulsion, and LSDA correlation adds a spurious correlation energy to a system with one electron. The net result is an electron that repels itself by 0.022 Eh (14 kcal/mol). This is the self-interaction error in its simplest form. In Hartree–Fock this error is exactly zero (Lecture 4).




6.4 What LSDA gets right, and what it gets wrong
It is surprising that a model built on a uniform gas works at all for molecules, where the density varies by orders of magnitude between the nuclei and the tails. It works better than it should, for a deep reason: the exchange–correlation hole of the uniform gas obeys the same exact sum rules as the true hole (it contains exactly one electron, removed from around each electron), and the energy depends only on a spherical average of the hole. Errors in exchange and in correlation also partly cancel.
What LSDA does well:

Geometries: bond lengths are usually within a few hundredths of an ångström (often slightly too short), and bond angles are good.
Vibrational frequencies of reasonable quality, and good properties of simple metals and many solids, which is why LSDA was the workhorse of solid-state physics for decades.

What LSDA does badly:

Overbinding. Atomization energies are much too large, typically by tens of kcal/mol for small molecules, and the error grows with molecular size. Bond energies, hydrogen bonds and weak complexes are all too strong.
Barrier heights are too low, often far too low.
Ionization energies from orbital energies are much too small, and anions are often not bound.

These errors are the reason LSDA was never popular in chemistry. Chemists started to use DFT only after the gradient corrections of the late 1980s and the hybrids of 1993 (the subject of Lecture 6). In Experiment 3 you will compute SPW92 alongside fifteen other methods and see where it stands.

title: Lecture 5 · Approximating the Hamiltonian II: density functional theory
section: 7 How a DFT program evaluates \(E_{xc}\): the integration grid
text:
7 How a DFT program evaluates \(E_{xc}\): the integration grid
In Hartree–Fock, every integral in the energy is a product of Gaussian basis functions that can be done analytically. In DFT, the terms \(T_s\), \(E_{ne}\) and \(J\) are computed in the same way. But \(E_{xc}\) is not. Integrals like \(\int\rho^{4/3}\,d\mathbf{r}\), and the more complicated ones of the next chapter, have no analytic solution for a density built from Gaussians. Programs compute them numerically, as a weighted sum over a grid of points placed around each atom:
\[
E_{xc} \approx \sum_{k} w_k\, \rho(\mathbf{r}_k)\,\varepsilon_{xc}\big(\rho(\mathbf{r}_k), \ldots\big).
\]
The grid is an extra approximation that Hartree–Fock does not have. A grid that is too coarse gives energies with numerical noise, which can be larger than you expect. You will meet grids in detail in Lecture 11 and test them in Experiment 7. For now, remember that the grid is the second reason, after the choice of \(E_{xc}\), why two DFT calculations with “the same” functional and basis can disagree.
One more preview. Nothing forces \(E_{xc}\) to be a pure density functional. Hybrid functionals replace part of the approximate exchange by exact (Hartree–Fock) exchange, computed from the Kohn–Sham orbitals with the \(\hat K\) operator of Lecture 4. This partly cures the self-interaction error. Hybrids are the fourth rung of Jacob’s ladder, in Lecture 6.

title: Lecture 5 · Approximating the Hamiltonian II: density functional theory
text:
8 Known errors of approximate functionals
Every functional you will use in this course is an approximation, and approximations fail in characteristic ways. Three of them are worth knowing by name from the start. Each returns in later classes, with experiments designed to expose it.
1. Self-interaction and delocalization error. In approximate functionals, the approximate \(E_x\) does not exactly cancel the self-repulsion contained in \(J[\rho]\) (as in the hydrogen atom above). Perdew and Zunger made this precise in 1981 and proposed a correction (Perdew and Zunger 1981). Because an electron that repels itself prefers to be spread out, approximate functionals systematically over-stabilize delocalized charge. This is called delocalization error (Cohen et al. 2012). Its symptoms are striking. In stretched H₂⁺, a one-electron system, LSDA and GGAs predict an energy far too low, with the electron shared between two distant protons. Reaction barriers come out too low, because transition states have stretched, delocalized bonds. Charge-transfer complexes are overbound, and orbital energies are too high. Mixing in Hartree–Fock exchange, which has no self-interaction, reduces this error (Lecture 6). It returns in Lecture 9.
2. Missing long-range dispersion. LSDA depends only on the density at each point. GGAs and meta-GGAs (Lecture 6) also look at its derivatives at that point, but still only locally. Dispersion, however, is a correlation between density fluctuations at two points that can be far apart, on two molecules whose densities do not overlap. A local or semilocal functional cannot see it: as two argon atoms are pulled apart, the energy of any such functional approaches the separated-atom value too quickly. The functional may give some spurious binding where the densities overlap (LSDA often does), but for the wrong reason. Dispersion must be added, by an empirical correction like -D4 (Caldeweyher et al. 2017, 2019) or by a nonlocal correlation functional (VV10) (Vydrov and Van Voorhis 2010). This is the subject of Lecture 8 and Experiment 4.
3. Static correlation. The Kohn–Sham reference is a single determinant. When the true wave function needs two or more determinants with similar weights (stretched bonds, diradicals, ozone, many transition-metal compounds), approximate functionals struggle. In principle the exact \(E_{xc}\) would handle it. In practice, approximate functionals do it badly or not at all, and often the unrestricted calculation breaks spin symmetry, just as UHF does for stretched H₂ (Lecture 4). Static correlation and self-interaction are related, and they pull in opposite directions: adding Hartree–Fock exchange reduces self-interaction error but makes static-correlation problems worse. This tension is one reason why no single functional is best for everything. It returns in Lecture 9 and Lecture 12.






WarningCommon mistake: “DFT includes correlation, so it is always better than HF”



Approximate DFT includes approximate exchange and correlation. For most chemistry it is far better than HF. But it can also be worse, and in ways that HF is not: HF has no self-interaction error, so for some properties dominated by that error (for example, the dissociation of one-electron bonds) HF is qualitatively right and LSDA or GGA functionals are qualitatively wrong. Always ask which errors your problem is sensitive to.

title: Lecture 5 · Approximating the Hamiltonian II: density functional theory
text:
Key points

The electron density \(\rho(\mathbf{r})\) depends on 3 coordinates, while the wave function depends on \(3N\). It integrates to \(N\), has cusps at the nuclei, and is measurable.
Hohenberg–Kohn (1964): the ground-state density determines the external potential and therefore everything; the energy is a functional of the density, minimized by the true density. The theorems prove existence but do not give the functional.
Thomas–Fermi theory approximates the kinetic energy as a local density functional and binds no molecules. Lesson: don’t approximate \(T\) that way.
Kohn–Sham (1965): a fictitious non-interacting system with the same density. Its kinetic energy \(T_s\) is computed exactly from orbitals. \(E[\rho] = T_s + E_{ne} + J + E_{xc}\).
\(E_{xc}\) contains exchange, correlation, and the kinetic correction \(T - T_s\). It is the only unknown term, and KS-DFT would be exact with the exact \(E_{xc}\).
The KS equations look like the HF equations, with the exchange operator replaced by a local potential \(v_{xc}\). They are solved by the same SCF machinery, and the output looks the same.
LSDA takes \(E_{xc}\) from the uniform electron gas: exchange \(\propto\rho^{4/3}\) (Dirac/Slater), correlation from quantum Monte Carlo data fitted by VWN or PW92. SPW92 is the LSDA of this course.
LSDA gives good geometries but overbinds: atomization energies far too large, barriers too low.
\(E_{xc}\) is evaluated numerically on a grid (Lecture 11).
Three error types to remember: self-interaction/delocalization error, missing dispersion, and static correlation.

title: Lecture 5 · Approximating the Hamiltonian II: density functional theory
text:
Study questions

How many spatial coordinates does the wave function of a water molecule depend on? And its electron density? Why does this matter for the cost of a calculation?
State the first Hohenberg–Kohn theorem in your own words. Then reproduce the proof by contradiction for a nondegenerate ground state.
What is a functional? Give two examples from this chapter or from Lecture 4, and say what each takes as input and what it returns.
Thomas–Fermi theory and Kohn–Sham DFT both write the energy as a functional of the density. What is the key difference that makes Kohn–Sham useful for chemistry while Thomas–Fermi binds no molecules?
Write the Kohn–Sham energy decomposition, name each term, and say which terms are computed exactly. List the three physical effects collected in \(E_{xc}\).
Compare the Hartree–Fock and Kohn–Sham one-electron operators term by term. Which term is nonlocal in HF and local in LSDA?
Show that Equation 10 reduces to Equation 9 for a closed-shell density. Then use dimensional analysis to explain why exchange in the LDA must scale as \(\rho^{4/3}\).
For the hydrogen atom, the exact exchange–correlation energy must equal \(-J[\rho]\). Explain why, and use the worked-example numbers to compute the self-interaction error of LSDA in kcal/mol.
A DFT calculation and an HF calculation on the same molecule with the same basis set both print an SCF table. Name two numerical approximations that are present in the DFT job but absent from the HF job.
Name the three main error types of approximate functionals. For each, give one chemical situation where you would expect it to matter.

title: Lecture 5 · Approximating the Hamiltonian II: density functional theory
text:
Further reading

Koch and Holthausen (2001), chapters 3–6: the standard introduction to DFT for chemists, from Hohenberg–Kohn to the LSDA and beyond. Written for exactly the audience of this course.
Kohn (1999): Walter Kohn’s Nobel lecture, an elegant and readable account of why the density is enough.
Burke (2012): a short perspective on what DFT is, what it is not, and where approximations come from.
Parr and Yang (1989): the classic, more mathematical textbook.
Cohen et al. (2012): a review of the main errors of approximate functionals (self-interaction, delocalization, static correlation), for after Lecture 9.
Peverati and Truhlar (2014) and Mardirossian and Head-Gordon (2017): reviews of modern functionals, useful for Experiment 2.

Lecture 2 opened the second one. A pair of choices, written method/basis, is a model chemistry:

Two more choices complete the definition of a calculation, and you must also report them: the geometry (here always given to you, as an .xyz file) and the electronic state, set by the total charge and the spin multiplicity. title: Lecture 3 · From theory to a calculation: IQmol, Q-Chem and Experiment 1
text:
2 The tools
The workflow of every experiment is the same (Figure 1).






Figure 1: The workflow of every job in this lab. You prepare the geometry and input on your computer, Q-Chem runs on a remote server, and you extract four numbers from the output to compute reaction energies and their errors.




2.1 Q-Chem and IQmol
Q-Chem (Epifanovsky et al. 2021) is the quantum-chemistry program that actually solves the equations. It reads a plain-text input file and writes a plain-text output file. You will not install it: it runs on a remote server.
IQmol (Gilbert, n.d.) is the free graphical program you install on your laptop (Guide 1). It does four jobs for you:

Builder and viewer. It opens .xyz files (File → Open) and shows the molecule in 3D. You can also build molecules, though in this lab all geometries are provided.
Q-Chem setup window. Calculation → Q-Chem Setup opens a window where you choose the job type, method, basis, charge and multiplicity, and which shows the text of the input file it will send. You can also paste a ready-made input there.
Submission to a server. In the Server menu of the setup window you select the free Q-Chem server and click Submit.
Job Monitor. It shows each job as queued → running → finished and lets you open or save the output when the job is done.







ImportantThe free server and its 10-minute limit



The free Q-Chem server is shared by many users (Guide 4). Each job is stopped after 10 minutes of run time, and a killed job gives no energy. All jobs in Experiment 1 are small and well within the limit. If a job is killed, suspect a typo in the input first, for example a much larger basis than intended. Start early: queues are longest right before deadlines.




2.2 Anatomy of a Q-Chem input
A Q-Chem input is a set of sections, each starting with $name and ending with $end. For a single-point energy you need two. Here is the test job of Guide 2, with the geometry of the HCl molecule from Experiment 1:
$molecule
0 1
Cl     0.00000000     0.00000000     0.00000000
H      0.00000000     0.00000000     1.27907000
$end

$rem
   JOBTYPE              SP
   METHOD               HF
   BASIS                def2-SVP
   SCF_CONVERGENCE      8
$end
$molecule describes the system:

the first line holds the total charge and the spin multiplicity \(2S+1\), here 0 1 (neutral singlet);
each following line holds an element symbol and its \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) coordinates in ångström (Q-Chem converts to bohr internally).

$rem holds the instructions, one keyword and one value per line:



Table 2: The four $rem keywords used in Experiment 1.










Keyword
Value here
Meaning




JOBTYPE
SP
single-point energy at the given geometry (no optimization, no frequencies)


METHOD
HF
the method: HF, or a functional name such as B3LYP, PBE, wB97M-V


BASIS
def2-SVP
the basis set


SCF_CONVERGENCE
8
a tight convergence threshold for the SCF iterations, \(10^{-8}\) (Lecture 4 explains what is converged)






A model chemistry maps directly onto two lines: method/basis becomes METHOD and BASIS. To run the same molecule with B3LYP/def2-TZVP, you change only those two values. Everything else stays.






NoteCharge and multiplicity: line 2 of every .xyz file



Standard .xyz files use their second line as a free comment. In this lab, line 2 always holds charge multiplicity, so you never have to guess. Copy it into the first line of $molecule. Recall from Lecture 1: 1 = singlet (all electrons paired, like HCl), 2 = doublet (one unpaired electron, like an H atom or a radical), 3 = triplet (two parallel unpaired electrons, like ground-state O₂). All the species of Experiment 1 are closed-shell singlets. A wrong multiplicity gives a perfectly converged energy for the wrong electronic state.




2.3 The experiment pages do the typing for you
You will run hundreds of jobs this semester. Typing inputs by hand is slow and error-prone, so each experiment page has a Run the calculations section that generates them from the experiment’s data:

a job checklist with one entry per job, named systematically (for example ex01_hf_def2-svp_hcl), with a rough cost flag (quick, a few minutes, may hit the 10-min limit);
a Copy input button for each job, to paste into IQmol’s input editor, replacing what is there;
an All inputs (.zip) button to download every input at once;
the molecule gallery, with the 3D structures and a button to download all geometries.

The checklist ticks itself off as you enter results, so you can see at a glance what is missing. Use the generated inputs: they are already consistent with the reference calculations, and they avoid typos.

3 A first job, step by step
In class we run the test job of Guide 2 live: HCl with HF/def2-SVP. Repeat it on your own before starting Experiment 1. The steps are:

Download the HCl geometry from the molecule gallery of Experiment 1 and open it in IQmol (File → Open).
Open Calculation → Q-Chem Setup. Either fill in the fields (Energy, HF, def2-SVP, charge 0, multiplicity 1), or paste the input from the experiment page.
Choose the free server in the Server menu, give the job a systematic name, and click Submit.
Follow the job in the Job Monitor. When it has finished, open the output file and save it in a folder for Experiment 1.
Find the total energy (next section). It should be close to −460 \(E_\text{h}\). If it is, everything works.

Then try the most important experiment of the semester in miniature: change only BASIS (for example to def2-TZVP), submit again, and compare. The total energy changes, and so do the number of basis functions and the time. Everything in Experiment 1 is a systematic version of this one change. Do not draw conclusions from a single molecule, though: what matters is how the reaction energy changes, and that needs both species of the reaction computed at the same level.






TipGood habits from day one




Run one job first, check its output, then submit the rest in batches.
Keep every output file, one folder per experiment, with systematic names.
Never resubmit a failed job blindly: read the end of its output first.

An output file is long, but you need only a few lines. Search for the phrases below with your editor’s find function (Guide 3 has a fully annotated example):

What each number means:

Number of basis functions. \(K\) of Lecture 2. Check it against what you expect from the shell compositions; it confirms that the right basis was used. It is also the \(N\) in the cost scaling you will measure.
SCF cycles. Hartree–Fock and Kohn–Sham DFT are solved iteratively (Lecture 4). The table of cycles shows the energy settling down; the line ending in Convergence criterion met is the last one. If instead you see a message that the SCF failed to converge, the energy is meaningless.
Total energy. Electronic energy plus nuclear repulsion at the fixed input geometry, in hartree (Lecture 1): no zero-point energy, no thermal corrections. If the output also prints an “SCF energy”, always use the total energy: with extra terms such as a dispersion correction (-D4), the two can differ.
Wall time vs CPU time. Wall time is what a stopwatch on the wall would measure. CPU time adds up the time of every processor core, so on a multi-core server it is larger. We always compare wall times, and only between jobs run on the same server. Timings are noisy: a busy server or a slow disk adds seconds that have nothing to do with the chemistry.
“Thank you very much for using Q-Chem. Have a nice day.” The last line of a finished job. If it is missing, the job crashed or was killed, and nothing in the file should be trusted.







ImportantFive checks before you trust a number




The job finished (the “Thank you” line is there).
The SCF converged (Convergence criterion met).
The charge and multiplicity echoed near the top are right.
The method and basis echoed in $rem are the ones you intended.
The number of basis functions is what you expect for that basis.

title: Lecture 3 · From theory to a calculation: IQmol, Q-Chem and Experiment 1
section: 5 From total energies to a reaction energy
text:
5 From total energies to a reaction energy

5.1 Signed stoichiometric coefficients
For any reaction, the reaction energy is a single sum over all the species \(i\) that take part:
\[
\Delta E = \sum_i \nu_i E_i ,
\tag{1}\]
where \(E_i\) is the total energy of species \(i\) and \(\nu_i\) is its signed stoichiometric coefficient: \(\nu_i > 0\) for products and \(\nu_i < 0\) for reactants. The minus sign of “products minus reactants” is already inside the coefficients, so you never subtract separately. This is the convention of the whole course, and the results forms check your \(\Delta E\) with exactly this sum (Guide 5).
For Experiment 1, the reaction is the dissociation of the HCl dimer:
\[
(\mathrm{HCl})_2 \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{HCl}, \qquad \nu_\text{dimer} = -1,\quad \nu_\text{HCl} = +2,
\]
\[
\Delta E = (+2)\,E(\mathrm{HCl}) + (-1)\,E\big((\mathrm{HCl})_2\big) .
\tag{2}\]
A positive \(\Delta E\) means the dimer is lower in energy than the separated molecules: energy must be supplied to pull them apart.
Total energies come in hartree. Convert the reaction energy to kcal/mol at the end, with
\[
1\ E_\text{h} = 627.5095\ \text{kcal/mol}.
\]


5.2 Keep all the digits
A reaction energy is a small difference between large numbers. In Experiment 1 the total energies are hundreds of hartree and the reference reaction energy is 2.01 kcal/mol, which is only 0.0032 \(E_\text{h}\). Rounding each total energy to 4 decimals can introduce errors of almost 0.1 kcal/mol (Lecture 1). Copy every digit Q-Chem prints, and round only the final reaction energy, to two decimals in kcal/mol.


5.3 Signed and absolute errors
To judge a method, compare the computed reaction energy with a reliable reference value (for the reactions in this lab, high-level wave-function results from benchmark databases):
\[
\varepsilon = \Delta E_\text{comp} - \Delta E_\text{ref} .
\tag{3}\]
The signed error \(\varepsilon\) tells you the direction: positive means the method overestimates the reaction energy. The absolute error \(|\varepsilon|\) tells you how far off it is, regardless of direction. Over several reactions, the mean signed error (MSE) reveals systematic bias and the mean absolute error (MAE) measures overall accuracy; Lecture 7 returns to these statistics. An error of about 1 kcal/mol is traditionally called chemical accuracy.






TipWorked example: a reaction energy and its error



Consider the water dimer, \((\mathrm{H_2O})_2 \to 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}\), with hypothetical total energies \(E(\mathrm{H_2O}) = -76.4203184\ E_\text{h}\) and \(E\big((\mathrm{H_2O})_2\big) = -152.8487052\ E_\text{h}\), and a reference of 5.00 kcal/mol.

Coefficients: \(\nu(\mathrm{H_2O}) = +2\), \(\nu(\text{dimer}) = -1\).
Sum: \(\Delta E = 2(-76.4203184) + (-1)(-152.8487052) = -152.8406368 + 152.8487052 = 0.0080684\ E_\text{h}\).
Convert: \(0.0080684 \times 627.5095 = 5.06\) kcal/mol.
Error: \(\varepsilon = 5.06 - 5.00 = +0.06\) kcal/mol (slight overestimate); \(|\varepsilon| = 0.06\) kcal/mol.

Now repeat step 2 with the total energies rounded to 3 decimals, \(-76.420\) and \(-152.849\): \(\Delta E = -152.840 + 152.849 = 0.009\ E_\text{h} = 5.65\) kcal/mol. The rounding alone created an error ten times larger than the method’s.








ImportantCommon mistakes with reaction energies




Forgetting a coefficient. The dimer dissociates into two monomers: \(E(\mathrm{HCl})\) must be multiplied by 2.
Sign flip. Writing reactants minus products gives the right magnitude and the wrong sign. With signed \(\nu\) this cannot happen.
Mixing levels of theory. Every species in one reaction energy must be computed with the same method and basis. Combining a def2-SVP dimer with a def2-TZVP monomer gives a meaningless number.
Forgetting the conversion, or dividing instead of multiplying by 627.5095.

title: Lecture 3 · From theory to a calculation: IQmol, Q-Chem and Experiment 1
text:
6 Experiment 1 briefing
Everything above comes together in Experiment 1: Basis Set Incompleteness Error. Read the experiment page in full before you start; this section explains what you will do and why it matters.






Figure 2: The reaction of Experiment 1: dissociation of the HCl dimer into two HCl molecules.




6.1 The question
Lecture 2 claimed that larger basis sets give results that converge toward the CBS limit, at a steeply growing cost. Experiment 1 tests that claim on a real reaction energy, for four different methods, with two families of basis sets. The reaction is the dissociation of the HCl dimer, a weakly bound complex held together by noncovalent interactions, from the NCCE30 subset (Peverati and Truhlar 2014) of the Minnesota 2015B database (Yu et al. 2016). Its reference energy is 2.01 kcal/mol. Weakly bound complexes are a demanding test for basis sets: the interaction energy is small, so even small basis-set errors are large in relative terms.


6.2 What you will run



Table 4: The Experiment 1 design. Each method/basis pair gives one reaction energy, so you obtain 24 reaction energies.











Choices

(HCl)₂ and HCl, both neutral singlets (0 1)
