All jobs are single points (JOBTYPE SP) with SCF_CONVERGENCE 8, and all are short. The two basis-set families are matched by ζ: double (SVP, DZ), triple (TZVP, TZ) and quadruple (QZVP, QZ). The methods span the range from no electron correlation at all (HF) to a modern, heavily parametrized functional (ωB97M-V); Lectures 4–6 explain what each one is.
For each job, record from the output the total energy, the number of SCF cycles, the wall time and the number of basis functions. Then compute each reaction energy yourself with Equation 2, convert it to kcal/mol, and enter it. The results form recomputes \(\Delta E\) from the total energies you entered and flags inconsistencies (a sign, a missing factor of 2, a unit slip). It never shows you the correct value.


6.3 What you will look at
Once your table is complete, the page draws two charts from your own data:

Error vs ζ. The signed error of each method as the basis grows from double- to quadruple-ζ, for each family. This is BSIE made visible: does the error shrink steadily, for every method? Do the two families behave the same way at the same ζ?
Cost scaling. Wall time against the number of basis functions on log–log axes, with a straight-line fit for each method. The slope is the exponent \(n\) in time \(\propto K^n\). Lecture 2 said the formal scaling of HF and hybrid DFT is \(K^4\), and that practice is usually kinder. You will measure your own \(n\), and decide which points to trust (very short jobs are dominated by fixed overhead).

The questions at the end of the page ask you to describe the trend with ζ for each method, compare the two families, classify each method’s behavior, report and interpret your measured exponent, and choose the best combination of method and basis for this reaction, considering both accuracy and cost.






ImportantLock your predictions first



Before running anything, answer the warm-up quiz and lock your predictions in the Predict first section of the experiment page. You will predict, among other things, how the error of ωB97M-V and of Hartree–Fock changes from double- to quadruple-ζ, which family gives smaller errors at the same ζ, and which method comes closest to the reference with def2-QZVP. Predictions are not graded on being right: they are part of your submission so you (and we) can see how your intuition changes. Think about them using Lectures 1 and 2, commit, and then let your data answer. Once locked, they cannot be changed.




6.4 How to submit

Work through the page in order: warm-up quiz, predictions, calculations, results, charts, questions. Your entries are saved only in your own browser, so download your file often.
In the Submit section, enter your name and your Florida Tech email (ending in @my.fit.edu or @fit.edu), and confirm that you ran the calculations yourself.
Download your submission file (a .json file).
Open the Microsoft Form linked on the page, sign in with your Florida Tech email, and upload the file. You can resubmit until the deadline; the latest upload counts.

The optional Colab notebook at the bottom of the page extrapolates the HCl dimer to the CBS limit with PySCF, using the ideas of Lecture 2.

text:
8 Key points

A calculation is defined by a model chemistry (method/basis), a geometry and an electronic state (charge and multiplicity). Report all of them.
A Q-Chem single-point input has $molecule (charge, multiplicity, coordinates in Å) and $rem (JOBTYPE, METHOD, BASIS, SCF_CONVERGENCE). Method/basis maps onto METHOD and BASIS.
Line 2 of every .xyz file in this lab is “charge multiplicity”.
IQmol opens the geometry, writes and submits the input to the free server (10-minute limit), and monitors the job. The experiment pages generate every input and keep a job checklist.
From each output take the total energy (all digits), the SCF cycle count, the wall time and the number of basis functions; check that the job finished and the SCF converged.
\(\Delta E = \sum_i \nu_i E_i\) with \(\nu > 0\) for products and \(\nu < 0\) for reactants; multiply by 627.5095 to get kcal/mol. Never round total energies.
Signed error \(\varepsilon = \Delta E_\text{comp} - \Delta E_\text{ref}\); absolute error \(|\varepsilon|\).
Experiment 1: (HCl)₂ → 2 HCl, reference 2.01 kcal/mol; 4 methods × 6 basis sets × 2 species = 48 jobs; lock predictions first; submit the JSON file through the Microsoft Form with your Florida Tech email.

9 Study questions

Write the complete Q-Chem input for a single-point B3LYP/def2-TZVP energy of the HCl molecule of Experiment 1. Which lines change if you switch to ωB97M-V/cc-pVQZ?
The second line of an .xyz file reads 0 2. What does it tell you about the species? Give an example of a molecule or atom that could have it.
An output ends with SCF cycles and no “Thank you very much for using Q-Chem” line. List two possible causes and what you would check.

Why must both species of a reaction be computed with the same method and the same basis set?
If the wall time grew as \(K^4\), and a job with \(K = 50\) took 4 s, how long would a job with \(K = 200\) take? Why might a log–log fit of your Experiment 1 timings give a smaller exponent?

title: Lecture 1 · The molecular Schrödinger equation
Lecture 1 · The molecular Schrödinger equation
text:
1 Why compute?
Quantum chemistry programs such as Q-Chem (Epifanovsky et al. 2021) solve, approximately, one equation: the Schrödinger equation for the electrons of a molecule. From its solution we get an energy for a given arrangement of atoms. Almost everything a computational chemist predicts is built from such energies:

Reaction energies. Compute the energy of every reactant and product, then combine them with the stoichiometric coefficients. Is the reaction uphill or downhill, and by how much?
Barrier heights. Compute the energy of a transition state and compare it with the reactants. The barrier controls the rate.
Structures. Move the atoms until the energy is as low as possible. The result is a predicted equilibrium geometry, with bond lengths and angles.
Spectroscopic and thermodynamic properties. The curvature of the energy around a minimum gives vibrational frequencies; from those, statistical mechanics gives zero-point energies, enthalpies and free energies.
Noncovalent interactions. How strongly do two molecules stick together? This needs very accurate energy differences, often of only one or two kcal/mol.

The energies involved are tiny compared with the total energies the program prints. A water molecule has a total energy of about −76 hartree, which is about −48,000 kcal/mol. A typical reaction energy is a few to a few tens of kcal/mol, and a hydrogen bond is a few kcal/mol. In this lab you will constantly subtract large numbers to get small ones. That is why the accuracy of each calculation matters so much, and why you must keep all the digits.

1.1 The course roadmap
This lab has ten experiments. Each one isolates one source of error or one practical decision:



Exp.
Topic
What it teaches




1

how big a basis set must be


2

3, 4
Organic chemistry, parts A and B
how functionals perform on “easy” and dispersion-bound reactions


5

where approximate functionals break down


6

7

8

whether the SCF found the right solution


9

from electronic energies to measured quantities


10
Final review
choosing and defending a method yourself



Behind all ten sits a single idea, which this chapter develops: every practical calculation makes two approximations. We approximate the wave function Ψ by expanding it in a finite set of functions (the basis set, Lecture 2 and Experiment 1). And we approximate the Hamiltonian Ĥ, or more precisely the way electrons interact, by choosing a method such as Hartree–Fock or a density functional (Lectures 4–6 and Experiments 2–5). Most of the semester is about understanding the errors these two approximations introduce, and how they can add up or cancel.

title: Lecture 1 · The molecular Schrödinger equation
section: 2 Review: the Schrödinger equation and the hydrogen atom
text:
2 Review: the Schrödinger equation and the hydrogen atom

2.1 Operators, eigenfunctions, eigenvalues
The time-independent Schrödinger equation (TISE) (Schrödinger 1926) is an eigenvalue equation:
\[
\hat{H}\Psi = E\Psi .
\tag{1}\]
Here \(\hat{H}\) is the Hamiltonian operator, the operator associated with the total energy. An operator acts on a function and returns another function. When the result is the same function multiplied by a number, the function is an eigenfunction of the operator and the number is the eigenvalue. Equation 1 says that the allowed stationary states of a system are the eigenfunctions \(\Psi\) of \(\hat{H}\), and the allowed energies are its eigenvalues \(E\).
Three facts from P-Chem 2 matter for everything that follows:

The Hamiltonian is a Hermitian operator, so its eigenvalues are real and its eigenfunctions can be chosen orthonormal: \(\int \Psi_i^* \Psi_j \, d\tau = \delta_{ij}\).
The Hamiltonian is a sum of a kinetic part and a potential part, \(\hat{H} = \hat{T} + \hat{V}\). For one particle of mass \(m\), \(\hat{T} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2\), and \(\hat{V}\) simply multiplies the wave function by the potential energy \(V(\mathbf{r})\).
For any normalized function \(\Psi\), the expectation value of the energy is \(\langle E \rangle = \int \Psi^* \hat{H} \Psi \, d\tau\). If \(\Psi\) is an eigenfunction, \(\langle E \rangle\) equals its eigenvalue exactly.







NoteNotation in this course



The P-Chem 2 textbook writes kinetic-energy operators as \(\hat{K}\) and uses \(\chi\) for spin orbitals. In these handouts we follow the convention of most quantum-chemistry programs and papers: \(\hat{T}\) for kinetic energy, \(\Psi\) for the many-electron wave function, \(\phi_i\) (or \(\psi_i\)) for orbitals, and \(\chi_\mu\) for basis functions (from Lecture 2 on). Bold symbols such as \(\mathbf{r}\) are vectors.




2.2 The hydrogen atom: the one exactly solvable atom
The hydrogen atom has one electron moving in the Coulomb field of one proton. Its Schrödinger equation can be solved exactly. In atomic units (Section 3.2) the energies are
\[
E_n = -\frac{1}{2n^2}\ E_\text{h}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots
\tag{2}\]
so the ground state lies at exactly \(-0.5\ E_\text{h}\). The eigenfunctions factor into a radial part and an angular part,
\[
\psi_{n\ell m_\ell}(r,\theta,\varphi) = R_{n\ell}(r)\, Y_\ell^{m_\ell}(\theta,\varphi),
\]
labeled by three quantum numbers: the principal quantum number \(n = 1, 2, \dots\); the angular-momentum quantum number \(\ell = 0, \dots, n-1\) (s, p, d, f, …); and the magnetic quantum number \(m_\ell = -\ell, \dots, +\ell\). The radial function \(R_{n\ell}\) has \(n - \ell - 1\) radial nodes, and the angular part has \(\ell\) angular nodes. Figure 1 shows the first six radial functions and the corresponding radial probability densities.






Figure 1: Hydrogen-atom radial functions \(R_{n\ell}(r)\) (a) and radial probability densities \(r^2R_{n\ell}^2(r)\) (b), in atomic units. The 2s function has one radial node, 3s has two, 3p has one; 2p and 3d have none (\(n-\ell-1=0\)). Note two features that will matter in Lecture 2: s functions have a sharp, finite cusp at the nucleus, and every function decays exponentially, as \(e^{-r/n}\), at large \(r\).



The hydrogen orbitals are one-electron wave functions. That idea is the seed of everything we do: for many-electron systems we will build approximate wave functions out of one-electron functions (orbitals), and we will build the orbitals themselves out of simpler functions that look like the hydrogen solutions near each nucleus. Two properties of \(\psi_{1s} \propto e^{-r}\) are worth noticing now, because Gaussian basis functions will get both of them wrong (Lecture 2):

The cusp. At \(r = 0\) the 1s function has a finite value and a sharp corner: its slope is \(d\psi/dr = -Z\psi(0)\), not zero. This is not an accident of hydrogen; it is required of any exact wave function wherever an electron meets a nucleus (Kato 1957).
The exponential tail. Far from the nucleus, bound wave functions decay as \(e^{-\sqrt{2I}\,r}\), where \(I\) is the ionization energy in hartree. For hydrogen, \(I = 0.5\ E_\text{h}\) and the decay is \(e^{-r}\).

title: Lecture 1 · The molecular Schrödinger equation
text:
3 The molecular Hamiltonian

3.1 Five terms
A molecule is a collection of \(M\) nuclei (charges \(Z_A\), masses \(M_A\), positions \(\mathbf{R}_A\)) and \(N\) electrons (mass \(m_e\), charge \(-e\), positions \(\mathbf{r}_i\)). Its nonrelativistic Hamiltonian has five terms:
\[
\hat{H} = \hat{T}_n + \hat{T}_e + \hat{V}_{ne} + \hat{V}_{ee} + \hat{V}_{nn} .
\tag{3}\]
In SI units, each term reads
\[
\begin{aligned}
\hat{T}_n &= -\sum_{A=1}^{M} \frac{\hbar^2}{2M_A}\nabla_A^2 &&\text{kinetic energy of the nuclei}\\
\hat{T}_e &= -\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\hbar^2}{2m_e}\nabla_i^2 &&\text{kinetic energy of the electrons}\\
\hat{V}_{ne} &= -\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{A=1}^{M} \frac{Z_A e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{R}_A|} &&\text{nucleus–electron attraction}\\
\hat{V}_{ee} &= \sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j>i}^{N} \frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j|} &&\text{electron–electron repulsion}\\
\hat{V}_{nn} &= \sum_{A=1}^{M}\sum_{B>A}^{M} \frac{Z_A Z_B e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,|\mathbf{R}_A - \mathbf{R}_B|} &&\text{nucleus–nucleus repulsion}
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}\]
The two attraction/repulsion sums over pairs use \(j > i\) and \(B > A\) so that each pair is counted once. The P-Chem 2 textbook writes the same five terms in §11.1, with \(\hat{K}\) for kinetic energy.
This Hamiltonian is called “exact”, but it already leaves out some physics: relativistic effects (important for core electrons of heavy atoms) and spin–orbit coupling. For the light molecules in most of this lab they are small. For heavy elements (Experiment 8 has ruthenium; Experiment 10 has palladium) the def2 basis sets include relativistic effects through effective core potentials, which you will meet in Lecture 2.


3.2 Atomic units
All the constants in Equation 4 are a nuisance. Quantum chemistry therefore works in atomic units, in which
\[
\hbar = m_e = e = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 = 1 .
\]
With this choice the Hamiltonian becomes much cleaner:
\[
\hat{H} = -\sum_{A}\frac{1}{2M_A}\nabla_A^2 - \sum_{i}\frac{1}{2}\nabla_i^2 - \sum_{i}\sum_{A}\frac{Z_A}{r_{iA}} + \sum_{i}\sum_{j>i}\frac{1}{r_{ij}} + \sum_{A}\sum_{B>A}\frac{Z_A Z_B}{R_{AB}} ,
\tag{5}\]
where \(r_{iA} = |\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{R}_A|\), \(r_{ij} = |\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j|\), \(R_{AB} = |\mathbf{R}_A - \mathbf{R}_B|\), and the nuclear masses \(M_A\) are now in units of the electron mass (about 1836 for a proton).
The unit of length is the bohr (\(a_0\)), the most probable distance of the 1s electron from the proton in hydrogen. The unit of energy is the hartree (\(E_\text{h}\)), twice the ionization energy of hydrogen. These are the units of every number Q-Chem prints internally, so you need the conversions at your fingertips:



Table 1: Atomic units used in this course. In this lab, total energies are always reported in hartree and reaction energies in kcal/mol, with 1 \(E_\text{h}\) = 627.5095 kcal/mol.

TipWorked example: units



(a) The ground-state energy of hydrogen is \(-0.5\ E_\text{h}\). In other units: \(-0.5 \times 627.5095 = -313.75\) kcal/mol, \(-0.5 \times 27.2114 = -13.606\) eV, which is the familiar 13.6 eV ionization energy.
(b) Experiment 1 studies the dissociation of the HCl dimer, with a reference energy of 2.01 kcal/mol. In hartree, that is \(2.01 / 627.5095 = 0.003203\ E_\text{h}\). The total energy of one HCl molecule is about \(-460\ E_\text{h}\). The quantity you want is therefore about one part in \(10^5\) of the numbers you subtract. Rounding each total energy to 4 decimals introduces up to \(0.00005\ E_\text{h}\) per energy. In \(\Delta E = 2E(\text{HCl}) - E(\text{dimer})\) the worst case is \(3 \times 0.00005 = 0.00015\ E_\text{h}\), or 0.09 kcal/mol: almost 5% of the answer.
(c) The bond length of HCl in the Experiment 1 geometry file is 1.27907 Å. In bohr: \(1.27907 / 0.529177 = 2.41709\ a_0\).

title: Lecture 1 · The molecular Schrödinger equation
text:
4 The Born–Oppenheimer approximation

4.1 Clamped nuclei
Equation 5 still describes all particles at once. Even for H₂ (two nuclei, two electrons) it is a problem in 12 coordinates. The first and most important simplification uses the fact that nuclei are heavy: a proton is 1836 times heavier than an electron, and a ³⁵Cl nucleus about 64,000 times. For the same kinetic energy, nuclei move far more slowly. To the electrons, the nuclei look almost frozen; to the nuclei, the electrons adjust instantly to wherever the nuclei are.
The Born–Oppenheimer approximation (Born and Oppenheimer 1927) makes this precise. We fix (“clamp”) the nuclei at positions \(\mathbf{R}\), drop the nuclear kinetic energy \(\hat{T}_n\), and solve for the electrons alone. The electronic Hamiltonian is
\[
\hat{H}_\text{el} = -\sum_{i}\frac{1}{2}\nabla_i^2 - \sum_{i}\sum_{A}\frac{Z_A}{r_{iA}} + \sum_{i}\sum_{j>i}\frac{1}{r_{ij}} ,
\tag{6}\]
and the electronic Schrödinger equation is
\[
\hat{H}_\text{el}\,\Psi_\text{el}(\mathbf{r};\mathbf{R}) = E_\text{el}(\mathbf{R})\,\Psi_\text{el}(\mathbf{r};\mathbf{R}) .
\tag{7}\]
The semicolon means that the electronic wave function depends on the electron coordinates \(\mathbf{r}\) as variables and on the nuclear positions \(\mathbf{R}\) only as parameters: change the geometry, and you get a different equation to solve. With the nuclei fixed, \(V_{nn}\) is just a number, and we add it at the end.


4.2 The potential energy surface
The sum
\[
U(\mathbf{R}) = E_\text{el}(\mathbf{R}) + V_{nn}(\mathbf{R})
\tag{8}\]
is the potential energy surface (PES): the energy the nuclei feel as they move. Its minima are stable structures, its first-order saddle points are transition states, and its curvature at a minimum gives the vibrational frequencies. Every concept of a “molecular structure” lives on this surface, and it exists only because of the Born–Oppenheimer approximation.
Figure 2 shows the PES of H₂ (a single coordinate, the bond length), split into its two pieces. The electronic energy alone is attractive at all distances; it is the nuclear repulsion that turns it into a curve with a minimum.






Figure 2: Potential energy curve of H₂, modeled with a Morse function using experimental constants (\(D_e\) = 4.75 eV, \(R_e\) = 0.741 Å, \(\tilde{\nu}_e\) = 4401 cm⁻¹), in atomic units. The total energy \(U(R)\) (solid) is the sum of the electronic energy \(E_\text{el}(R)\) (dashed) and the nuclear repulsion \(V_{nn} = 1/R\) (dotted, shifted down by 1 \(E_\text{h}\) to fit on the same axes). At large \(R\) the curve approaches the energy of two separate H atoms, \(2 \times (-0.5) = -1\ E_\text{h}\).





4.3 What “total energy” means in a Q-Chem output
When Q-Chem prints
 Total energy in the final basis set =     -460.xxxxxxxxxx
that number is \(U(\mathbf{R})\) of Equation 8, computed at the one geometry you gave in the input: the electronic energy plus the nuclear repulsion. It is the energy of a motionless molecule. In particular, it does not contain:

the zero-point vibrational energy (ZPE): even at 0 K, a molecule vibrates, and that costs energy;
thermal energy at room temperature (translation, rotation, populated vibrational levels);
entropy, so it is not a free energy.

The reaction energies you compute in Experiments 1–8 are therefore electronic reaction energies, \(\Delta E_\text{el}\), and they are compared with reference values of the same kind. Comparing with experiment requires the corrections listed above; that is the subject of Lecture 13 and Experiment 9.






TipWorked example: nuclear repulsion of HCl



For HCl at \(R = 2.41709\ a_0\) (from the previous worked example), \(V_{nn} = Z_\text{Cl} Z_\text{H}/R = 17 \times 1 / 2.41709 = 7.0332\ E_\text{h}\). That is a large positive number, about 4,400 kcal/mol. The total energy is about \(-460\ E_\text{h}\), so the electronic energy is about \(-467\ E_\text{h}\). You never need to add \(V_{nn}\) yourself: the “total energy” already includes it. Q-Chem also prints the nuclear repulsion energy separately near the top of the output, which is a quick check that the geometry was read correctly.








ImportantCommon mistake



“Total energy” in a quantum-chemistry output does not mean “energy including everything”. It means the electronic energy plus nuclear repulsion at a fixed geometry. Never compare it directly with an experimental enthalpy.

title: Lecture 1 · The molecular Schrödinger equation
text:
5 Many electrons

5.1 Why we cannot solve it
For a one-electron system, such as H or He⁺ or H₂⁺, the electronic Schrödinger equation can be solved exactly (analytically for atoms, numerically to any precision for H₂⁺). With two or more electrons the term
\[
\hat{V}_{ee} = \sum_{i}\sum_{j>i}\frac{1}{r_{ij}}
\]
couples the coordinates of every electron to every other one. The motion of electron 1 depends on where electron 2 is, and vice versa. The equation no longer separates into one-electron problems, and no analytic solution exists. Numerically, the difficulty is the dimension: \(\Psi\) is a function of \(3N\) spatial coordinates (plus \(N\) spin coordinates). A benzene molecule has 42 electrons, so its wave function lives in a 126-dimensional space. Storing it on even a coarse grid of 10 points per coordinate would take \(10^{126}\) numbers.
The helium atom shows how big the effect of \(\hat{V}_{ee}\) is:



Table 2: The helium atom. Ignoring electron repulsion is a disaster; a single determinant of the best orbitals gets most of the energy; the remaining 0.042 \(E_\text{h}\) (26 kcal/mol) is the correlation energy of Lecture 4.









Model for He
Energy (\(E_\text{h}\))




Ignore \(\hat{V}_{ee}\) entirely (two independent hydrogen-like electrons with \(Z = 2\))
\(2 \times (-Z^2/2) = -4.000\)


Best possible single determinant (Hartree–Fock limit)
\(-2.8617\)


Exact nonrelativistic energy
\(-2.9037\)






Notice the size of the last difference. The error of the best single-determinant wave function is “only” 1.4% of the total energy, yet 26 kcal/mol is far larger than the reaction energies we care about. This is why approximations to the electron–electron interaction are the heart of quantum chemistry.


5.2 Spin and the Pauli principle
Electrons have spin, an intrinsic angular momentum with two possible projections, \(m_s = +\tfrac{1}{2}\) (\(\alpha\), “up”) and \(m_s = -\tfrac{1}{2}\) (\(\beta\), “down”). It has no classical analogue and does not appear in the Hamiltonian of Equation 6, yet it has dramatic consequences through the Pauli principle: the wave function of a system of electrons must be antisymmetric with respect to the exchange of any two electrons,
\[
\Psi(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \dots, \mathbf{x}_N) = -\Psi(\mathbf{x}_2, \mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_N),
\tag{9}\]
where \(\mathbf{x}_i = (\mathbf{r}_i, s_i)\) collects the three spatial coordinates and the spin coordinate of electron \(i\). The familiar “no two electrons in the same state” rule is a consequence of Equation 9, not the other way around.
Spin matters for every calculation you run. The second line of each geometry file in this lab gives the charge and the spin multiplicity \(2S+1\), where \(S\) is the total spin quantum number. Closed-shell molecules such as HCl have all electrons paired: \(S = 0\), a singlet (multiplicity 1). A hydrogen atom has one unpaired electron, \(S = \tfrac{1}{2}\), a doublet (2). The ground state of O₂ and of the O atom has two unpaired electrons with parallel spins, \(S = 1\), a triplet (3). Get the multiplicity wrong and you compute a different electronic state, with a different energy.


5.3 Orbitals and the Slater determinant
How do we write down a wave function that is automatically antisymmetric? Start from one-electron functions. A spatial orbital \(\phi(\mathbf{r})\) times a spin function, \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\), is a spin orbital \(\varphi(\mathbf{x})\). Each spatial orbital can therefore hold two electrons, one with each spin.
A simple product of spin orbitals, \(\varphi_1(\mathbf{x}_1)\varphi_2(\mathbf{x}_2)\), is not antisymmetric. The fix, for two electrons, is to subtract the swapped product:
\[
\Psi(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\Big[\varphi_1(\mathbf{x}_1)\varphi_2(\mathbf{x}_2) - \varphi_2(\mathbf{x}_1)\varphi_1(\mathbf{x}_2)\Big]
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\left|\begin{matrix}
\varphi_1(\mathbf{x}_1) & \varphi_2(\mathbf{x}_1) \\
\varphi_1(\mathbf{x}_2) & \varphi_2(\mathbf{x}_2)
\end{matrix}\right| .
\tag{10}\]
The second form is a determinant, and it generalizes to \(N\) electrons. The Slater determinant (Slater 1930) is
\[
\Psi(\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_N) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N!}}
\left|\begin{matrix}
\varphi_1(\mathbf{x}_1) & \varphi_2(\mathbf{x}_1) & \cdots & \varphi_N(\mathbf{x}_1) \\
\varphi_1(\mathbf{x}_2) & \varphi_2(\mathbf{x}_2) & \cdots & \varphi_N(\mathbf{x}_2) \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\varphi_1(\mathbf{x}_N) & \varphi_2(\mathbf{x}_N) & \cdots & \varphi_N(\mathbf{x}_N)
\end{matrix}\right| .
\tag{11}\]
Rows are electrons, columns are spin orbitals. Two properties of determinants do all the work:

Swapping two rows changes the sign of a determinant. Swapping two rows means exchanging two electrons, so Equation 11 obeys Equation 9 automatically.
A determinant with two identical columns is zero. Two electrons in the same spin orbital give \(\Psi = 0\): this is the Pauli exclusion principle.

The Slater determinant is the simplest antisymmetric wave function we can build from orbitals. It is the wave function of Hartree–Fock theory (Lecture 4), and the Kohn–Sham determinant of density functional theory (Lecture 5) has the same form. It is not the exact wave function: a single determinant describes each electron as moving in the average field of the others, and misses the way electrons instantaneously avoid each other. That missing piece is electron correlation.






NoteOrbitals are building blocks, not observables



For one-electron systems, orbitals are exact wave functions. For many-electron systems they are a mathematical device for building an approximate \(\Psi\). This is why the orbital pictures in IQmol are so useful for intuition, and also why you should not over-interpret them: different methods give somewhat different orbitals for the same molecule.




5.4 The variational principle
We cannot solve Equation 7 exactly, so how can we tell whether one approximate wave function is better than another? The variational principle gives the answer. For any normalized, well-behaved trial function \(\Psi_\text{trial}\) that satisfies the right boundary conditions and symmetry,
\[
E[\Psi_\text{trial}] = \int \Psi_\text{trial}^* \hat{H} \Psi_\text{trial}\, d\tau \;\geq\; E_0 ,
\tag{12}\]
where \(E_0\) is the exact ground-state energy. Equality holds only if \(\Psi_\text{trial}\) is the exact ground state.
The proof takes three lines. Expand the trial function in the (unknown) exact eigenfunctions, \(\Psi_\text{trial} = \sum_k c_k \Psi_k\), with \(\sum_k |c_k|^2 = 1\). Then \(E[\Psi_\text{trial}] = \sum_k |c_k|^2 E_k\). Since every \(E_k \geq E_0\), the weighted average can never be below \(E_0\).
The consequences are practical:

Lower is better. Among trial wave functions of the same Hamiltonian, the one with the lower energy is closer to the exact ground state (in energy).
Optimize parameters. Give the trial function adjustable parameters and minimize the energy with respect to them. The result is the best approximation of that form.
More flexibility can only help. If one family of trial functions contains another (for example, a bigger set of basis functions that includes all the functions of a smaller one), the minimum energy of the bigger family is lower or equal.

Point 3 is the reason basis sets work, as you will see in Lecture 2.






TipWorked example: the variational principle for helium



Take as a trial function for He a product of two hydrogen-like 1s orbitals with an adjustable exponent \(\zeta\) (an “effective nuclear charge”), \(\Psi = \frac{\zeta^3}{\pi} e^{-\zeta r_1} e^{-\zeta r_2}\), times the singlet spin function. Evaluating \(\langle \hat{H} \rangle\) for helium (\(Z = 2\)) gives
\[
E(\zeta) = \zeta^2 - 2Z\zeta + \tfrac{5}{8}\zeta .
\]
Setting \(dE/d\zeta = 0\) gives \(\zeta = Z - \tfrac{5}{16} = 1.6875\) and \(E = -\zeta^2 = -2.8477\ E_\text{h}\). Compare with Table 2. The optimized energy is above the exact \(-2.9037\ E_\text{h}\), as the variational principle guarantees, and well below the unscreened \(\zeta = 2\) result (\(E = 4 - 8 + 1.25 = -2.75\ E_\text{h}\)). The optimized \(\zeta < 2\) has a physical meaning: each electron partly screens the nucleus from the other. Adding more flexibility (more parameters) would bring the energy closer to \(-2.9037\).








ImportantWhen “lower is better” does not apply



The variational principle compares energies computed with the same Hamiltonian. Hartree–Fock and the basis-set expansion are variational, so a bigger basis always gives a lower or equal HF energy. But approximate density functionals (Lectures 5–6) use approximate Hamiltonians: a functional that gives a lower total energy is not, for that reason, a better functional. Comparing total energies across methods is meaningless; comparing reaction energies with a reliable reference is how methods are judged (Lecture 7).

title: Lecture 1 · The molecular Schrödinger equation
section: 6 The two approximations of every calculation
text:
6 The two approximations of every calculation
We can now state precisely what any practical electronic-structure calculation does. It makes two approximations, and they are independent of each other.
Approximation 1: the wave function (the basis set). The orbitals are unknown functions in three dimensions. A computer cannot store an arbitrary function, so we expand each orbital in a finite set of known functions, the basis set. The finite expansion restricts the shapes the orbitals can take, and by the variational principle the energy is too high. As the basis grows, this basis-set incompleteness error (BSIE) shrinks toward the complete-basis-set (CBS) limit. This is Lecture 2 and Experiment 1.
Approximation 2: the Hamiltonian (the method). Even with a complete basis, we cannot handle \(\hat{V}_{ee}\) exactly. A method decides how to treat it. Hartree–Fock replaces it by an average field (Lecture 4). Density functional theory replaces the hard part by an approximate exchange–correlation functional (Lectures 5–6). Wave-function methods such as MP2 or CCSD(T) add correlation on top of Hartree–Fock, at a much higher cost.
The pair of choices is called a model chemistry or level of theory, and it is written method/basis:



Table 3: Decoding a model chemistry. You will meet each of these names in Experiment 1.










Model chemistry
Method (approximates Ĥ)
Basis set (approximates Ψ)




HF/cc-pVTZ
Hartree–Fock
Dunning triple-ζ


B3LYP/def2-SVP
B3LYP hybrid functional
Karlsruhe double-ζ


ωB97M-V/def2-QZVP
ωB97M-V range-separated hybrid meta-GGA
Karlsruhe quadruple-ζ






The total error of a computed reaction energy is, roughly, method error + basis-set error (+ smaller numerical errors such as integration grids and SCF convergence). One of the goals of this lab is to learn to keep these errors separate. Experiment 1 holds the method fixed and varies the basis; Experiments 3–5 hold the basis fixed and vary the method; Experiment 6 shows what happens when the two errors cancel each other.






NoteWhat comes next



Lecture 2 opens the first approximation: what basis functions look like, why everyone uses Gaussians, and how to read names such as 6-31G*, def2-TZVP and cc-pVQZ. Lecture 3 turns all of this into a real calculation in IQmol and Q-Chem.

title: Lecture 1 · The molecular Schrödinger equation
text:
7 Key points

A quantum-chemistry program computes an energy for a fixed arrangement of nuclei. Reaction energies, barriers, structures and frequencies are all built from such energies.
The molecular Hamiltonian has five terms: \(\hat{T}_n\), \(\hat{T}_e\), \(\hat{V}_{ne}\), \(\hat{V}_{ee}\) and \(\hat{V}_{nn}\). In atomic units (\(\hbar = m_e = e = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 = 1\)) energies are in hartree and lengths in bohr.
1 \(E_\text{h}\) = 627.5095 kcal/mol = 2625.50 kJ/mol = 27.2114 eV; 1 bohr = 0.529177 Å.
The Born–Oppenheimer approximation clamps the nuclei and gives the electronic Schrödinger equation; \(E_\text{el}(\mathbf{R}) + V_{nn}(\mathbf{R})\) is the potential energy surface.
Q-Chem’s “total energy” is \(E_\text{el} + V_{nn}\) at one fixed geometry: no zero-point energy, no thermal corrections, no entropy.
The electron–electron repulsion couples all electrons, so no system with two or more electrons can be solved exactly.
Electrons are fermions: the wave function must be antisymmetric. A Slater determinant of spin orbitals is the simplest antisymmetric wave function and enforces the Pauli principle automatically.
The variational principle: any trial wave function gives an energy at or above the exact ground-state energy, for the same Hamiltonian. Lower is better, and more flexibility can only lower the energy.
Every calculation approximates Ψ (the basis set) and Ĥ (the method). A model chemistry is written method/basis.

title: Lecture 1 · The molecular Schrödinger equation
text:
8 Study questions

Write the five terms of the molecular Hamiltonian for the H₂⁺ ion in atomic units. Which term is absent compared with H₂, and why does its absence make H₂⁺ exactly solvable within the Born–Oppenheimer approximation?
The total energy of a molecule is printed as −76.4 \(E_\text{h}\). Express it in kcal/mol, kJ/mol and eV. Which unit would you use to report a reaction energy in this lab?
A reaction energy is computed as 0.0158 \(E_\text{h}\). Convert it to kcal/mol. If each of the two total energies used to compute it had been rounded to 3 decimal places, what is the largest error (in kcal/mol) the rounding could introduce?
Why does the Born–Oppenheimer approximation work so well? Give the mass ratio between a ³⁵Cl nucleus and an electron, and explain why the approximation is expected to be slightly worse for molecules containing hydrogen.
Compute the nuclear repulsion energy of H₂ at its equilibrium bond length of 0.741 Å, in hartree and in kcal/mol.
Explain in your own words what the “total energy” in a Q-Chem output contains, and list three contributions that would be needed to compare it with an experimental reaction enthalpy at 298 K.
Write the Slater determinant for the ground state of the lithium atom (configuration 1s² 2s¹) using spin orbitals \(1s\alpha\), \(1s\beta\), \(2s\alpha\). Show that putting the third electron in \(1s\alpha\) instead gives \(\Psi = 0\).
Give the spin multiplicity of: HCl, the H atom, the Cl atom, the O atom (ground state), O₂ (ground state), and the CH₃ radical.
Calculation A gives \(E = -2.8477\ E_\text{h}\) for He and calculation B gives \(-2.8617\ E_\text{h}\), both with the exact Hamiltonian. Which wave function is better, and how do you know? Could a calculation with the exact Hamiltonian give \(-2.95\ E_\text{h}\)?
Two students compute the total energy of water with two different density functionals and get −76.42 and −76.38 \(E_\text{h}\). One argues the first functional is better “because of the variational principle”. Is the argument correct? Explain.

title: Computational Chemistry Lab
text: Welcome to the computational lab of Advanced Physical Chemistry. Over ten experiments you will use density functional theory (DFT) the way researchers do: choose a method, run real quantum-chemistry jobs on a shared server, compare your numbers with high-level reference data, and decide which results you can trust. Every experiment comes from real benchmark databases, and every one hides a lesson about where DFT works well and where it doesn’t.

title: Working on a shared machine
text: The Q-Chem server you use through IQmol is shared: by everyone in this class, by students in other courses, and by users around the world. Research clusters work the same way. Learning to use a shared resource well is one of the skills this lab teaches.

title: Working on a shared machine
text:
How a queue works
When you click Submit, your job doesn’t start right away. It joins a queue. A scheduler starts jobs as resources free up, usually first come, first served, sometimes with limits per user. Your job’s life:

queued → running → finished (or failed / killed)

The Job Monitor in IQmol shows which stage each job is in.

title: Working on a shared machine
section: The limits of the free server
text:
The limits of the free server

Run time: each job can run for at most 10 minutes. After that it is killed and you get no energy.
Concurrency: you may not be able to run many jobs at the same time. Extra jobs just wait in the queue.
Availability: the server is a free service. It can be slow at busy times, and very occasionally unavailable. Never leave the calculations for the night before the deadline.

Every experiment page shows a rough cost flag next to each job: quick, a few minutes, or may hit the 10-min limit. These are estimates based on the molecule size, the basis set and the type of functional, not guarantees.

title: Working on a shared machine
text:
Good habits

Test one job first. Before submitting 128 jobs, run one, open the output and check it.
Submit in batches. For example, all the molecules for one functional, then check them, then the next functional.
Name jobs systematically, e.g. ex03_b3lyp_def2-tzvp_eth_st. The input generator does it for you.
Keep a job log. The checklist on each experiment page ticks itself off as you enter energies, so you can see at a glance what’s missing.
Keep every output, organized in one folder per experiment.
Don’t resubmit blindly. If a job fails, read the end of the output first. Resubmitting a broken input just wastes everyone’s queue time.
Start early. Queues are longest right before deadlines, for every class, everywhere.







NoteWhy not run everything on your laptop?



For these small molecules you could, but real research calculations need hundreds of cores and days of time. The workflow you learn here (prepare locally → submit to a queue → retrieve and analyze) is exactly how computational chemists work on university clusters and national supercomputers.

title: Install IQmol and connect to Q-Chem
text:
All calculations in this lab run in Q-Chem (Epifanovsky et al. 2021), a professional quantum-chemistry program. You won’t install Q-Chem on your laptop. Instead you’ll use IQmol (Gilbert, n.d.), a free graphical program that builds the molecule, writes the Q-Chem input and sends the job to a remote server where Q-Chem actually runs. When the job finishes, IQmol brings the results back.
This is how research computing works: you prepare jobs on your own computer, submit them to a shared machine, and analyze the output when it comes back.

title: Experiment 8: Stability Analysis and Transition Metals
text:
Background
As you know, the coefficients of the basis functions in the Kohn–Sham orbitals come from an iterative procedure, the self-consistent field (SCF) procedure. Starting from an initial set of coefficients (the initial density matrix, or “guess”), it produces the final, optimized coefficients, which computational chemists call the converged SCF solution.
A converged SCF solution is a stationary point, but we can’t know in advance whether it is a minimum, a maximum or a saddle point. To be sure we have the lowest energy, we must characterize the stationary point and correct it if needed. This stability analysis requires the second derivatives of the energy with respect to orbital rotations (the electronic Hessian), and it can be repeated more than once. When an instability is detected, two constraints can be lifted to lower the energy (Seeger and Pople 1977): we can change the theoretical framework (from restricted to unrestricted), or we can allow complex instead of real orbitals. The wave function obtained after a stability analysis is stable and has a lower energy than the unstable one.
How can an SCF end on an unstable solution? For example, it can land on an excited state while you are computing the ground state. With a reasonable guess this is unlikely for molecules made mostly of main-group elements, but it is much more likely for systems with nearly degenerate low-lying states, such as transition-metal atoms. Without a stability analysis you would never notice. Good descriptions of the procedure are in Seeger and Pople (1977), Bauernschmitt and Ahlrichs (1996) and Fukutome (1981).
In this experiment you will use five functionals with the def2-TZVP basis set (Weigend and Ahlrichs 2005): PBE (Perdew et al. 1996) for both atoms, BP86 (Becke 1988; Perdew 1986a, 1986b) and PBE0 (Adamo and Barone 1999; Ernzerhof and Scuseria 1999) for Ru⁺, and M06-2X (Zhao and Truhlar 2008) and B97M-V (Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2015; Vydrov and Van Voorhis 2010) for Fe. These are the combinations whose calculations converge reliably both with and without stability analysis. Other functionals (SPW92, B3LYP, SCAN, ωB97M-V) and Hartree–Fock were left out because their SCF often fails to converge for these atoms, itself a lesson about transition metals. Ru needs an effective core potential (ECP = def2-ECP).
You will compute the excitation energies of two atoms, Fe (reference 34.32 kcal/mol) and Ru⁺ (reference 21.96 kcal/mol). The data come from the 3dAEE8 (Hoyer et al. 2014; Luo et al. 2014; Yu and Truhlar 2014) and 4dAEE5 (Luo and Truhlar 2012) subsets of the Minnesota 2015B database (Yu et al. 2016). Run two sets of calculations:

Without stability analysis: compute the excitation energy E(excited) − E(ground).
With stability analysis: add INTERNAL_STABILITY TRUE to the $rem section, and check in the output whether an instability was found and the wave function re-optimized.

As usual, compute the errors with respect to the reference values.

title: Experiment 6: Why is the B3LYP/6-31G* Level of Theory so Successful?
text:
Background
The B3LYP functional (Vosko et al. 1980; Becke 1988, 1993; Lee et al. 1988; Stephens et al. 1994) with the 6-31G* basis set of Pople and co-workers (Ditchfield et al. 1971; Hehre et al. 1972; Hariharan and Pople 1973; Dill and Pople 1975; Binkley and Pople 1977; Francl et al. 1982; Gordon et al. 1982; Rassolov et al. 1998, 2001) is the de facto standard method in the organic chemistry community. The functional is based on the three-parameter hybrid scheme Becke introduced in 1993 (Becke 1993). The original three-parameter functional combined his 1988 exchange functional (Becke 1988) with the Perdew–Wang (PW91) correlation functional (Perdew and Wang 1992, 2018; Perdew et al. 1992). One year later, Frisch and co-workers introduced B3LYP by replacing PW91 with LYP (Lee et al. 1988), which gave better results in a computational study of circular dichroism spectra (Stephens et al. 1994). B3LYP became more popular than B3PW91, even though their performance and theoretical foundations are almost identical.
6-31G* is a double-ζ split-valence polarized basis set, so it contains a moderate number of basis functions. Its use with B3LYP became popular in the 1990s and early 2000s because it allowed calculations on relatively large molecules relevant to organic chemistry, with performance far better than the methods available before, such as semi-empirical methods and Hartree–Fock. Given how much computers have improved in the last two decades, however, a double-ζ basis set in a research setting is sometimes dangerous, as you saw in Experiment 1.
In this experiment you will test B3LYP with several double-ζ polarized basis sets to understand why B3LYP/6-31G* is so “special”:

6-31G* (Pople)
cc-pVDZ (Dunning) (Dunning 1989; Woon and Dunning 1993, 1994; Wilson et al. 1999; Koput and Peterson 2002; Balabanov and Peterson 2005; Prascher et al. 2011)
def2-SVP (Ahlrichs) (Weigend and Ahlrichs 2005)
pc-1 (Jensen) (Jensen 2001, 2002, 2007, 2012; Jensen and Helgaker 2004). If it is not available, use def2-SV(P), the smallest of the Ahlrichs basis sets.

Run them on three reactions you already know: the Diels–Alder reaction 4a, the alkane isomerization 4b and the CaO dissociation 5b. They were chosen because they respond to the small basis sets in very different ways; find out how. Compare with the def2-TZVP results you obtained in Experiments 4 and 5 with the same functionals. As before, report each computed reaction energy with its error with respect to the reference value.

title: Experiment 6: Why is the B3LYP/6-31G* Level of Theory so Successful?
text:
Questions

Loading the questions…







TipTip



This experiment shows that B3LYP/6-31G* works so well because it benefits from a fortuitous error cancellation (Kruse et al. 2012). Theory says a functional’s error with a small basis set should always be larger than with a big one. That B3LYP/6-31G* doesn’t follow this expectation when compared with B3LYP/def2-TZVP is worrisome: it points to a lucky cancellation of errors. Lucky cancellations are unpredictable. Sometimes they work in your favor, as for the reactions of Experiment 4, and sometimes against you, as for those of Experiment 5. The 6-31G* basis set does not make B3LYP better or more physically sound. Instead of trying to work out which chemical problems B3LYP/6-31G* can solve, we suggest moving away from it toward a more modern functional with predictable behavior with respect to the basis set. If that’s not possible because of limited computing resources, put more appropriate corrections in place, such as those suggested by Kruse, Goerigk and Grimme, with the help of an expert. In 2012, Cohen, Mori-Sánchez and Yang wrote that uniformly outperforming B3LYP was still a challenge for xc functionals (Cohen et al. 2012). Recent reviews have shown that this is no longer true (Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2017; Goerigk and Mehta 2019; Peverati and Truhlar 2014; Yu et al. 2016). We feel the real challenge now is to get rid of B3LYP/6-31G* altogether, though, as Kruse, Goerigk and Grimme noted, we don’t expect this to happen anytime soon.

In this experiment you will deal with four more organic reactions commonly found in textbooks:

4a: the Diels–Alder reaction between ethene and butadiene to give cyclohexene, ΔEref = –45.40 kcal/mol.
4b: the isomerization of n-hexane to neohexane (2,2-dimethylbutane), ΔEref = –2.49 kcal/mol.

4d: the formation of the methanol dimer, held together by a hydrogen bond, ΔEref = –5.81 kcal/mol.

title: Experiment 2: Jacob’s Ladder
text:
Background
The design of a computational experiment starts with the chemical problem you want to study. Next you read the published literature (Goerigk et al. 2017; Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2017; Yu et al. 2015; Yu, He, and Truhlar 2016; Yu, He, Li, et al. 2016; Mehta et al. 2018; Najibi and Goerigk 2018; Rappoport et al. 2009; Cramer and Truhlar 2009) to identify the best-performing method for that problem. Only after this bibliographical research do you start submitting calculations and analyzing results. The next decision in setting up a good computational experiment is the choice of an exchange–correlation (xc) functional and a basis set. We use the term method for a specific combination of xc functional and basis set.
Choosing a good method is not easy, which is why you should rely on suggestions from experts in the field (Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2016, 2017; Goerigk et al. 2017; Yu et al. 2015; Yu, He, and Truhlar 2016; Yu, He, Li, et al. 2016; Mehta et al. 2018; Najibi and Goerigk 2018; Rappoport et al. 2009; Cramer and Truhlar 2009; Goerigk and Mehta 2019; Peverati and Truhlar 2014; Yu, Li, et al. 2016). The functionals used in this lab were chosen for teaching purposes, and we are not implicitly encouraging their use in a general research context. For good reviews of DFT, read Mardirossian and Head-Gordon (2017), Goerigk and Mehta (2019), Peverati and Truhlar (2014) or Yu, Li, et al. (2016).
Before starting the experiments, you should know the most common acronyms in the DFT literature. In particular, you should be familiar with the jargon of the “Jacob’s ladder of density functional approximations”, introduced by Perdew and Schmidt in 2001 (Perdew and Schmidt 2001). The local spin-density approximation (LSDA), the generalized gradient approximation (GGA), meta-GGA (mGGA), and hybrid and double-hybrid functionals should not be new to you. If they are, review them in Koch and Holthausen (2001) or in the reviews above before moving on.

title: Experiment 1: Basis Set Incompleteness Error
text:
Background



The reaction studied in this experiment: dissociation of the HCl dimer.


There are many different “families” of basis sets (Jensen 2013; Nagy and Jensen 2017), developed over the past sixty years by different computational chemists. Head-Gordon and co-workers (Witte et al. 2016) found that the most cost-effective basis sets for DFT belong to the Ahlrichs family (Weigend and Ahlrichs 2005). In this experiment you will analyze how they perform for the dissociation of the HCl dimer, taken from the NCCE30 subset (Peverati and Truhlar 2014; Marshall et al. 2011; Vydrov and Van Voorhis 2012; Lange and Lane 2011; McMahon and Lane 2011) of the Minnesota 2015B database (Yu et al. 2016). The reference energy for this dissociation is 2.01 kcal/mol.
You will calculate the dissociation energy with three functionals, B3LYP (Vosko et al. 1980; Becke 1988, 1993; Lee et al. 1988; Stephens et al. 1994), PBE (Perdew et al. 1996) and ωB97M-V (Vydrov and Van Voorhis 2010; Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2016), and with the Hartree–Fock (HF) method (Hartree 1928b, 1928a; Fock 1930; Slater 1930). You will use two families of basis sets:

the Ahlrichs def2-SVP, def2-TZVP and def2-QZVP basis sets (Weigend and Ahlrichs 2005);
the Dunning correlation-consistent basis sets (Dunning 1989; Woon and Dunning 1993, 1994; Wilson et al. 1999; Koput and Peterson 2002; Balabanov and Peterson 2005; Prascher et al. 2011), written cc-pVnZ, where “cc” means correlation consistent and n is D for double-ζ, T for triple-ζ or Q for quadruple-ζ.

For each method/basis combination, compute the reaction energy and its error with respect to the reference.
\[
\Delta E = 2\,E(\mathrm{HCl}) - E\big((\mathrm{HCl})_2\big)
\]
\[
\varepsilon = \Delta E_\text{comp} - \Delta E_\text{ref}
\]

TipTip



When performing calculations, errors arise from different sources. Each basis set carries an error because it is a truncated expansion. This is the basis set incompleteness error (BSIE; computational chemists love acronyms). To minimize its impact, run calculations with the largest basis set you can afford. Put differently, you want the error from the basis set to be small, so that the error from the exchange–correlation functional is always the dominant one.

Background

In Experiment 4 we found that the -D4 dispersion correction can improve reaction energies. Unfortunately, -D4, like every other scheme designed to account for dispersion, is not a universal fix for more complicated problems.
In this last experiment on functionals, you will deal with four reactions:

5a: ethene + ozone → the first intermediate (primary ozonide) of ozonolysis, as found in many textbooks. ΔEref = –58.7 kcal/mol.
5b: homolytic dissociation of CaO into calcium and oxygen atoms. ΔEref = 96.15 kcal/mol.
5c: total atomization of sulfuric acid, H2SO4 → S + 4 O + 2 H. ΔEref = 602.18 kcal/mol.
5d: conversion of ozone into molecular oxygen, 2 O3 → 3 O2. ΔEref = –67.60 kcal/mol.

title: Experiment 5: Difficult Cases for DFT
text:
Questions

Loading the questions…







TipTip



The reactions in these experiments appear in organic chemistry textbooks and involve very simple molecules. Yet even in these conceptually simple cases the results are unpredictable, and different functionals behave in different ways. When a functional fails, it is not a failure of DFT as a whole but of the approximation in use. DFT is exact in principle, but in practice we rely on approximations to the exact theory, and our results are only as good as those approximations (the xc functionals).

title: Experiment 5: Difficult Cases for DFT
text:
Practice comment
The “easy” reactions (Experiment 3). You may have noticed that almost all functionals give good results for the first group. For each reaction we compare electronic energies of very similar molecules: only the conformation, or for pent-2-ene the configuration, changes. The electron density barely changes, so even a functional that gets the density badly wrong in some regions can still give good results, as long as it describes the change consistently. Errors in regions that don’t change cancel when you take products minus reactants. This is known as cancellation of errors. Error cancellation is hard to generalize, though: we cannot say that rotations around single bonds, conformational changes or cis–trans isomerizations are always easy to compute. There is no way to know in advance whether a reaction is easy, medium or hard. Before starting a computational study, analyze in detail the database subsets that contain molecules or properties close to the ones you want to study.
The “medium” reactions (Experiment 4). Here we need a functional that gets the electron density right. Reactants and products are generally very different, so we can’t rely on the error cancellation that helped in the simpler cases. In the Diels–Alder reaction, for example, two fragments combine into a larger molecule. The same holds for isomerizations, which are very difficult for DFT. The other two reactions involve dimers held together by noncovalent interactions. In the 1990s it was recognized that many xc functionals fail to describe bonding in the van der Waals region (Kristyán and Pulay 1994; Hobza et al. 1995; Allen and Tozer 2002), and in 2012 correctly modeling van der Waals interactions was still listed as a challenge for DFT (Cohen et al. 2012). The problem has been tackled many times (Grimme et al. 2011; Vydrov and Van Voorhis 2010; Grimme 2006b; Caldeweyher et al. 2017, 2019; Dion et al. 2004; Lee et al. 2010). The two most used corrections today are the D corrections of Grimme, Goerigk and co-workers (Grimme 2006b; Grimme et al. 2011; Caldeweyher et al. 2017, 2019) and the VV10 nonlocal functional of Vydrov and Van Voorhis (Vydrov and Van Voorhis 2010). As you may have noticed, adding the -D4 correction to B3LYP and PBE improved their results. Using -D4 whenever possible is a good idea, especially for geometry optimizations (Kruse et al. 2012), but it can sometimes overcorrect. B97M-V and ωB97M-V include VV10 nonlocal correlation, and they are among the best-performing functionals overall. Dispersion corrections for the Minnesota functionals have also been proposed (Goerigk et al. 2017; Goerigk and Grimme 2011; Goerigk 2015), but since those functionals were parametrized on van der Waals complexes too, in principle they don’t need them.
The “hard” reactions (Experiment 5). This group gave the worst results. No functional performs satisfactorily, apart from occasional exceptions: MN15 does well for CaO because that molecule was in its training set, i.e. MN15 was parametrized on the database that contains it. Yet these reactions don’t look complicated chemically; the two largest molecules have only five atoms heavier than hydrogen. This is why we can’t run calculations blindly. Always seek expert advice when different functionals give wildly different results. In an editorial in Organometallics (Hopmann 2019), Kathrin Hopmann discusses what makes a computational paper interesting and advises: “Do not use DFT for mechanisms it cannot handle.” That sums up the take-home message of Experiments 3–5. Every functional published over the past 40 years has strengths and weaknesses (Becke 2014), and much of the effort in functional development has gone into broadening the former and narrowing the latter. As a result, xc functionals are improving statistically: on average, modern functionals give better results than older ones. But it is always up to the researcher to use judgment when choosing among them.

title: Experiment 7: Integration Grids
text:
Background
This experiment looks at a subtle issue that can affect the results of any exchange–correlation functional. Kohn–Sham (KS) DFT (Hohenberg and Kohn 1964; Kohn and Sham 1965) needs a real-space grid to evaluate the exchange–correlation integrals. Most programs build it with an algorithm Becke introduced in 1988 (Becke 1988a): the integrals become weighted sums over a finite number of points arranged on spheres around each atom. A grid’s “density” is described by its number of radial shells and angular points per shell; (75,302), for example, means 75 radial shells with 302 points each. The choice of grid can change the results significantly, as Wheeler and Houk showed for the M06 family (Wheeler and Houk 2010; Zhao and Truhlar 2008) and Mardirossian and Head-Gordon for two generations of Minnesota functionals (Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2016b, 2013). They also point out that meta-GGA functionals usually need finer grids than GGAs.
Choosing the grid is often overlooked, and many practitioners are unaware of the issue. Relying on a program’s defaults is not a good idea, even though some programs pick the grid according to the functional (Q-Chem, Inc., n.d.). In this experiment you will study the dissociation curve of the argon dimer. The geometries come from the RG10 subset (Tang and Toennies 2003) of the MGCDB84 database (Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2017), with the Ar–Ar distance between 3.0 and 6.0 Å. The interaction energy at each distance is
\[
\Delta E(r) = E\big(\mathrm{Ar}_2(r)\big) - 2\,E(\mathrm{Ar}).

Background
This experiment analyzes two bond dissociation reactions from the Minnesota 2015B database (Yu, He, Li, et al. 2016), one from the SR-MGN-BE107 subset (Peverati and Truhlar 2014, 2011; Zhao et al. 2006) and one from the SR-TM-BE17 subset (Peverati and Truhlar 2014, 2012; Zhang et al. 2013; Averkiev et al. 2010; Xu et al. 2015). title: Experiment 9: Comparison with Experimental Results
text:
Practice comment
Bond dissociation energies are everywhere in benchmark databases (Goerigk et al. 2017; Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2017; Yu et al. 2015; Yu, He, and Truhlar 2016; Yu, He, Li, et al. 2016) because xc functionals must describe them correctly. Even simple reactions can be tricky. Breaking the C–O bond is easy in principle, but it produces two radicals, which are hard for theoretical methods (remember that KS-DFT, like HF, is in principle a single-determinant theory) (Hait et al. 2019). For FeCl, the heavier element complicates things further. There is also no simple way to compare a computed result with an experimental one, as Truhlar and co-workers explain (Zhang et al. 2013; Xu et al. 2015): going from the experimental value to a purely electronic one requires several corrections (zero-point energy, thermal contributions, spin–orbit coupling, …). That is why comparing computed and experimental values directly is discouraged unless you get help from a theoretician.
The atomization energies are one more example of why you should rely on modern functionals. A functional must describe not only the molecule but also the atoms, which are a completely different chemical species. HF lacks electron correlation, so it describes atoms very poorly and gives large errors. All density functional approximations include electron correlation in some approximate way (He et al. 2000; Cremer 2001; Polo et al. 2002; Mok et al. 1996; Handy and Cohen 2001), so they do better for atoms. Even so, we again advise non-experts to seek help from a theoretician in such cases.

text:
Step 1 · Get the geometry
Download 37_HCl_NCCE30.xyz from the molecule gallery of Experiment 1. Open it in a text editor and you’ll see the format:

In this lab we always put the charge and the spin multiplicity (2S+1) there, so you never have to guess them: 1 = singlet (all electrons paired), 2 = doublet (one unpaired electron, e.g. a radical or an H atom), 3 = triplet (e.g. O₂ or the O atom), and so on.

title: Reading a Q-Chem output
section: Sanity checks before you trust a number
text:
Sanity checks before you trust a number

Did the job finish? The last lines should say “Thank you very much for using Q-Chem. Have a nice day.” If they don’t, the job crashed or ran out of time.
Did the SCF converge? Look for Convergence criterion met. If you see a warning that the SCF failed to converge, the energy is meaningless.
Right charge and multiplicity? Near the top, Q-Chem repeats the $molecule section. A triplet O atom run as a singlet gives a perfectly converged, perfectly wrong energy.
Right method and basis? The $rem section is echoed at the top as well. One typo (e.g. def2-QZVP instead of def2-SVP) changes everything.
Do the significant figures look sensible? Copy all the digits Q-Chem prints. Reaction energies are small differences between big numbers, so rounding total energies to 4 decimals adds errors of up to 0.03 kcal/mol.







TipWall time vs CPU time



Wall time is what you’d measure with a stopwatch; CPU time adds up the time of every processor core used. On a multi-core server CPU time is larger. In this lab we always compare wall times, and only between jobs run on the same server.

title: Units, reaction energies and errors
text:
Q-Chem gives total electronic energies in hartree (Eh), the atomic unit of energy. For any reaction, the reaction energy is a single sum over all species i taking part in it:
\[
\Delta E = \sum_i \nu_i\,E_i
\]
where Ei is the total energy of species i and νi is its stoichiometric coefficient.






ImportantSign convention: the coefficients carry their own sign



Each stoichiometric coefficient includes its sign: νi > 0 for products and νi < 0 for reactants. With this convention you never write “products minus reactants” separately. The minus sign is already inside the reactants’ coefficients, so ΔE is always just Σ νi Ei.


For example, for 2 O3 → 3 O2 the coefficients are ν(O3) = −2 and ν(O2) = +3, so
\[
\Delta E = (+3)\,E(\mathrm{O_2}) + (-2)\,E(\mathrm{O_3}).
\]
The same convention is used throughout this site: the results table checks your ΔE with exactly this sum.
Then convert to kcal/mol:
\[
1\ E_\text{h} = 627.5095\ \text{kcal/mol}.
\]






TipWorked example



For 2 O3 → 3 O2 (ν = +3 for O2, −2 for O3): ΔE = (+3) E(O2) + (−2) E(O3). If E(O2) = −150.300000 Eh and E(O3) = −225.350000 Eh (made-up numbers), then ΔE = −450.900000 + 450.700000 = −0.200000 Eh = −125.50 kcal/mol.


Keep all the digits of the total energies until the very end. Total energies are hundreds of hartree, while reaction energies are often a few kcal/mol (thousandths of a hartree).

title: Units, reaction energies and errors
text:
Errors
For each method we compare the computed reaction energy with a high-level reference value:

Signed error: ε = ΔEcomp − ΔEref. Positive means the method overestimates the reaction energy.
Absolute error: |ε|. It tells you how far off the method is, regardless of direction.

Over a set of N reactions:
\[
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_k \varepsilon_k
\]
\[
\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_k |\varepsilon_k|
\]
The mean signed error (MSE) reveals systematic bias: does the method always overshoot? The mean absolute error (MAE) measures overall accuracy. A method can have a small MSE but a large MAE, with big errors in both directions that cancel on average. That is why we look at both.






NoteChemical accuracy



An error of about 1 kcal/mol is traditionally called “chemical accuracy”: roughly the precision needed to predict reaction rates and equilibria in a useful way. Keep it in mind as a yardstick when you judge your results.

title: Units, reaction energies and errors
section: How the website checks your arithmetic
text:
How the website checks your arithmetic
When you enter a reaction energy, the page recomputes it from the total energies you entered and compares the two (allowing for rounding). Green means they agree; red means something is off (sign, stoichiometry, or unit conversion). The page never shows you the correct value. It only tells you whether your own numbers are consistent.

title: Lecture 2 · Approximating the wave function: basis sets
Lecture 2 · Approximating the wave function: basis sets
text:
1 Molecular orbitals from basis functions

1.1 The LCAO expansion
Lecture 1 ended with the first of the two approximations of every calculation: the orbitals are unknown functions of three coordinates, and a computer cannot store an arbitrary function. The solution is to write each molecular orbital \(\phi_i\) as a linear combination of a finite number \(K\) of known functions \(\chi_\mu\), the basis functions:
\[
\phi_i(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{\mu=1}^{K} c_{\mu i}\, \chi_\mu(\mathbf{r}) .
\tag{1}\]
The basis functions are fixed in advance; only the coefficients \(c_{\mu i}\) are optimized. In P-Chem 2 you met this as LCAO, the linear combination of atomic orbitals: for H₂⁺, one 1s function on each proton; for water, a 1s, 2s and three 2p functions on oxygen plus one 1s on each hydrogen, seven functions in total. Modern basis functions are not atomic orbitals in the strict sense (they are not eigenfunctions of any atom), but they are still centered on the atoms and look like atomic orbitals, so the name has stuck.
With Equation 1, the hard problem of finding unknown functions becomes the much easier problem of finding unknown numbers: a \(K \times K\) matrix of coefficients. In Hartree–Fock and Kohn–Sham DFT this leads to a matrix eigenvalue equation, the Roothaan–Hall equation \(\mathbf{FC} = \mathbf{SC}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\), which you will meet in Lecture 4. Here \(\mathbf{S}\) is the overlap matrix, \(S_{\mu\nu} = \int \chi_\mu^* \chi_\nu \, d\mathbf{r}\). Basis functions on different atoms overlap, so \(\mathbf{S}\) is not the identity matrix; §13.2 of the P-Chem 2 textbook shows it for water.
\(K\) basis functions give exactly \(K\) molecular orbitals. Of these, \(N/2\) are occupied in a closed-shell molecule with \(N\) electrons; the rest are virtual (unoccupied) orbitals. The number of basis functions \(K\) is printed in every Q-Chem output and is one of the four numbers you record in Experiment 1.


1.2 The variational principle and the CBS limit
If the set \(\{\chi_\mu\}\) were complete, any function could be expanded exactly in it, and Equation 1 would be no approximation at all. A complete set is infinite, so any real basis is a truncation. The orbitals can only take the shapes that the chosen functions allow.
The variational principle of Lecture 1 tells us what happens as we enlarge the basis. For Hartree–Fock and for Kohn–Sham DFT with a given functional, the energy is minimized with respect to the coefficients. Adding basis functions enlarges the space of allowed orbitals, so the minimum can only go down or stay the same:
\[
E(\text{basis}_1) \;\geq\; E(\text{basis}_2) \quad \text{if basis}_2 \supseteq \text{basis}_1 .
\]
As the basis grows toward completeness, the energy converges from above to a limit, the complete-basis-set (CBS) limit. The difference between the energy in a finite basis and the CBS energy (with the same method) is the basis-set incompleteness error (BSIE). It is the error that Experiment 1 is designed to measure.






NoteStrictly nested or not?



The inequality is guaranteed only if the bigger basis contains the smaller one. Real basis-set families are re-optimized at each size, so def2-TZVP does not literally contain def2-SVP. In practice the total energy still decreases monotonically along a well-designed family, which is what matters for us. Reaction energies, being differences, do not have to converge monotonically, and Experiment 1 asks you to look at exactly this.

title: Lecture 2 · Approximating the wave function: basis sets
text:
2 Slater-type and Gaussian-type functions
What should the basis functions look like? Two choices dominate the history of quantum chemistry.

2.1 Slater-type orbitals
Slater-type orbitals (STOs) mimic the hydrogen-atom solutions:
\[
\chi^\text{STO}(r,\theta,\varphi) = N\, r^{n-1} e^{-\zeta r}\, Y_\ell^{m}(\theta,\varphi) .
\tag{2}\]
The exponent \(\zeta\) (zeta) sets the size: a large \(\zeta\) gives a tight function close to the nucleus; a small \(\zeta\) gives a diffuse one. STOs have the right physics. They have a cusp at the nucleus (a finite slope at \(r = 0\), as every exact wave function must (Kato 1957)) and an exponential tail at large \(r\), like real bound states (Lecture 1).
Their weakness is computational. A molecular calculation needs huge numbers of integrals over basis functions, the worst being the two-electron integrals
\[
(\mu\nu|\lambda\sigma) = \iint \frac{\chi_\mu(\mathbf{r}_1)\chi_\nu(\mathbf{r}_1)\,\chi_\lambda(\mathbf{r}_2)\chi_\sigma(\mathbf{r}_2)}{|\mathbf{r}_1-\mathbf{r}_2|}\, d\mathbf{r}_1 d\mathbf{r}_2 ,
\tag{3}\]
in which the four functions may sit on four different atoms. For STOs these multicenter integrals have no closed form and must be computed numerically, which is slow.


2.2 Gaussian-type orbitals
In 1950, Boys proposed using Gaussian-type orbitals (GTOs) instead (Boys 1950):
\[
\chi^\text{GTO}(x,y,z) = N\, x^{a} y^{b} z^{c}\, e^{-\alpha r^2}, \qquad \ell = a + b + c .
\tag{4}\]
The sum \(\ell = a + b + c\) sets the angular momentum: \(\ell = 0\) is an s function, \(\ell = 1\) a p function (\(x\), \(y\) or \(z\) in front), \(\ell = 2\) a d function, and so on. The exponent \(\alpha\) plays the role of \(\zeta\).
GTOs have the wrong physics in two places, visible in Figure 2:

No cusp. A Gaussian is flat at the nucleus (\(d\chi/dr = 0\) at \(r = 0\)), and its value there is too small.
Wrong tail. \(e^{-\alpha r^2}\) decays much faster than \(e^{-\zeta r}\). Far from the nucleus, a single Gaussian underestimates the wave function by orders of magnitude.



2.3 The Gaussian product theorem
Why use the wrong functions? Because of one beautiful property. The product of two Gaussians centered on two different points \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) is a single Gaussian centered at a point \(\mathbf{P}\) on the line between them:
\[
e^{-\alpha|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{A}|^2}\, e^{-\beta|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{B}|^2}
= K_{AB}\, e^{-p|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{P}|^2},
\qquad p = \alpha+\beta,\quad
\mathbf{P} = \frac{\alpha\mathbf{A}+\beta\mathbf{B}}{\alpha+\beta},\quad
K_{AB} = e^{-\frac{\alpha\beta}{\alpha+\beta}|\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B}|^2} .
\tag{5}\]
This is the Gaussian product theorem (Figure 1). It collapses every pair of functions in Equation 3 to a single center, so a four-center integral becomes a two-center one, which has an analytic formula. Gaussian integrals are so cheap that it pays to use several Gaussians to imitate one STO. This trade, more functions but much faster integrals, is the reason virtually every molecular quantum-chemistry program, Q-Chem included, uses Gaussian basis functions.






Figure 1: The Gaussian product theorem in one dimension. The product (black) of a Gaussian centered at A (exponent 1.0) and one centered at B (exponent 0.6) is exactly a single Gaussian centered at P, with exponent 1.6 and height reduced by the constant \(K_{AB}\) of Equation 5.





2.4 Contracted Gaussians: STO-3G
A contracted Gaussian is a fixed linear combination of several primitive Gaussians:
\[
\chi_\mu(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{k=1}^{L} d_{k\mu}\, g_k(\alpha_k, \mathbf{r}) .
\tag{6}\]
The exponents \(\alpha_k\) and the contraction coefficients \(d_{k\mu}\) are chosen once, when the basis set is designed, and never change during a calculation. The program optimizes only the coefficients \(c_{\mu i}\) of Equation 1, one per contracted function. Contraction gives functions with a better shape without increasing \(K\).
The simplest example is STO-3G (Hehre et al. 1969): each Slater-type orbital is replaced by a contraction of three primitive Gaussians, fitted to reproduce it as closely as possible. For the hydrogen 1s function, which in STO-3G mimics a Slater function with \(\zeta = 1.24\) (slightly tighter than the free-atom value of 1.0, because a hydrogen in a molecule holds its electron more tightly), the published primitives are:



Table 1: STO-3G contraction for the hydrogen 1s function (coefficients for normalized primitives).

The tight primitive (\(\alpha \approx 3.4\)) builds up the peak near the nucleus; the diffuse one (\(\alpha \approx 0.17\)) supplies the tail. Figure 2 compares the result with the Slater function it imitates and with the best single Gaussian (the one with maximum overlap with the STO, \(\alpha = 0.417\)). The single Gaussian has an overlap of 0.978 with the STO; the three-Gaussian contraction reaches 0.9998. Even so, STO-3G still misses the cusp, and its tail still falls too fast beyond about 5 bohr.






Figure 2: The hydrogen 1s Slater function with \(\zeta = 1.24\) (black), the best single Gaussian (dashed red) and the STO-3G contraction of three Gaussians (blue), using the exponents and coefficients of Table 1. (a) Near the nucleus, the Slater function has a cusp; Gaussians are flat at \(r = 0\). The dotted curves are the three weighted primitives that add up to the STO-3G function. (b) On a logarithmic scale, the Slater function decays as a straight line (\(e^{-\zeta r}\)); Gaussians bend down (\(e^{-\alpha r^2}\)).



The shell composition of a basis set is often written as (primitives)/[contracted functions]. For STO-3G on oxygen, (6s3p)/[2s1p]: six s primitives contracted to two s functions (1s and 2s), and three p primitives contracted to one set of p functions. A “set” of p functions means \(p_x\), \(p_y\) and \(p_z\), so [2s1p] is \(2 + 3 = 5\) basis functions.


2.5 Cartesian and spherical d functions
Equation 4 with \(\ell = 2\) gives six Cartesian d functions: \(x^2\), \(y^2\), \(z^2\), \(xy\), \(xz\), \(yz\) (times the Gaussian). But a true d shell has only five components. The extra one is the combination \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = r^2\), which is spherical: it behaves like an s function. Spherical (or pure) d functions keep only the five real combinations with \(\ell = 2\) (\(d_{z^2}\), \(d_{x^2-y^2}\), \(d_{xy}\), \(d_{xz}\), \(d_{yz}\)). The same happens for higher \(\ell\):

The choice changes \(K\), the energy (slightly) and the cost. Each basis set was designed with one convention in mind: the Pople sets such as 6-31G* were defined with six Cartesian d functions, while the def2 and correlation-consistent sets were designed for spherical functions. Programs have defaults that you can override, so always check the number of basis functions in your output against what you expect. This is one of the checks you will do in Experiment 1.

title: Lecture 2 · Approximating the wave function: basis sets
text:
3 Building better basis sets
A minimal basis such as STO-3G has a fundamental limitation: each occupied atomic orbital gets exactly one function, with a fixed size and shape. In a molecule, orbitals need to change in three ways, and each one is addressed by a different kind of extra function.

3.1 Split valence: letting orbitals change size
The core orbitals (1s on C, N, O; 1s2s2p on Cl) hardly change when atoms form bonds. The valence orbitals change a lot: they expand or contract depending on the bonding partner and on the charge. A split-valence basis gives each valence orbital two or more functions with different exponents, a tight one and a loose one. The variational optimization then chooses the right mixture, effectively tuning the size of the orbital in each direction and in each molecule.
The number of functions per valence orbital is called ζ (“zeta”, from the STO exponent):

minimal (single-ζ): one function per occupied orbital (STO-3G);
double-ζ (DZ): two functions per valence orbital;
triple-ζ (TZ): three;
quadruple-ζ (QZ): four; and so on.

In the Dunning families, ζ is labeled by the cardinal number \(n\) = 2 (D), 3 (T), 4 (Q), 5, 6.






TipWorked example: what does split valence buy?



For oxygen, a minimal basis has 1s, 2s, 2p: \(1 + 1 + 3 = 5\) functions. A split-valence double-ζ basis keeps one core 1s function but doubles the valence: \(1 + 2 + 2\times 3 = 9\) functions (written [3s2p]). Water goes from \(5 + 2 \times 1 = 7\) functions (minimal) to \(9 + 2 \times 2 = 13\) (double-ζ valence on both O and H, no polarization). Splitting the valence nearly doubles the size of the basis, before adding anything else.




3.2 Polarization functions: letting orbitals change shape
An s function is spherical; a p function points along one axis. When an atom sits in a molecule, the electric field of its neighbors distorts its electron cloud: the orbitals need to bend and shift off-center. The way to allow this is to add functions with higher angular momentum than any occupied orbital of the free atom: p functions on hydrogen, d functions on C, N, O and Cl, f functions on top of those, and so on. Mixing a little p into an s function shifts its center of charge; mixing d into p bends it. These are polarization functions.
Polarization functions are essential for almost every property: bond angles (NH₃ is too flat without them), reaction energies, dipole moments and, very importantly for this lab, the weak interactions between molecules. In larger basis sets, they come in several layers: def2-TZVP has 2d1f on oxygen; cc-pVQZ has 3d2f1g.


3.3 Diffuse functions: the far tail
Diffuse functions are extra functions with very small exponents, so they extend far from the nucleus. They are needed whenever electrons spend time far out:

anions, whose extra electron is weakly bound and spread out;
weak intermolecular interactions (hydrogen bonds, dispersion), which depend on the overlap of the outer tails of two molecules;
Rydberg excited states and properties such as polarizabilities.

Diffuse functions are expensive and can cause numerical problems (near-linear dependence of the basis) in larger molecules. Use them when the chemistry needs them.






NoteThree questions, three kinds of functions



Size → more ζ (split valence). Shape → polarization (higher ℓ). Reach → diffuse (small α). A good basis set is balanced: it improves all three together rather than piling up one kind.

text:
4 Pople basis sets
The basis sets developed by John Pople and co-workers in the 1970s and 1980s are the most widely known, and you will see their names in thousands of papers. Their names are a code for how the functions are contracted.



Table 3: Reading a Pople basis-set name. The numbers before “G” describe contractions: the digit before the hyphen is the core, the digits after it are the valence functions.









Name
Meaning




STO-3G

core: 3 primitives in 1 function; valence split in two: 2 primitives + 1 primitive (Binkley et al. 1980)

core: 6 primitives; valence: 3 + 1 (double-ζ) (Ditchfield et al. 1971; Hehre et al. 1972)


6-311G
core: 6; valence: 3 + 1 + 1 (triple-ζ) (Krishnan et al. 1980)


6-31G* = 6-31G(d)
6-31G plus one set of d polarization functions on heavy (non-hydrogen) atoms (Hariharan and Pople 1973; Francl et al. 1982)

as above, plus p functions on hydrogen


6-31+G*

6-31++G**

6-311G**
