TipWorked example: counting functions in 6-31G*



Water. Oxygen in 6-31G: one core 1s function, two 2s functions and two sets of 2p functions, [3s2p] = \(3 + 6 = 9\). The star adds one set of d functions: 6 if Cartesian (as 6-31G* was defined), 5 if spherical. Hydrogen in 6-31G has two s functions and no polarization in 6-31G* (only the second star adds p on H). Total: \(9 + 6 + 2 \times 2 = 19\) (Cartesian d) or 18 (spherical d).
HCl. Chlorine in 6-31G: one 1s, then the 2s2p shell (one s + one p set), then the valence 3s3p split in two (two s + two p sets): [4s3p] = \(4 + 9 = 13\); plus d: 6 or 5. Hydrogen: 2. Total: \(13 + 6 + 2 = 21\) (Cartesian) or 20 (spherical). For comparison, STO-3G gives HCl only 10 functions: [3s2p] = 9 on Cl, 1 on H.


Pople sets were designed for Hartree–Fock in the era of slow computers, and they were extraordinarily successful. Their limitations are well known today: the s and p functions of each valence shell share exponents (to save time, which no longer matters), polarization is added in an ad hoc way, and the sequence 6-31G* → 6-311G** is not designed to converge systematically toward the CBS limit. You should recognize them, and you will meet 6-31G* again in Experiment 6, where its famous partnership with B3LYP gets a closer look. For new work, the families in the next section are better choices.

title: Lecture 2 · Approximating the wave function: basis sets
section: 5 The modern families used in this course
text:
5 The modern families used in this course

5.1 Karlsruhe def2 basis sets
The def2 basis sets of Weigend and Ahlrichs (Weigend and Ahlrichs 2005) (the “Ahlrichs” or “Karlsruhe” family) were designed to give consistent quality across almost the whole periodic table, H to Rn. The names describe the valence quality:

def2-SVP: split valence (double-ζ) plus polarization;
def2-TZVP: triple-ζ valence plus polarization;
def2-QZVP: quadruple-ζ valence plus polarization.

Variants with an extra P (def2-TZVPP, def2-QZVPP) add more polarization, and variants ending in D add diffuse functions. “def2” stands for the second generation of the Karlsruhe default sets. For elements beyond krypton, def2 replaces the inner-core electrons with an effective core potential (ECP): a fixed potential that represents the core and includes the scalar-relativistic effects that matter for heavy atoms. Only the outer electrons are treated explicitly. You will use this in Experiments 8 and 10 for ruthenium and palladium.
The def2 family has been found to be among the most cost-effective choices for DFT (Witte et al. 2016), which is one reason it is the default basis of most experiments in this lab.


5.2 Dunning correlation-consistent basis sets
The correlation-consistent basis sets of Dunning and co-workers are written cc-pVnZ: correlation-consistent polarized valence n-zeta, with \(n\) = D, T, Q, 5, 6 (Dunning 1989; Woon and Dunning 1993). They were built for correlated wave-function methods (MP2, CCSD(T)). The design rule is that functions are added in groups that each recover a similar amount of correlation energy. Going from cc-pVDZ to cc-pVTZ adds one more s, p and d function and the first f function on oxygen, because these contribute comparably. The result is a family that converges systematically toward the CBS limit, so results at several \(n\) can be extrapolated (Section 6.2).
The prefix aug- adds one diffuse function of each angular momentum present (Kendall et al. 1992): aug-cc-pVTZ is the standard choice for anions and weak interactions with correlated methods. (Other prefixes, such as cc-pCVnZ for core correlation, exist but are not used here.)


5.3 Jensen polarization-consistent basis sets
Jensen’s pc-n basis sets (pc-0, pc-1, pc-2, pc-3, pc-4) apply the same systematic idea, but are optimized for Hartree–Fock and DFT instead of correlated methods (Jensen 2001). pc-1 is double-ζ quality. You will use pc-1 in Experiment 6 to compare double-ζ basis sets from different families.


5.4 Counting basis functions
The size of every basis set follows from the shell composition of each atom. With spherical (pure) functions, each shell contributes \(2\ell+1\) functions: s = 1, p = 3, d = 5, f = 7, g = 9.

Both are “triple-ζ”, but they distribute the functions differently. cc-pVTZ gives hydrogen much more polarization (2p1d instead of 1p), because correlated methods need it. def2-TZVP puts more s functions on oxygen. Same label, different size: the name tells you the quality class, not the cost.

Third, hydrogen atoms are cheap at double-ζ but not at quadruple-ζ (30 functions each).

title: Lecture 2 · Approximating the wave function: basis sets
text:
6 Convergence, cost and basis-set errors

6.1 More functions, better results
The central message of this chapter fits in one sentence: in a systematic family, more functions give results that converge toward the CBS limit. Figure 3 (a) sketches the typical behavior of the total energy. The first step, double- to triple-ζ, is large; each further step is smaller.
For Hartree–Fock and DFT, the total energy converges fast, roughly exponentially with the cardinal number (Feller 1992):
\[
E(n) = E_\text{CBS} + A\, e^{-\alpha n} .
\tag{7}\]
The correlation energy of wave-function methods converges much more slowly, as an inverse power (Helgaker et al. 1997; Halkier et al. 1998):
\[
E_\text{corr}(n) = E_\text{corr,CBS} + A\, n^{-3} .
\tag{8}\]
The reason is physical. Near the point where two electrons meet, the exact wave function has a cusp in the inter-electron distance \(r_{12}\), and smooth orbital products converge to it only slowly. HF and DFT have no such cusp to describe, so they converge faster.






Figure 3: (a) Schematic convergence of a variational energy with the cardinal number \(n\) of a systematic basis-set family, toward the CBS limit (Equation 7; the curve is illustrative, not data). (b) Real numbers of basis functions \(K\) for water in the def2 and cc-pVnZ families (Table 4), with the formal \(K^4\) cost relative to the double-ζ basis written above each bar.





6.2 Extrapolation to the CBS limit
Because the convergence is systematic, two or three results at consecutive \(n\) can be fit to Equation 7 or Equation 8 to estimate the CBS limit without ever computing it. For the \(n^{-3}\) form, two points \(m < n\) give
\[
E_\text{CBS} = \frac{n^3 E_n - m^3 E_m}{n^3 - m^3} .
\tag{9}\]






TipWorked example: two-point extrapolation



Suppose (hypothetical numbers) the MP2 correlation energy of a molecule is \(-0.2950\ E_\text{h}\) with cc-pVTZ (\(m = 3\)) and \(-0.3080\ E_\text{h}\) with cc-pVQZ (\(n = 4\)). Then
\[
E_\text{corr,CBS} = \frac{64(-0.3080) - 27(-0.2950)}{64 - 27} = \frac{-19.712 + 7.965}{37} = -0.3175\ E_\text{h} .
\]
The extrapolated value lies 0.0095 \(E_\text{h}\) (6 kcal/mol) below the QZ result: the correlation energy is far from converged even at quadruple-ζ. This is why reference values such as those you compare with in this lab are usually CCSD(T)/CBS estimates.


The optional Colab notebook of Experiment 1 lets you try an extrapolation on the HCl dimer yourself.


6.3 The price: cost grows steeply with K
Better results cost more. The number of two-electron integrals (Equation 3) grows as \(K^4\): with permutational symmetry there are about \(K^4/8\) unique ones. For water, that is about 41,000 with def2-SVP (\(K = 24\)), 430,000 with def2-TZVP (43), and 23 million with def2-QZVP (117). Going from double- to quadruple-ζ multiplies the formal cost by about 565 (Figure 3 b).
This \(K^4\) is the formal scaling of Hartree–Fock and hybrid DFT. In practice, programs do better: integrals between functions far apart are negligible and are skipped (screening), and approximations such as density fitting reduce the work. For small molecules, fixed overheads (starting the program, reading files) also blur the picture. The measured exponent is therefore lower than 4, and it depends on the method and the size of the system. In Experiment 1 you will measure it yourself from your own wall times.






ImportantThe 10-minute limit is a basis-set limit



On the free IQmol server every job must finish in 10 minutes. For the molecules in this lab, the basis set is usually what decides whether a job fits. A one-character typo, such as def2-QZVP instead of def2-SVP, can multiply the cost by hundreds and get your job killed.




6.4 Two basis-set errors: BSIE and BSSE

Basis-set incompleteness error (BSIE). The difference between a result in a finite basis and the CBS limit, with the same method. It affects every calculation. It shrinks as the basis grows, and it is what Experiment 1 measures for a reaction energy.
Basis-set superposition error (BSSE). A specific artifact of incomplete basis sets in systems made of fragments, such as a dimer. In the dimer, each monomer can “borrow” the basis functions centered on its partner to improve its own description, lowering its energy. The isolated monomers have no partner functions to borrow. The dimer is therefore artificially stabilized, and the interaction energy is too large in magnitude. BSSE also vanishes in the CBS limit. The standard correction, the counterpoise method of Boys and Bernardi (Boys and Bernardi 1970), recomputes each monomer in the full dimer basis. We return to BSSE in Lectures 8 and 10.







TipPractical rules of thumb




Double-ζ (def2-SVP, cc-pVDZ) is fine for quick tests and geometries of large systems, but rarely converged for energies.
Triple-ζ (def2-TZVP) is the usual compromise between accuracy and cost for DFT, and it is the default basis of Experiments 3–5 and 9.
Quadruple-ζ is close to the CBS limit for HF and DFT, and expensive.
Add diffuse functions for anions and when weak interactions matter most.
Report the basis set exactly, including stars, plus signs and prefixes: “6-31G” and “6-31G*” are different basis sets.

title: Lecture 2 · Approximating the wave function: basis sets
text:
7 Key points

Molecular orbitals are expanded in a finite set of \(K\) atom-centered basis functions, \(\phi_i = \sum_\mu c_{\mu i}\chi_\mu\). Only the coefficients are optimized.
For HF and DFT, a bigger basis gives a lower (or equal) energy; the limit is the complete-basis-set (CBS) limit, and the difference is the basis-set incompleteness error.
Slater functions have the correct cusp and tail but expensive integrals; Gaussians have neither, but the Gaussian product theorem makes their integrals fast. Contracted Gaussians combine several primitives to imitate one Slater function (STO-3G).
Cartesian d shells have 6 components and spherical ones 5 (f: 10 vs 7). The convention changes \(K\); check it in the output.
Split valence (more ζ) lets orbitals change size; polarization (higher ℓ) lets them change shape; diffuse functions (small α) extend their reach.
Pople names encode contractions (6-31G*, 6-311+G**). Pople sets are historical and not designed to converge systematically.
def2-SVP/TZVP/QZVP cover almost the whole periodic table, with ECPs beyond Kr. cc-pVnZ (n = D, T, Q, 5) converges systematically for correlated methods; aug- adds diffuse functions. pc-n is optimized for DFT.
The number of basis functions follows from the shell composition: for water, 24 (def2-SVP, cc-pVDZ), 43 (def2-TZVP), 58 (cc-pVTZ), 117 (def2-QZVP), 115 (cc-pVQZ).
The formal cost of HF and hybrid DFT grows as \(K^4\); the measured exponent is lower. HF/DFT energies converge roughly exponentially with \(n\); correlation energies as \(n^{-3}\).
BSSE makes complexes artificially too stable in small basis sets; it vanishes at the CBS limit.

title: Lecture 2 · Approximating the wave function: basis sets
text:
8 Study questions

Explain in your own words why the energy cannot increase when functions are added to a basis set (for HF or DFT). Why is this guarantee weaker when comparing def2-SVP and def2-TZVP, and why does it not apply to reaction energies?
List two physical shortcomings of Gaussian functions compared with Slater functions, and the one mathematical property that makes Gaussians the standard anyway.
Using Equation 5, find the center \(P\) and the exponent \(p\) of the product of an s Gaussian with \(\alpha = 2.0\) at \(x = 0\) and one with \(\beta = 0.5\) at \(x = 1.0\) bohr. Which original Gaussian is \(P\) closer to, and why?
What is the difference between a primitive and a contracted Gaussian? In STO-3G, how many primitives and how many contracted functions does a hydrogen atom have? How many coefficients \(c_{\mu i}\) does the SCF optimize for an H atom?
Decode each name: 3-21G, 6-31+G**, 6-311++G(d,p), def2-TZVPP, aug-cc-pVQZ. For each, say whether it has polarization functions on H, and whether it has diffuse functions.
Count the basis functions of HCl in def2-SVP from the shell compositions H [2s1p] and Cl [4s3p1d], with spherical functions. Then predict \(K\) for the HCl dimer. (Check your answer against your first Experiment 1 output.)
Count the basis functions of methane (CH₄) in cc-pVDZ, cc-pVTZ and def2-TZVP. Carbon has the same shell composition as oxygen in Table 4.
A water calculation reports 25 basis functions with 6-31G**. Another program reports 24 for the same basis. Explain the difference.
If the time of a calculation grew exactly as \(K^4\), how much longer would a water job take with def2-QZVP than with def2-TZVP? Give two reasons why the real ratio is smaller.
Why does BSSE make the binding energy of a dimer too large in a small basis set, rather than too small? Why does it disappear at the CBS limit?

title: Lecture 2 · Approximating the wave function: basis sets
text:
9 Further reading

F. Jensen, “Atomic orbital basis sets” (Jensen 2013), and B. Nagy and F. Jensen, “Basis sets in quantum chemistry” (Nagy and Jensen 2017): modern, readable reviews of everything in this chapter.
A. Szabo and N. S. Ostlund, Modern Quantum Chemistry (Szabo and Ostlund 1996), §3.6: the classic derivation of STO-nG and the minimal-basis H₂ calculation.
T. Helgaker, P. Jørgensen and J. Olsen, Molecular Electronic-Structure Theory (Helgaker et al. 2000), chapters 6 and 8: Gaussian functions, basis-set design and convergence in depth.
F. Weigend and R. Ahlrichs (Weigend and Ahlrichs 2005): the original def2 paper, with tables of the shell compositions for every element.
The Basis Set Exchange lists the exponents and coefficients of nearly every published basis set; you can look up any of the sets in Table 4 there.

title: Lecture 4 · Approximating the Hamiltonian I: Hartree–Fock and the SCF
Lecture 4 · Approximating the Hamiltonian I: Hartree–Fock and the SCF
text:
1 Where we are
Every calculation in this course makes two approximations. In Lecture 1 you wrote the electronic Hamiltonian (atomic units, nuclei clamped):
\[
\hat H_{\mathrm{el}} = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\nabla_i^2 \;-\; \sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{A}\frac{Z_A}{|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{R}_A|} \;+\; \sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j>i}^{N}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{r}_j|}.
\tag{1}\]
The three terms are the kinetic energy of the electrons, their attraction to the nuclei, and the electron–electron repulsion. The last term couples every electron to every other, and that is why no analytic solution exists for \(N \geq 2\).
In Lecture 2 you approximated the wave function’s flexibility with a basis set: orbitals are written as a finite sum of basis functions \(\chi_\mu\). That is the first approximation. This lecture and the next two are about the second one: how we approximate the Hamiltonian, or more precisely, how we treat the electron–electron repulsion. Together, the two choices make a model chemistry, written method/basis, such as HF/def2-TZVP or B3LYP/def2-SVP.
Hartree–Fock (HF) is the starting point for everything else. It is a method in its own right (you are running it in Experiment 1), it is the reference for the correlated wave-function methods that produce the benchmark numbers of this lab, and its machinery (orbitals, the Fock matrix, the SCF loop) is reused almost unchanged by density functional theory in Lecture 5.






NoteExperiment 1 check-in



By now you should have submitted your first jobs for Experiment 1. If anything did not work (the server, IQmol, a job that never finished), check the guides on setting up IQmol, your first job and reading the output, and ask in class. We will discuss the results of Experiment 1 in Lecture 7, after everyone has submitted.

title: Lecture 4 · Approximating the Hamiltonian I: Hartree–Fock and the SCF
text:
2 The mean-field idea

2.1 Hartree’s average field
In 1928 Douglas Hartree proposed a simple way out of the many-electron problem (Hartree 1928). Instead of following every electron as it dodges every other electron, let each electron move in the average electrostatic field created by the nuclei and by the charge cloud of all the other electrons. Each electron then obeys its own one-electron Schrödinger equation, with an effective potential that depends on where the other electrons are on average.
This is a mean-field approximation. It replaces the instantaneous repulsion \(1/|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j|\) by an interaction with a smeared-out charge density. The catch is that the average field depends on the orbitals of the other electrons, which are themselves the solutions we are looking for. Hartree solved the problem iteratively: guess the orbitals, compute the field, solve for new orbitals, compute a new field, and repeat until the orbitals that come out produce the same field that went in. He called the result a self-consistent field (SCF). The name survives in every quantum chemistry program, including the “SCF” lines of your Q-Chem outputs.
Hartree wrote the many-electron wave function as a simple product of orbitals, \(\Psi = \varphi_1(\mathbf{r}_1)\varphi_2(\mathbf{r}_2)\cdots\varphi_N(\mathbf{r}_N)\). A product like this is not antisymmetric. It violates the Pauli principle, and it misses an important energy term, as we will see.


2.2 The Slater determinant
In 1930 Fock (Fock 1930) and Slater (Slater 1930) fixed this by using a determinant of spin orbitals instead of a product. A spin orbital \(\phi_i(\mathbf{x})\) is a spatial orbital times a spin function, \(\phi_i(\mathbf{x}) = \varphi_i(\mathbf{r})\,\sigma(\omega)\) with \(\sigma = \alpha\) or \(\beta\), and \(\mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{r},\omega)\) collects the space and spin coordinates of one electron. The Slater determinant is
\[
\Psi(\mathbf{x}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{x}_N) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N!}}
\left|\begin{matrix}
\phi_1(\mathbf{x}_1) & \phi_2(\mathbf{x}_1) & \cdots & \phi_N(\mathbf{x}_1)\\
\phi_1(\mathbf{x}_2) & \phi_2(\mathbf{x}_2) & \cdots & \phi_N(\mathbf{x}_2)\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
\phi_1(\mathbf{x}_N) & \phi_2(\mathbf{x}_N) & \cdots & \phi_N(\mathbf{x}_N)
\end{matrix}\right|.
\tag{2}\]
Swapping two electrons swaps two rows, which changes the sign of the determinant: the wave function is antisymmetric, as the Pauli principle requires. Putting two electrons in the same spin orbital makes two columns equal, and the determinant vanishes: no two electrons can share all their quantum numbers. You met this determinant in Lecture 1 and in P-Chem 2. We will write it compactly as \(\Psi = |\phi_1\phi_2\cdots\phi_N|\).
The Hartree–Fock approximation is a single statement: the wave function is one Slater determinant, and the best determinant is the one with the lowest energy. “Best” comes from the variational principle, \(E[\Psi_{\mathrm{trial}}] \ge E_0\), which you used for basis sets in Lecture 2. Everything else in this chapter follows from that statement.


2.3 The energy of a Slater determinant
Take the expectation value of the Hamiltonian (Equation 1) with a normalized determinant of orthonormal spin orbitals. The algebra is long but standard (see Szabo and Ostlund (1996), chapter 2). The result is short:
\[
E_{\mathrm{HF}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} h_{i} \;+\; \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\left(J_{ij} - K_{ij}\right) \;+\; V_{nn}.
\tag{3}\]
Here \(V_{nn}\) is the constant nuclear repulsion, and the three kinds of integrals are:

the one-electron (core) energy of spin orbital \(i\), its kinetic energy plus its attraction to all nuclei: \[
h_{i} = \int \phi_i^*(\mathbf{x}) \left[-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^2 - \sum_A \frac{Z_A}{|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{R}_A|}\right]\phi_i(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x};
\]
the Coulomb integral, the classical repulsion between the charge clouds \(|\phi_i|^2\) and \(|\phi_j|^2\): \[
J_{ij} = \iint \frac{|\phi_i(\mathbf{x}_1)|^2\,|\phi_j(\mathbf{x}_2)|^2}{r_{12}}\,d\mathbf{x}_1\,d\mathbf{x}_2;
\]
the exchange integral, which has the two orbitals swapped between the electrons on one side: \[
K_{ij} = \iint \frac{\phi_i^*(\mathbf{x}_1)\phi_j(\mathbf{x}_1)\,\phi_j^*(\mathbf{x}_2)\phi_i(\mathbf{x}_2)}{r_{12}}\,d\mathbf{x}_1\,d\mathbf{x}_2.
\]

The first two terms are what you would write for classical charge clouds. The third is new. It comes entirely from the antisymmetry of the determinant: a simple Hartree product gives only \(h\) and \(J\). Because the spin parts must match on both sides of \(K_{ij}\), the exchange integral is zero unless electrons \(i\) and \(j\) have the same spin. Exchange is always positive (\(K_{ij} \ge 0\)), so it always lowers the energy.






NoteExchange has no classical analogue



Exchange is not a new force. It is a correction to the Coulomb repulsion that appears because two electrons with the same spin cannot be at the same place (the determinant vanishes when \(\mathbf{x}_1 = \mathbf{x}_2\)). Around each electron there is a region, the Fermi hole or exchange hole, where same-spin electrons are unlikely to be found. Less overlap means less repulsion, and \(-K_{ij}\) is that energy saving. Nothing in classical electrostatics gives this term. It is a pure consequence of the Pauli principle.








ImportantRemember this: no self-interaction in Hartree–Fock



Look at the double sum in Equation 3. It includes the terms with \(i = j\). The term \(J_{ii}\) is the repulsion of electron \(i\) with its own charge cloud, which is unphysical: an electron does not repel itself. But from the definitions, \(K_{ii} = J_{ii}\), so the two cancel exactly: \(J_{ii} - K_{ii} = 0\). Hartree–Fock is free of self-interaction. Hartree’s original product method was not, and, as you will see in Lecture 5, approximate density functionals are not either. This single fact explains why mixing some Hartree–Fock exchange into a functional helps (Lecture 6).




2.4 The Hartree–Fock equations and the Fock operator
We want the spin orbitals that minimize Equation 3 while staying orthonormal. This is a constrained minimization, done with Lagrange multipliers. After a unitary rotation that makes the multiplier matrix diagonal (the canonical orbitals), the condition for a minimum becomes a set of one-electron eigenvalue equations, the Hartree–Fock equations:
\[
\hat f\,\phi_i = \varepsilon_i\,\phi_i, \qquad i = 1,\ldots,N.
\tag{4}\]
The Fock operator \(\hat f\) is an effective one-electron Hamiltonian:
\[
\hat f(\mathbf{x}_1) = \hat h(\mathbf{x}_1) + \sum_{j=1}^{N}\left[\hat J_j(\mathbf{x}_1) - \hat K_j(\mathbf{x}_1)\right].
\tag{5}\]

\(\hat h = -\tfrac12\nabla^2 - \sum_A Z_A/|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{R}_A|\) is the core Hamiltonian: kinetic energy plus nuclear attraction of one electron.
\(\hat J_j\) is the Coulomb operator: it multiplies the orbital by the electrostatic potential of the charge cloud of electron \(j\), \[
\hat J_j(\mathbf{x}_1)\,\phi_i(\mathbf{x}_1) = \left[\int \frac{|\phi_j(\mathbf{x}_2)|^2}{r_{12}}\,d\mathbf{x}_2\right]\phi_i(\mathbf{x}_1).
\]
\(\hat K_j\) is the exchange operator: it swaps the orbitals inside the integral, \[
\hat K_j(\mathbf{x}_1)\,\phi_i(\mathbf{x}_1) = \left[\int \frac{\phi_j^*(\mathbf{x}_2)\,\phi_i(\mathbf{x}_2)}{r_{12}}\,d\mathbf{x}_2\right]\phi_j(\mathbf{x}_1).
\] \(\hat K_j\) is a nonlocal operator: the result at point \(\mathbf{x}_1\) depends on the value of \(\phi_i\) everywhere in space, not only at \(\mathbf{x}_1\). Keep this in mind. Density functional approximations replace this nonlocal operator by a local potential, and that is the root of several of their errors.

The sum \(\sum_j(\hat J_j - \hat K_j)\) is the Hartree–Fock potential: the average field that each electron feels from all the others. This is the mean-field idea in equation form. The term \(j = i\) is included in the sum, but, as above, its Coulomb and exchange parts cancel when acting on \(\phi_i\).
Each eigenvalue \(\varepsilon_i\) is an orbital energy. It equals \(h_i + \sum_j (J_{ij} - K_{ij})\): the kinetic and nuclear-attraction energy of electron \(i\) plus its average repulsion with all other electrons. Note that the total energy is not the sum of the orbital energies. Summing \(\varepsilon_i\) over all occupied orbitals counts every electron pair twice, so
\[
E_{\mathrm{HF}} = \sum_i \varepsilon_i - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j}\left(J_{ij} - K_{ij}\right) + V_{nn}.
\]
This is exactly the bookkeeping check in §13.2 of P-Chem 2: twice the sum of the occupied orbital energies of water, plus the electron–electron repulsion counted once with the opposite sign, plus the nuclear repulsion, gives back the total energy.


2.5 Closed shells: restricted Hartree–Fock
Most of the molecules in this course have an even number of electrons, all paired. For these closed-shell molecules we let each spatial orbital \(\varphi_a\) hold two electrons, one \(\alpha\) and one \(\beta\). This is restricted Hartree–Fock (RHF). Doing the spin integration once and for all, the Fock operator for the \(N/2\) doubly occupied spatial orbitals becomes
\[
\hat f(\mathbf{r}) = \hat h(\mathbf{r}) + \sum_{a=1}^{N/2}\left[2\hat J_a(\mathbf{r}) - \hat K_a(\mathbf{r})\right],
\tag{6}\]
where the factor 2 counts the two electrons in each orbital, and the exchange term has no factor 2 because exchange acts only between electrons of the same spin. We come back to open shells in Section 3.4.

title: Lecture 4 · Approximating the Hamiltonian I: Hartree–Fock and the SCF
section: 3 The Roothaan–Hall equations and the SCF loop
text:
3 The Roothaan–Hall equations and the SCF loop

3.1 From integro-differential equations to matrices
Equations (Equation 4) are coupled integro-differential equations. For atoms they can be solved numerically on a radial grid, as Hartree did. For molecules this is impractical. In 1951 Roothaan (Roothaan 1951) and, independently, Hall (Hall 1951) used the LCAO idea from Lecture 2: expand each spatial orbital in a finite basis of \(K\) functions,
\[
\varphi_i(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{\mu=1}^{K} c_{\mu i}\,\chi_\mu(\mathbf{r}).
\tag{7}\]
Insert this into \(\hat f\varphi_i = \varepsilon_i\varphi_i\), multiply from the left by \(\chi_\nu^*\) and integrate. The unknown functions become unknown coefficients, and the equations become a matrix problem, the Roothaan–Hall equations:
\[
\mathbf{F}\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{S}\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
\tag{8}\]
All matrices are \(K \times K\):

\(\mathbf{C}\) holds the MO coefficients: column \(i\) is orbital \(\varphi_i\).
\(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) is diagonal, with the orbital energies \(\varepsilon_i\).
\(\mathbf{S}\) is the overlap matrix, \(S_{\mu\nu} = \int \chi_\mu^*\chi_\nu\,d\mathbf{r}\). It is not the identity matrix because basis functions on different atoms overlap (the same point is made in P-Chem 2 §11.3.1). This is why Equation 8 is a generalized eigenvalue problem.
\(\mathbf{F}\) is the Fock matrix, \(F_{\mu\nu} = \int\chi_\mu^*\hat f\chi_\nu\,d\mathbf{r}\). For RHF it is

\[
F_{\mu\nu} = H^{\mathrm{core}}_{\mu\nu} + \sum_{\lambda=1}^{K}\sum_{\sigma=1}^{K} P_{\lambda\sigma}\left[(\mu\nu|\lambda\sigma) - \frac{1}{2}(\mu\lambda|\nu\sigma)\right],
\tag{9}\]
with the core-Hamiltonian matrix \(H^{\mathrm{core}}_{\mu\nu} = \int\chi_\mu^*\hat h\chi_\nu\,d\mathbf{r}\), the two-electron integrals
\[
(\mu\nu|\lambda\sigma) = \iint \frac{\chi_\mu^*(\mathbf{r}_1)\chi_\nu(\mathbf{r}_1)\,\chi_\lambda^*(\mathbf{r}_2)\chi_\sigma(\mathbf{r}_2)}{r_{12}}\,d\mathbf{r}_1\,d\mathbf{r}_2,
\]
and the density matrix
\[
P_{\lambda\sigma} = 2\sum_{a=1}^{N/2} c_{\lambda a}\,c_{\sigma a}^*.
\tag{10}\]
The density matrix is the bridge between orbitals and electron density: \(\rho(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{\lambda\sigma}P_{\lambda\sigma}\chi_\lambda(\mathbf{r})\chi^*_\sigma(\mathbf{r})\). In Equation 9 the first bracket term is the Coulomb part and the second, with the swapped indices, is the exchange part. The notation in P-Chem 2 is slightly different (\(h = K + V\), \(G\) for the two-electron part, \(V_{ijkl}\) for the integrals), but the equation is the same.
Once the equations are solved, the energy is
\[
E_{\mathrm{RHF}} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mu\nu}P_{\nu\mu}\left(H^{\mathrm{core}}_{\mu\nu} + F_{\mu\nu}\right) + V_{nn}.
\tag{11}\]






NoteWhere the cost comes from



There are about \(K^4/8\) unique two-electron integrals \((\mu\nu|\lambda\sigma)\). With 7 basis functions (water in a minimal basis, as in P-Chem 2 §13.2) this is a few hundred. With the 200 or so functions of a medium-sized molecule in def2-TZVP it is about \(2\times 10^8\). Computing and contracting these integrals with \(\mathbf{P}\) is the formal \(K^4\) (often written \(N^4\)) cost of Hartree–Fock that you met in Lecture 2 and are measuring in Experiment 1. In practice programs skip integrals that are negligibly small (screening) or approximate them (density fitting), so the observed scaling is lower.




3.2 Why it must be solved iteratively
Equation 8 looks like an ordinary eigenvalue problem, but it is not linear: the Fock matrix depends on the density matrix (Equation 9), which depends on the coefficients (Equation 10), which are the solution of the equation. We need \(\mathbf{C}\) to build \(\mathbf{F}\), and \(\mathbf{F}\) to find \(\mathbf{C}\). The way out is Hartree’s: iterate until the input and output agree. This is the SCF procedure (Figure 1).






Figure 1: The self-consistent field (SCF) loop used by Hartree–Fock and by Kohn–Sham DFT. Each pass through the loop is one line (“cycle”) of the SCF table in a Q-Chem output.



Step by step:

Input. Geometry, charge, multiplicity and basis set: exactly the $molecule and $rem sections of a Q-Chem input.
One-time work. Compute \(\mathbf{S}\) and \(\mathbf{H}^{\mathrm{core}}\) (cheap), and decide how to handle the two-electron integrals (store them, or recompute them each cycle, which modern programs usually do).
Initial guess. Make a first density matrix \(\mathbf{P}\). A crude choice is to diagonalize \(\mathbf{H}^{\mathrm{core}}\) alone (no electron repulsion at all). A much better one, and the default in Q-Chem, is a superposition of precomputed atomic densities (SAD). A good guess saves cycles and makes it more likely that the SCF lands on the right solution.
Build the Fock matrix from the current \(\mathbf{P}\) with Equation 9. This is the expensive step.
Solve \(\mathbf{FC} = \mathbf{SC}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\). First transform to an orthonormal basis (for example with \(\mathbf{S}^{-1/2}\)), so the problem becomes an ordinary eigenvalue problem \(\mathbf{F}'\mathbf{C}' = \mathbf{C}'\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\). Diagonalize, then transform the coefficients back.
Occupy the \(N/2\) orbitals with the lowest \(\varepsilon_i\) (the aufbau principle), build the new \(\mathbf{P}\) with Equation 10, and compute the energy with Equation 11.
Check convergence. If the new density is (almost) the same as the old one, stop. If not, go back to step 4 with the new density.



3.3 Convergence, DIIS and the SCF table in your output
What does “the same” mean in step 7? At self-consistency the Fock matrix and the density matrix commute in the metric of the overlap matrix:
\[
\mathbf{F}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{S} - \mathbf{S}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0}.
\tag{12}\]
Away from convergence this commutator is not zero, and its size is a natural error measure. Pulay’s DIIS method (direct inversion in the iterative subspace) (Pulay 1980) uses it twice. First, the largest element of the commutator is the DIIS error that Q-Chem prints in the third column of the SCF table. Second, instead of using only the newest Fock matrix, DIIS builds the next one as a linear combination of the Fock matrices from the last several cycles, with coefficients chosen to make the combined error as small as possible. This extrapolation is what makes modern SCF calculations converge in 10–20 cycles instead of hundreds.
Here is what this looks like in a Q-Chem output (see the guide on reading the output):
 ---------------------------------------
  Cycle       Energy         DIIS error
 ---------------------------------------
    1    -920.4153225231      4.31e-02
    2    -920.6017766913      7.45e-03
    ...
   11    -920.6431907518      1.12e-07
   12    -920.6431907520      4.05e-09  Convergence criterion met
 ---------------------------------------
Each line is one pass through Figure 1. The energy goes down and settles. The DIIS error shrinks by orders of magnitude. The job stops when the DIIS error falls below \(10^{-n}\), where \(n\) is the value of SCF_CONVERGENCE in the $rem section. All experiments in this course use SCF_CONVERGENCE 8, a tight threshold: the energy is then converged far beyond the digits you need for a reaction energy, because the energy error is roughly the square of the density error. That is a consequence of the variational principle: at the minimum, first-order errors in the orbitals give only second-order errors in the energy.






WarningWhen the SCF goes wrong



The SCF is a numerical procedure, and it can fail in three ways. Learn to recognize them now. You will meet all three later in the course.

Oscillation. The energy jumps up and down from cycle to cycle and never settles. This happens when two or more orbitals are close in energy near the HOMO–LUMO gap and swap occupation back and forth. Typical for transition-metal compounds and stretched bonds.
Slow convergence. The DIIS error decreases, but very slowly, and the job hits the maximum number of cycles (Q-Chem prints a warning that the SCF failed to converge). The energy of a job that did not converge is meaningless. Never use it.
Convergence to the wrong solution. The SCF converges perfectly, but to a stationary point that is not the lowest-energy solution: an excited configuration, or a saddle point that is a minimum only within the constraints you imposed (for example, RHF for a molecule that wants unpaired electrons). The output looks normal. Only a stability analysis can tell. This is the subject of Lecture 12 and Experiment 8.

Programs have many tools against the first two: better initial guesses, damping, level shifting, and second-order algorithms such as geometric direct minimization. You will not need them for the organic molecules of Experiments 1–7.




3.4 Restricted and unrestricted Hartree–Fock
Molecules with unpaired electrons (radicals, the O and S atoms, triplet states, many transition-metal complexes) cannot use Equation 6, because their \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) electrons are not paired up in the same spatial orbitals. There are two common ways to handle them:

Unrestricted Hartree–Fock (UHF) (Pople and Nesbet 1954) gives the \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) electrons their own sets of spatial orbitals, \(\{\varphi_i^\alpha\}\) and \(\{\varphi_i^\beta\}\). There are two Fock matrices and two density matrices, coupled through the Coulomb term (the \(\alpha\) electrons repel the \(\beta\) electrons and vice versa). In a basis these are the Pople–Nesbet equations, \(\mathbf{F}^\alpha\mathbf{C}^\alpha = \mathbf{S}\mathbf{C}^\alpha\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^\alpha\) and the same for \(\beta\). UHF has more freedom than RHF, so its energy is lower or equal. The price is that the UHF determinant is not, in general, an eigenfunction of \(\hat S^2\): it is contaminated by higher spin states. Q-Chem prints \(\langle \hat S^2\rangle\) for unrestricted jobs so you can check (a pure doublet has \(0.75\), a pure triplet \(2.0\)).
Restricted open-shell Hartree–Fock (ROHF) keeps doubly occupied orbitals for the paired electrons and singly occupied orbitals for the unpaired ones. It gives a pure spin state, at a slightly higher energy than UHF.

In this course, open-shell species are run unrestricted (Q-Chem does this automatically when the multiplicity is larger than 1). The same choice exists in DFT, where we speak of restricted and unrestricted Kohn–Sham. You will use unrestricted calculations for atoms and radicals in Experiment 5 and later.






TipMultiplicity reminder



The multiplicity is \(2S+1\), where \(S\) is the total spin: 1 for a closed shell (singlet), 2 for one unpaired electron (doublet), 3 for two parallel unpaired electrons (triplet). It is the second number on line 2 of every .xyz file of this lab (“charge multiplicity”). A triplet O atom run as a singlet gives a perfectly converged, perfectly wrong energy.

title: Lecture 4 · Approximating the Hamiltonian I: Hartree–Fock and the SCF
text:
4 Orbital energies and Koopmans’ theorem
Diagonalizing the Fock matrix gives \(K\) orbitals, but only the lowest \(N/2\) (for RHF) are occupied. The remaining \(K - N/2\) are virtual (unoccupied) orbitals. The highest occupied one is the HOMO and the lowest unoccupied one the LUMO. The number of virtual orbitals grows with the basis set, while the number of occupied orbitals is fixed by the number of electrons.
Q-Chem prints the orbital energies after the SCF table, under a heading “Orbital Energies (a.u.)”, split into “Occupied” and “Virtual” lists (for unrestricted jobs, separately for \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\)). Occupied orbital energies are negative: these electrons are bound. Their pattern follows chemical intuition: very low core levels (about \(-20.5\) Eh for the O 1s orbital in water), then valence levels between about \(-1.5\) and \(-0.3\) Eh. Compare the minimal-basis water numbers in P-Chem 2 §13.2.
Koopmans’ theorem (Koopmans 1934) gives the occupied orbital energies a physical meaning. If we remove an electron from orbital \(i\) and keep all the other orbitals frozen, the energy of the resulting cation, minus the energy of the neutral molecule, is exactly \(-\varepsilon_i\). So the first ionization energy is approximately
\[
\mathrm{IE} \approx -\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HOMO}}.
\tag{13}\]
Two errors are hidden in this approximation. Orbital relaxation: in the real cation the remaining electrons rearrange to the new field, which lowers the cation energy, so Koopmans’ value is too large. Correlation: the neutral molecule has one more electron pair to correlate than the cation, so including correlation increases the true ionization energy, and Koopmans’ value is too small. The two errors have opposite signs and partly cancel, so Koopmans IEs of closed-shell molecules are often within about 1 eV of experiment. The cancellation is fortunate, not guaranteed. The analogous estimate of the electron affinity from the LUMO, \(\mathrm{EA} \approx -\varepsilon_{\mathrm{LUMO}}\), is much worse, because the two errors now add up.






NoteWorked example: water



An HF calculation on water with a large basis gives \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HOMO}} \approx -0.507\) Eh. Then \(\mathrm{IE} \approx 0.507 \times 27.211 \approx 13.8\) eV. The experimental vertical ionization energy of water is 12.6 eV. Koopmans’ estimate is about 1.2 eV too high, as expected when relaxation wins over correlation. Try it yourself: run water with HF and a triple-ζ basis and look for the last “Occupied” number in the output. Your value will depend slightly on the geometry and basis.








TipWhat the orbital pictures in IQmol show



IQmol can plot any orbital from a Q-Chem job as an isosurface (a surface of constant \(|\varphi_i|\), with two colors for the two signs). These pictures are useful for chemical intuition: the HOMO of ethene is the C=C π orbital, the LUMO is the π*. Keep two things in mind. First, the canonical orbitals of Equation 4 are delocalized over the whole molecule and do not look like Lewis bonds and lone pairs (water’s two “lone pairs” are two quite different orbitals). Any unitary rotation of the occupied orbitals gives the same determinant and the same energy, so localized orbitals are equally valid. Second, the virtual orbitals depend strongly on the basis set, and adding diffuse functions changes them a lot.

title: Lecture 4 · Approximating the Hamiltonian I: Hartree–Fock and the SCF
text:
5 What Hartree–Fock misses: electron correlation

5.1 The correlation energy
The Hartree–Fock wave function is the best single determinant, but it is still only one determinant. In the mean-field picture, each electron sees the average position of the others. Real electrons react to each other’s instantaneous positions: they avoid each other more than the average field suggests. Their motions are correlated. Exchange already keeps same-spin electrons apart (the Fermi hole), but nothing in HF keeps opposite-spin electrons apart.
Löwdin defined the correlation energy as the difference between the exact energy and the Hartree–Fock energy (Löwdin 1955):
\[
E_{\mathrm{corr}} = E_{\mathrm{exact}} - E_{\mathrm{HF}}.
\tag{14}\]
Because of the variational principle, \(E_{\mathrm{corr}}\) is always negative. Two details matter. “Exact” means the exact nonrelativistic Born–Oppenheimer energy. And both energies should be in the same basis set, or, ideally, both at the complete-basis-set (CBS) limit. Otherwise the basis-set error gets mixed into the correlation energy.
How big is it? For the helium atom, \(E_{\mathrm{HF}} = -2.8617\) Eh at the basis-set limit, while the exact energy is \(-2.9037\) Eh. The correlation energy is \(-0.042\) Eh, or \(-26\) kcal/mol: about 1.4% of the total energy. For the water molecule it is roughly \(-0.37\) Eh (about \(-230\) kcal/mol), about 0.5% of the total. As a rule of thumb, the correlation energy is around 1% of the total energy, or very roughly 25 kcal/mol per electron pair.
One percent sounds small. It is not. Chemistry happens in energy differences. A typical reaction energy is 1–100 kcal/mol, and the conformational energies of Experiment 3 are 1–3 kcal/mol. The total energy of a small organic molecule is about 100,000–500,000 kcal/mol. If the correlation energy changed by just 1% between reactants and products, it would shift a reaction energy by a few kcal/mol. When bonds are broken or formed, or when the number of electron pairs changes, the change in correlation energy is much larger than that.






NoteHartree–Fock has no dispersion at all



London dispersion, the attraction between two neutral, nonpolar molecules (two argon atoms, two methane molecules, the stacked layers of graphite), comes from correlated, instantaneous fluctuations of the electron clouds. A mean-field method cannot describe it: in HF each molecule sees only the static average charge of the other. At long range, HF gives no dispersion attraction at all. Weakly bound complexes held together mainly by dispersion are unbound, or far too weakly bound, at the HF level, no matter how large the basis set. Keep this in mind when you look at your Experiment 1 results. Dispersion returns in Lecture 8.




5.2 Dynamic and static correlation
It is useful to split correlation into two kinds, although there is no sharp boundary between them.
Dynamic correlation is the short-range dodging of electrons: each electron creates a small “Coulomb hole” around itself where other electrons, of either spin, are less likely to be. It is present in every molecule with more than one electron. Describing it requires mixing in many determinants, each with a small weight. It converges slowly with the basis set, because the wave function has a cusp where two electrons meet.
Static (nondynamic) correlation appears when one determinant is not even qualitatively right: when two or more electron configurations have nearly the same energy and must be mixed with comparable weights. Typical examples are stretched or breaking bonds, diradicals, ozone, and many transition-metal compounds.
The textbook example is the dissociation of H₂ (Figure 2). Near the equilibrium distance, one doubly occupied bonding orbital \(\sigma_g\) is a good description, and RHF is qualitatively right. The minimum is a little too shallow, and the difference from the exact curve is the dynamic correlation energy. But as the bond is stretched, the RHF determinant \(|\sigma_g\alpha\,\sigma_g\beta|\) still forces both electrons into the same spatial orbital. Expanded in atomic orbitals, it is 50% covalent (H· + ·H) and 50% ionic (H⁺ + H⁻), at any distance. At infinite separation it should be 100% covalent. The ionic half costs a lot of energy, so the RHF curve rises far above the energy of two H atoms. The exact wave function fixes this by mixing in a second determinant, \(|\sigma_u\alpha\,\sigma_u\beta|\), with a weight that grows until both have equal weight at dissociation. That second determinant is the static correlation.






Figure 2: Dissociation of H₂ computed with a minimal basis set (STO-3G), where the full configuration interaction (full CI) curve is the exact answer within this basis. RHF is good near equilibrium but goes to an energy far above two H atoms. UHF breaks the spin symmetry beyond about 1.2 Å and dissociates correctly, at the cost of a spin-contaminated wave function. The gap between RHF and full CI at the minimum is the dynamic correlation energy; the growing gap at long distance is static correlation. Computed with images/src/l04_l06_figures.py.



UHF also “fixes” the dissociation: past a certain distance (the Coulson–Fischer point) the \(\alpha\) electron localizes on one atom and the \(\beta\) electron on the other, and the energy goes correctly to two H atoms. But the UHF wave function is then a 50/50 mixture of a singlet and a triplet, and the curve has a kink. UHF solutions that are lower than RHF are an example of an instability of the RHF solution: the topic of Lecture 12.






WarningCommon mistake: “a converged SCF means the method is right”



A converged SCF tells you that the equations were solved, not that the approximation behind them is good. RHF for H₂ at 3 Å converges without trouble to a number that is 200 kcal/mol too high. Convergence is about numerics. Accuracy is about the method.

title: Lecture 4 · Approximating the Hamiltonian I: Hartree–Fock and the SCF
text:
6 Ways forward
There are two broad families of methods that go beyond Hartree–Fock.
Correlated wave-function methods keep the HF determinant as a starting point (the reference) and add excited determinants to it.

Møller–Plesset perturbation theory treats the difference between the real Hamiltonian and the sum of Fock operators as a perturbation (Møller and Plesset 1934). Its second-order version, MP2, recovers a large part of the dynamic correlation and describes dispersion, at a cost that scales as \(N^5\).
Coupled-cluster theory includes excitations to all orders in an exponential form. CCSD(T) (singles, doubles and a perturbative estimate of triples) (Raghavachari et al. 1989) is called the “gold standard” of quantum chemistry: for molecules without strong static correlation, CCSD(T) near the CBS limit is typically within about 1 kcal/mol of experiment for reaction energies. Its cost scales as \(N^7\): doubling the size of the molecule makes the calculation about 128 times slower. The reference values of most reactions in this lab come from CCSD(T)/CBS or similar high-level calculations collected in benchmark databases (Goerigk et al. 2017), as you will see in Lecture 7.
Multireference methods (CASSCF, MRCI, CASPT2) start from several determinants and are needed when static correlation is strong. They are outside the scope of this course.

Density functional theory takes a different path. It keeps a one-determinant, mean-field machinery, with the same SCF loop and the same \(N^3\)–\(N^4\) cost as HF, but it changes the Hamiltonian of that machinery so that it includes, approximately, both exchange and correlation. How that is possible, and why the hard part is a single term called the exchange–correlation energy, is the subject of Lecture 5.

title: Lecture 4 · Approximating the Hamiltonian I: Hartree–Fock and the SCF
text:
Key points

Hartree–Fock approximates the wave function by one Slater determinant and finds the best one with the variational principle. Each electron moves in the average field of the others.
The HF energy contains one-electron terms, classical Coulomb terms \(J_{ij}\), and exchange terms \(K_{ij}\) between same-spin electrons. Exchange comes from antisymmetry and has no classical analogue.
Because \(J_{ii} = K_{ii}\), HF is free of self-interaction. Approximate density functionals are not.
The Fock operator is \(\hat f = \hat h + \sum_j(\hat J_j - \hat K_j)\). In a basis, the HF equations become the Roothaan–Hall equations \(\mathbf{FC} = \mathbf{SC}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\).
\(\mathbf{F}\) depends on its own solution through the density matrix, so the equations are solved iteratively (the SCF loop). DIIS accelerates the loop, and the DIIS error in the output measures how far from self-consistency you are. SCF_CONVERGENCE 8 means a DIIS error below \(10^{-8}\).
The SCF can oscillate, converge slowly, or converge to the wrong solution. A converged SCF is not proof of a correct answer.
RHF pairs electrons in the same spatial orbitals; UHF gives \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) electrons their own orbitals and is used for open shells.
Koopmans’ theorem: \(\mathrm{IE} \approx -\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HOMO}}\), thanks to a partial cancellation of relaxation and correlation errors.
The correlation energy \(E_{\mathrm{exact}} - E_{\mathrm{HF}}\) is about 1% of the total energy but as large as or larger than most reaction energies. It has dynamic and static parts. HF has no dispersion.
Correlated wave-function methods (MP2, CCSD(T)) are accurate but scale as \(N^5\) to \(N^7\). DFT is the cheaper alternative.

title: Lecture 4 · Approximating the Hamiltonian I: Hartree–Fock and the SCF
text:
Study questions

Write the Hartree product and the Slater determinant for a two-electron system. Show that only the determinant changes sign when the two electrons are exchanged, and that it vanishes if both electrons occupy the same spin orbital.
In Equation 3, the double sum runs over all \(i\) and \(j\), including \(i = j\). Why is this harmless in Hartree–Fock? What would go wrong if the exchange term were approximated by something that does not exactly cancel \(J_{ii}\)?
Explain in words why \(K_{ij} = 0\) when electrons \(i\) and \(j\) have opposite spins. What does this imply about how HF treats opposite-spin electrons?
The Roothaan–Hall equations look like an eigenvalue problem, but they must be solved iteratively. Explain why, in two or three sentences, using the words “Fock matrix” and “density matrix”.
In the SCF table of a Q-Chem output, what is printed in the “DIIS error” column, and what does the job need to see there to stop with SCF_CONVERGENCE 8? Why can the energy be converged to more digits than the density?
A colleague’s job printed a final energy, but no “Convergence criterion met” line. Can the energy be used in a reaction energy? Why or why not?
Use Koopmans’ theorem to estimate the ionization energy (in eV) of a molecule with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HOMO}} = -0.40\) Eh. Name the two approximations hidden in this estimate and the direction of each error.
Using Figure 2, explain why RHF fails to dissociate H₂ into two H atoms. What does the exact wave function contain that the RHF wave function lacks? Is this dynamic or static correlation?
The correlation energy of a molecule is “only” about 1% of its total energy. Explain why it is still essential for computing reaction energies, using an order-of-magnitude argument.
Argon dimer is bound by about 0.3 kcal/mol. What would an HF calculation with a very large basis set predict for it, and why?

title: Lecture 6 · Approximating the Hamiltonian III: Jacob’s ladder
Lecture 6 · Approximating the Hamiltonian III: Jacob’s ladder
text:
1 Jacob’s ladder
In Lecture 5 we saw that Kohn–Sham DFT is exact except for one term, the exchange–correlation energy \(E_{xc}[\rho]\), and that the simplest approximation to it, LSDA, overbinds molecules badly. Since the late 1980s, hundreds of better approximations have been proposed. Their names can look like a random collection of letters and numbers: BLYP, PBE0, M06-2X, ωB97M-V, MN15-L. There is order behind them, and the most useful way to see it is a metaphor introduced by John Perdew and Karla Schmidt in 2001 (Perdew and Schmidt 2001; Perdew et al. 2005).
In the Book of Genesis, Jacob dreams of a ladder that connects earth to heaven. In Perdew’s version, the ladder rises from the “Hartree world” (no exchange or correlation at all, as in Hartree’s 1928 method) to the “heaven of chemical accuracy”, meaning errors below about 1 kcal/mol for energy differences. Each rung adds a new ingredient: a new kind of local information that the functional can use (Figure 1).






Figure 1: Perdew’s Jacob’s ladder of density functional approximations. Each rung keeps the ingredients of the rungs below it and adds a new one. Higher rungs are usually more accurate and always more expensive. Examples are typical functionals for each rung.






Table 1: The five rungs of Jacob’s ladder.











Rung
Name
New ingredient
Typical examples




1

2

4

Three facts about the ladder are worth stating clearly.

Each rung includes the lower ones. A GGA still uses the density, a meta-GGA still uses the gradient, a hybrid is built on top of a GGA or a meta-GGA.
Higher is usually better, but not always. A well-designed GGA can beat a poorly designed hybrid for some properties. The ladder ranks ingredients, not individual functionals.
Higher is always more expensive. Rungs 1–3 are semilocal: the energy density at a point depends only on information at that point, and the cost is small. Rung 4 needs the exchange matrix of Hartree–Fock, which is more expensive, and rung 5 needs a correlated wave-function step like MP2.

The rest of this chapter climbs the ladder one rung at a time. Rung 1 (LSDA) was the subject of Lecture 5.

title: Lecture 6 · Approximating the Hamiltonian III: Jacob’s ladder
text:
2 Rung 2: the generalized gradient approximation (GGA)

2.1 The reduced gradient and the enhancement factor
LSDA uses only the value of the density at each point. In a molecule, the density changes rapidly: near the nuclei, in bonds, and in the tails. The natural next ingredient is the gradient of the density, \(\nabla\rho\), which tells the functional how fast the density is changing. The early attempts to add a simple gradient correction (the gradient expansion) made things worse, because the expansion behaves badly where the gradient is large. The solution, developed in the 1980s, was the generalized gradient approximation (GGA): a more flexible function of \(\rho\) and \(\nabla\rho\) that is built to behave well everywhere.
To compare gradients in regions of very different density, GGAs use a dimensionless reduced density gradient:
\[
s(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{|\nabla\rho(\mathbf{r})|}{2\left(3\pi^2\right)^{1/3}\rho(\mathbf{r})^{4/3}}.
\tag{1}\]
\(s = 0\) in the uniform gas. In molecules, \(s\) is small (below about 1) in the valence and bonding regions, and it grows without limit in the exponential tails of the density, far from the nuclei.
Any GGA exchange functional can then be written as the LDA exchange energy density multiplied by an enhancement factor \(F_x(s)\):
\[
E_x^{\mathrm{GGA}}[\rho] = -C_x\int\rho(\mathbf{r})^{4/3}\,F_x\big(s(\mathbf{r})\big)\,d\mathbf{r}, \qquad C_x = \frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{3}{\pi}\right)^{1/3}.
\tag{2}\]
(For spin-polarized systems the same formula is applied to each spin density separately.) \(F_x = 1\) gives back LSDA. Different GGA exchange functionals are simply different choices of \(F_x(s)\). Because \(F_x > 1\), GGAs make the exchange energy more negative than LSDA, which, as we saw for the hydrogen atom in Lecture 5, is what is needed.


2.2 B88 exchange
In 1988 Axel Becke proposed the exchange functional that made DFT popular in chemistry (Becke 1988). In its original form, written for each spin density,
\[
E_x^{\mathrm{B88}} = E_x^{\mathrm{LSDA}} - \beta\sum_\sigma\int\rho_\sigma^{4/3}\,\frac{x_\sigma^2}{1 + 6\beta\,x_\sigma\sinh^{-1}x_\sigma}\,d\mathbf{r}, \qquad x_\sigma = \frac{|\nabla\rho_\sigma|}{\rho_\sigma^{4/3}},
\tag{3}\]
with a single parameter \(\beta = 0.0042\) a.u. Becke chose the form so that the exchange energy density has the correct \(-1/(2r)\) behavior far from an atom, and fitted \(\beta\) to the exact (Hartree–Fock) exchange energies of the noble-gas atoms. B88 is therefore a slightly empirical functional: one parameter, fitted to data. It is the “B” in BLYP, BP86 and B3LYP.


2.3 PBE exchange and the idea of exact constraints
In 1996 Perdew, Burke and Ernzerhof proposed a GGA with a different philosophy (Perdew, Burke, et al. 1996). Instead of fitting to data, they chose the simplest form that satisfies known exact constraints, properties that the exact functional is proven to have. The PBE enhancement factor is
\[
F_x^{\mathrm{PBE}}(s) = 1 + \kappa - \frac{\kappa}{1 + \mu s^2/\kappa}, \qquad \kappa = 0.804, \quad \mu \approx 0.2195.
\tag{4}\]
Each number has a physical origin. \(\mu\) is chosen so that, for small gradients, the gradient correction to exchange cancels that of PBE correlation, to recover the accurate linear response of the uniform gas. \(\kappa\) is chosen so that \(F_x\) never exceeds 1.804, a local version of the Lieb–Oxford bound, a proven lower limit on how negative the exchange–correlation energy can be. PBE is non-empirical: no parameter was fitted to molecular data. This makes it a safe, general-purpose functional for chemistry and especially for solids, where it is the default in many codes.
Figure 2 compares the two enhancement factors. They are almost identical for \(s < 1\), where most of the chemistry happens. They differ in the tails: B88 keeps growing, while PBE levels off toward its bound.






Figure 2: Exchange enhancement factors of B88 and PBE as functions of the reduced gradient \(s\), computed from Equation 3 and Equation 4 for a spin-unpolarized density. LSDA corresponds to \(F_x = 1\). The two GGAs agree closely in the valence region (\(s < 1\)) and differ in the low-density tails. Computed with images/src/l04_l06_figures.py.









NoteWorked example: GGA exchange for the hydrogen atom



In Lecture 5 we evaluated LSDA exchange for the exact density of the hydrogen atom and found \(-0.268\) Eh, against the exact \(-0.3125\) Eh. With the same density, the two GGAs give (computed with the course script):

The gradient correction removes most of the exchange error. The rest is a remaining self-interaction error, which a semilocal functional cannot remove completely.




2.4 GGA correlation and the names of GGA functionals
A GGA functional needs a correlation part too. The common ones are:

LYP (Lee, Yang and Parr, 1988) (Lee et al. 1988), derived from a correlation formula fitted to the helium atom. It is not built on the uniform gas at all, and it gives zero correlation for any one-electron system, as it should.
P86 (Perdew, 1986) (Perdew 1986a, 1986b), an early gradient correction to LSDA correlation.
PW91 (Perdew, Wang and co-workers, 1991–1992) (Perdew et al. 1992), a non-empirical GGA for both exchange and correlation, the predecessor of PBE.
PBE correlation (Perdew, Burke, et al. 1996), the non-empirical partner of PBE exchange.

GGA names usually combine the exchange part and the correlation part: BLYP is B88 exchange + LYP correlation, BP86 is B88 + P86, PBE is PBE exchange + PBE correlation. GGAs reduced the errors of LSDA in atomization energies by a large factor, from tens of kcal/mol to typically 5–10 kcal/mol for small molecules, and gave much better hydrogen bonds and barriers. This is why the 1990s were the decade in which chemists adopted DFT.
A third family of GGAs is built with Becke’s 1997 power-series form (Becke 1997), in which \(F_x\) and the correlation enhancement factors are written as short power series with coefficients fitted to data. Many modern empirical functionals use this form, including the B97 series and the ωB97 family that we will meet below.

title: Lecture 6 · Approximating the Hamiltonian III: Jacob’s ladder
text:
3 Rung 3: meta-GGAs

3.1 The kinetic-energy density
The third rung adds an ingredient that depends on the Kohn–Sham orbitals, but only in a semilocal way: the kinetic-energy density of each spin,
\[
\tau_\sigma(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}^{\mathrm{occ}}\left|\nabla\varphi_{i\sigma}(\mathbf{r})\right|^2.
\tag{5}\]
Integrated over space, \(\tau\) gives the Kohn–Sham kinetic energy \(T_s\) of Lecture 5. Some meta-GGAs use the Laplacian of the density, \(\nabla^2\rho\), instead of or in addition to \(\tau\). Both carry information about how the density is curved, which the gradient alone does not.
Why is \(\tau\) useful? Compare it with the von Weizsäcker kinetic-energy density, \(\tau_W = |\nabla\rho|^2/(8\rho)\), which is the exact kinetic-energy density whenever only one orbital is occupied. The ratio \(\tau_W/\tau\) equals 1 in regions dominated by a single orbital (for example, any one-electron system, or a region dominated by a single electron pair, like a covalent single bond) and is smaller elsewhere. Modern meta-GGAs use a closely related variable, \(\alpha = (\tau - \tau_W)/\tau^{\mathrm{unif}}\), which is

\(\alpha = 0\) in one-orbital regions,
\(\alpha = 1\) in the uniform electron gas,
\(\alpha \gg 1\) in the region between two closed shells that do not bond (for example, between two weakly interacting molecules).

So a meta-GGA can recognize the kind of chemical region it is in, which a GGA cannot. This lets it, for instance, make the correlation energy vanish for any one-electron density (removing the one-electron self-correlation error of LSDA and most GGAs), and treat single bonds, metallic-like regions and weak interactions differently.


3.2 Examples

TPSS (Tao, Perdew, Staroverov and Scuseria, 2003) (Tao et al. 2003), a non-empirical meta-GGA.
SCAN (“strongly constrained and appropriately normed”, 2015) (Sun et al. 2015), a non-empirical meta-GGA that satisfies all 17 exact constraints known to be appropriate for a meta-GGA, and is “normed” to reproduce exactly a few systems (such as the hydrogen atom and the uniform gas). SCAN is accurate but numerically delicate, and needs fine integration grids. Its revision r²SCAN (2020) (Furness et al. 2020) keeps most of its accuracy with much better numerical behavior.
Empirical meta-GGAs, fitted to large databases of reference energies. An example is B97M-rV (Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2015; Mardirossian et al. 2017).

Meta-GGAs cost only a little more than GGAs, because \(\tau\) is computed from the same orbitals that the program already has. They need finer integration grids, though, because \(\tau\) and \(\alpha\) vary rapidly in space and many fitted meta-GGAs have oscillating enhancement factors. You will see this directly in Experiment 7 and in Lecture 11.






Warning“Local” means “no Hartree–Fock exchange”, not “LSDA”



Rungs 1–3 together are called semilocal or simply local functionals: they use only information at each point (density, gradient, \(\tau\)), and no Hartree–Fock exchange. In the Minnesota family, the suffix -L marks such a local functional. The suffix does not tell you whether the functional is a GGA or a meta-GGA: for that, you need to know which ingredients it uses.

title: Lecture 6 · Approximating the Hamiltonian III: Jacob’s ladder
text:
4 Rung 4: hybrid functionals

4.1 Why mix in Hartree–Fock exchange? The adiabatic connection
So far, every functional has been a function of local quantities. The fourth rung adds a completely different ingredient: the occupied orbitals themselves, used to compute exact exchange, the Hartree–Fock exchange energy of Lecture 4 evaluated with the Kohn–Sham orbitals:
\[
E_x^{\mathrm{HF}} = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j}^{\mathrm{occ}}K_{ij}.
\tag{6}\]
Why would that help? A rigorous argument comes from the adiabatic connection. Imagine scaling the electron–electron repulsion by a factor \(\lambda\) that goes from 0 to 1, while adjusting the external potential to keep the density fixed. At \(\lambda = 0\) the electrons do not interact: this is the Kohn–Sham system, and its exchange–correlation energy is pure exchange, exactly \(E_x^{\mathrm{HF}}\) with KS orbitals. At \(\lambda = 1\) we have the real molecule. The exact \(E_{xc}\) is the average of the exchange–correlation energy over this path:
\[
E_{xc} = \int_0^1 W_\lambda\,d\lambda,
\tag{7}\]
where \(W_\lambda\) is the potential-energy part of exchange–correlation at coupling strength \(\lambda\). We know the \(\lambda = 0\) end exactly (\(W_0 = E_x^{\mathrm{HF}}\)). Semilocal functionals are best near the \(\lambda = 1\) end. A simple approximation to the integral therefore mixes the two. Becke tried exactly this in 1993, with a “half-and-half” mixture of HF exchange and LSDA (Becke 1993b). A few months later he proposed a more flexible, fitted version (Becke 1993a), the ancestor of B3LYP.
The chemical argument is simpler. Hartree–Fock is free of self-interaction (Lecture 4), while semilocal functionals are not (Lecture 5). Their errors often have opposite signs: HF underbinds and gives barriers that are too high, semilocal DFT overbinds and gives barriers that are too low. Mixing the two cancels part of both errors.


4.2 Global hybrids: B3LYP and PBE0
A global hybrid uses the same fraction \(a_0\) of HF exchange everywhere in space:
\[
E_{xc}^{\mathrm{hybrid}} = a_0\,E_x^{\mathrm{HF}} + (1 - a_0)\,E_x^{\mathrm{DFA}} + E_c^{\mathrm{DFA}},
\tag{8}\]
where DFA stands for the underlying semilocal density functional approximation (a GGA or a meta-GGA).
B3LYP is the most cited functional in the history of chemistry. Becke’s 1993 three-parameter form (Becke 1993a), with LYP correlation substituted by Stephens and co-workers in 1994 (Stephens et al. 1994), is
\[
E_{xc}^{\mathrm{B3LYP}} = (1 - a_0)\,E_x^{\mathrm{LSDA}} + a_0\,E_x^{\mathrm{HF}} + a_x\,\Delta E_x^{\mathrm{B88}} + (1 - a_c)\,E_c^{\mathrm{VWN}} + a_c\,E_c^{\mathrm{LYP}},
\tag{9}\]
with \(a_0 = 0.20\), \(a_x = 0.72\) and \(a_c = 0.81\). Here \(\Delta E_x^{\mathrm{B88}}\) is the gradient correction part of B88 (Equation 3, minus its LSDA part). So B3LYP contains 20% HF exchange. The three parameters were fitted by Becke to a small set of thermochemical data (with PW91 correlation in his original functional, today called B3PW91), and the same values were kept when LYP replaced PW91. B3LYP is an empirical hybrid GGA. Because different programs use different forms of VWN correlation (Lecture 5), “B3LYP” energies can differ slightly from code to code.
PBE0 (Adamo and Barone 1999; Ernzerhof and Scuseria 1999) is the non-empirical counterpart:
\[
E_{xc}^{\mathrm{PBE0}} = \frac{1}{4}E_x^{\mathrm{HF}} + \frac{3}{4}E_x^{\mathrm{PBE}} + E_c^{\mathrm{PBE}}.
\tag{10}\]
The 25% HF exchange is not fitted. Perdew, Ernzerhof and Burke argued from perturbation theory that 1/4 is a good general choice for molecules (Perdew, Ernzerhof, et al. 1996).
Hybrids built on meta-GGAs are hybrid meta-GGAs. Examples are TPSSh (TPSS with 10% HF exchange) (Staroverov et al. 2003) and several Minnesota functionals: M06-2X (Zhao and Truhlar 2008) has 54% HF exchange (the “2X” stands for doubled HF exchange relative to its parent functional), and MN15 (Yu, He, et al. 2016) has 44%. Notice how much the HF fraction varies between functionals. Fitted functionals designed for main-group thermochemistry and barrier heights tend to use more HF exchange (40–60%), while functionals meant also for transition metals use less, because HF exchange makes the static-correlation problems of Lecture 5 worse.






NoteThe cost of exact exchange



Exact exchange is computed exactly as in Hartree–Fock: the program must build the exchange matrix from the two-electron integrals, which costs more than the Coulomb part and much more than evaluating a semilocal functional on a grid. In practice, a hybrid calculation takes noticeably longer per SCF cycle than a GGA in the same basis. You will measure this in Experiment 3.




4.3 Range-separated hybrids
A global hybrid uses the same fraction of HF exchange for electrons that are close together and for electrons that are far apart. That is a compromise. At short range, semilocal exchange works reasonably well, and its errors partly cancel those of semilocal correlation. At long range, semilocal exchange is qualitatively wrong: the exchange–correlation potential of a semilocal functional decays exponentially far from a molecule, instead of as \(-1/r\). This makes orbital energies, charge-transfer excitations, Rydberg states and stretched bonds poorly described, and leaves residual self-interaction where it hurts most.
Range-separated hybrids use different amounts of HF exchange at different electron–electron distances. They split the Coulomb operator with the error function:
\[
\frac{1}{r_{12}} = \underbrace{\frac{\mathrm{erfc}(\omega r_{12})}{r_{12}}}_{\text{short range}} + \underbrace{\frac{\mathrm{erf}(\omega r_{12})}{r_{12}}}_{\text{long range}},
\tag{11}\]
where \(\mathrm{erf}\) is the error function, \(\mathrm{erfc} = 1 - \mathrm{erf}\), and the range-separation parameter \(\omega\) (in bohr\(^{-1}\)) sets where the switch happens: \(1/\omega\) is roughly the distance at which long range takes over (Figure 3, left). The exchange energy is then written as
\[
E_x = c_{\mathrm{SR}}\,E_x^{\mathrm{HF,SR}} + (1 - c_{\mathrm{SR}})\,E_x^{\mathrm{DFA,SR}} + c_{\mathrm{LR}}\,E_x^{\mathrm{HF,LR}} + (1 - c_{\mathrm{LR}})\,E_x^{\mathrm{DFA,LR}},
\tag{12}\]
where \(c_{\mathrm{SR}}\) and \(c_{\mathrm{LR}}\) are the fractions of HF exchange at short and long range. The effective fraction of HF exchange grows smoothly from \(c_{\mathrm{SR}}\) at \(r_{12} = 0\) to \(c_{\mathrm{LR}}\) at large \(r_{12}\) (Figure 3, right).






Figure 3: Left: the Coulomb interaction \(1/r\) split into a short-range part, \(\mathrm{erfc}(\omega r)/r\), and a long-range part, \(\mathrm{erf}(\omega r)/r\), for \(\omega = 0.3\) bohr\(^{-1}\). Right: the effective fraction of Hartree–Fock exchange as a function of the electron–electron distance for two range-separated hybrids (ωB97M-V with \(\omega = 0.3\) bohr\(^{-1}\), M11 with \(\omega = 0.25\) bohr\(^{-1}\)) and three global hybrids. Computed with images/src/l04_l06_figures.py.



The most common choice in chemistry is a long-range corrected hybrid, with \(c_{\mathrm{LR}} = 1\) (100% HF exchange at long range, which restores the correct \(-1/r\) potential). The idea goes back to Iikura, Tsuneda, Yanai and Hirao (Iikura et al. 2001). Examples:

title: Lecture 6 · Approximating the Hamiltonian III: Jacob’s ladder
text:
5 Rung 5: double hybrids and RPA
The fifth rung uses the virtual (unoccupied) Kohn–Sham orbitals as well. Double hybrids add a fraction of second-order perturbation (MP2-like) correlation, computed from the virtual orbitals, on top of a hybrid. The first widely used one, B2PLYP (Grimme, 2006) (Grimme 2006a), has 53% HF exchange and 27% MP2-like correlation, with B88 and LYP for the rest. The random-phase approximation (RPA) is a different fifth-rung method, which treats correlation through all virtual orbitals and naturally includes dispersion.
Fifth-rung methods are among the most accurate DFT approaches for main-group thermochemistry (Goerigk et al. 2017). The price is MP2-like cost (\(N^5\)) and slow basis-set convergence (like any correlated wave-function method, Lecture 4). We will not use them in the experiments, and there are no double hybrids in Experiment 2.

title: Lecture 6 · Approximating the Hamiltonian III: Jacob’s ladder
section: 6 Two design questions that cut across the ladder
text:
6 Two design questions that cut across the ladder
The rung tells you which ingredients a functional uses. Two other questions are independent of the rung, and you need both to understand a functional’s name and behavior.

6.1 How is dispersion included?
As we saw in Lecture 5, no semilocal functional describes long-range dispersion, and adding HF exchange does not help (HF has no dispersion at all, Lecture 4). There are four possibilities:

Not at all. Many classic functionals, including plain B3LYP, PBE and PBE0, have no long-range dispersion. They underbind dispersion-dominated complexes and get conformational energies of large flexible molecules wrong.
An empirical pairwise correction, -D. Grimme’s corrections add an atom–atom term \(-\sum_{AB} C_6^{AB}/R_{AB}^6\) (plus higher terms), switched off at short range by a damping function, on top of the DFT energy. The history: D2 (2006) (Grimme 2006b), D3 (2010) (Grimme et al. 2010), and the current D4 (2017–2019) (Caldeweyher et al. 2017, 2019), whose \(C_6\) coefficients depend on the atomic partial charges and so on the chemical environment. In this course we always use -D4: B3LYP-D4 is B3LYP plus the D4 correction. The correction costs almost nothing.
A nonlocal correlation functional, -V. Vydrov and Van Voorhis’s VV10 (Vydrov and Van Voorhis 2010) adds a correlation term that depends on the density at two points at once, \(\iint \rho(\mathbf{r})\,\Phi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}')\,\rho(\mathbf{r}')\,d\mathbf{r}\,d\mathbf{r}'\), so it can see two separate molecules. A “-V” at the end of a name (ωB97X-V, ωB97M-V, B97M-V) means VV10; “-rV” means the revised, faster rVV10 (Sabatini et al. 2013), as in B97M-rV. Note that VV10 is a correlation ingredient; it does not change the rung of the functional.
Built into a fitted functional. Highly parametrized functionals such as the Minnesota family were fitted to data that include noncovalent complexes, so they capture medium-range dispersion (at van der Waals contact distances) through their parameters, without any explicit term. At long range they behave like any semilocal functional. In the course data files this is labeled “fitted”.

Dispersion is the topic of Lecture 8, and Experiment 4 compares these options directly.


6.2 Non-empirical or empirical?
The second question is how the parameters were chosen.

Non-empirical (constraint-satisfying) functionals, like PBE, PBE0, TPSS and SCAN, are built to obey exact constraints of the true functional, with no fitting to molecular data (Perdew et al. 2005). Their strength is that they are expected to be reasonable for any system, including systems unlike anything their designers tested.
Empirical (fitted) functionals, like B3LYP (3 parameters), the B97 family, the Minnesota functionals and ωB97M-V, have parameters fitted to databases of reference energies. ωB97M-V was designed by a “combinatorial” search: its authors fitted thousands of candidate forms and kept the one with the best balance between training and test sets (Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2016). Highly parametrized functionals can be very accurate for the kinds of systems they were trained on.

The danger of fitting is overfitting: a functional with many parameters can reproduce its training set very well and still fail for systems unlike those in the training set. A fair test of a functional uses data it was not fitted to. This is not a reason to avoid empirical functionals (several of the best functionals available are empirical), but it is a reason to check what a functional was trained on before trusting a good result. You will meet a concrete case in Experiment 5 and in Lecture 9. In reality the line between the two groups is blurred: many “non-empirical” functionals use exact data for a few simple systems (norms), and most empirical functionals also impose some exact constraints.


6.3 Decoding functional names
There is no universal naming rule, but the following conventions cover most cases:
