M06-2X: Minnesota 2006, with “double” HF exchange (54%). Which rung? The name alone does not say; the paper does (it uses \(\tau\)).
MN15-L: Minnesota 2015, “N” for nonseparable (exchange and correlation are not fitted as separate pieces), “L” for local, so no HF exchange. Whether it is a GGA-type or a meta-GGA-type functional, the name does not say. You need the paper.

The last two examples carry the main message for Experiment 2: the name is a hint, the paper is the answer.

title: Lecture 6 · Approximating the Hamiltonian III: Jacob’s ladder
text:
7 Experiment 2: climbing the ladder yourself
Experiment 2 has no calculations. You will classify 20 functionals into five categories: LSDA, GGA, meta-GGA, hybrid GGA and hybrid meta-GGA (there are no double hybrids). The point is to learn how to find this information for any functional, which is something you will need every time you read a computational paper or choose a method.
A reliable procedure, for each functional:

Does it contain any Hartree–Fock exchange? If yes, it is a hybrid (global or range-separated). Look for a percentage of “exact” or “HF” exchange in the paper or the Q-Chem manual. If no, it is local (rungs 1–3).
Does it use the kinetic-energy density \(\tau\) or the Laplacian \(\nabla^2\rho\)? If yes, it is a meta-GGA (or a hybrid meta-GGA). Look for \(\tau\) in the equations, or for “meta” in the abstract.
Does it use the density gradient? If yes (and not \(\tau\)), it is a GGA. If it uses only the density, it is LSDA.

Note separately, for yourself, whether the functional is range-separated and how it handles dispersion. The form does not ask for these, but you will need them in Experiments 3–5.
Where to look. The best source is the original paper (the references for every functional appear on the pages of Experiments 3–5). Reviews are faster: Mardirossian and Head-Gordon (2017) and Goerigk et al. (2017) classify hundreds of functionals with consistent notation, and Peverati and Truhlar (2014) and Yu, Li, et al. (2016) explain the Minnesota family and the general landscape. The Q-Chem manual lists the functionals available in the program, with their references (Epifanovsky et al. 2021). Avoid unsourced web pages.
Common traps.

A functional named after its parameters or its year tells you nothing about its rung.
“Range-separated” does not imply “hybrid” (see above).
“-V” adds nonlocal correlation, not HF exchange, and does not move a functional up the ladder.
“-L” means no HF exchange, but it does not tell you GGA or meta-GGA.
MN-type (“nonseparable”) functionals are classified, on this simplified ladder, with the GGAs or meta-GGAs of the same ingredients.







ImportantBefore next week: lock your Experiment 3 predictions



Experiment 3 asks you to predict, before running anything, how methods on different rungs will perform on four “easy” organic reactions. Make those predictions with what you learned in Lectures 4–6, and lock them in before you start the calculations. Predictions are graded for being made, not for being right.

title: Lecture 6 · Approximating the Hamiltonian III: Jacob’s ladder
section: 8 The 16 methods of Experiments 3–5 on the ladder
text:
8 The 16 methods of Experiments 3–5 on the ladder
In Experiments 3, 4 and 5 you will run the same 16 methods: fifteen density functionals and Hartree–Fock, all with the def2-TZVP basis. Every chart in those experiments colors the methods by rung. Several of them are also in the Experiment 2 exercise, so place them on the ladder yourself first, using the procedure above. The complete table is in Lecture 7, which you should read after you submit Experiment 2.

title: Lecture 6 · Approximating the Hamiltonian III: Jacob’s ladder
text:
Key points

Jacob’s ladder (Perdew, 2001) orders functionals by their ingredients: LSDA (\(\rho\)), GGA (\(+\nabla\rho\)), meta-GGA (\(+\tau\) or \(\nabla^2\rho\)), hybrid (\(+\) occupied orbitals via HF exchange), double hybrid/RPA (\(+\) virtual orbitals). Higher rungs are usually more accurate and always more expensive.
GGA exchange is LSDA exchange times an enhancement factor \(F_x(s)\) of the reduced gradient \(s\). B88 (1988) has one fitted parameter; PBE (1996) is non-empirical, with parameters fixed by exact constraints.
Meta-GGAs use the kinetic-energy density \(\tau\), which lets them recognize one-orbital regions, uniform-gas-like regions and weak-interaction regions. Examples: TPSS, SCAN, r²SCAN. They need finer grids.
Global hybrids mix a fixed fraction of HF exchange: B3LYP 20%, PBE0 25%, M06-2X 54%, MN15 44%. The adiabatic connection justifies mixing; HF exchange reduces self-interaction error.
Range-separated hybrids split \(1/r_{12}\) with \(\mathrm{erf}(\omega r_{12})\). Long-range corrected hybrids reach 100% HF exchange at long range: ωB97M-V 15% → 100% (\(\omega = 0.3\)), M11 42.8% → 100% (\(\omega = 0.25\)).
Double hybrids (B2PLYP) add MP2-like correlation from virtual orbitals, at MP2-like cost.
Dispersion is independent of the rung: none, -D4, nonlocal VV10 (“-V”, “-rV”), or fitted (medium range only).
Functionals are non-empirical (constraints) or empirical (fitted). Fitted functionals can be excellent, but beware of overfitting and of judging a functional on its own training set.
The name is a hint, the paper is the answer.

title: Lecture 6 · Approximating the Hamiltonian III: Jacob’s ladder
text:
Study questions

List the five rungs of Jacob’s ladder and the ingredient each one adds. Why is each rung more expensive than the one below it?
Calculate the reduced gradient \(s\) for the hydrogen-atom density \(\rho = e^{-2r}/\pi\) as a function of \(r\). (Hint: \(|\nabla\rho| = 2\rho\).) Where is \(s\) small and where is it large? Which part of Figure 2 matters most for the hydrogen atom’s valence region?
B88 and PBE exchange agree closely for \(s < 1\). Why do they still give somewhat different energies for atoms and molecules?
What does the variable \(\alpha = (\tau - \tau_W)/\tau^{\mathrm{unif}}\) tell a meta-GGA? Give its value in a one-electron system and in the uniform gas.
Write the B3LYP and PBE0 formulas. Which parameters were fitted and which were derived? What fraction of HF exchange does each contain?
Using the adiabatic connection, explain in a few sentences why a hybrid functional should contain some but not 100% HF exchange.
Sketch the fraction of HF exchange as a function of electron–electron distance for B3LYP, for ωB97M-V and for a screened hybrid like HSE. Explain why long-range correction restores the correct asymptotic potential.
Decode the names B3PW91, ωB97X-V, PBE-D4 and B97M-rV: what does each part of the name mean? Which of them are hybrids, and which include dispersion, and how?
A colleague says: “M11 is range-separated, so it must be a hybrid; and B97M-V has a V, so it must be better at dispersion than B97M-rV.” Comment on both statements.
Why is overfitting a concern for functionals with many parameters? How would you test whether a fitted functional really is better than a non-empirical one?

title: Lecture 6 · Approximating the Hamiltonian III: Jacob’s ladder
text:
Further reading

Perdew and Schmidt (2001) and Perdew et al. (2005): the original Jacob’s ladder papers, and a clear statement of the constraint-satisfaction philosophy.
Mardirossian and Head-Gordon (2017): a long, careful review of 200 functionals tested on a large database, with a classification of each. The best single reference for Experiment 2.
Goerigk et al. (2017): the GMTKN55 database paper, which also ranks functionals on each rung of the ladder.
Peverati and Truhlar (2014): a review of the quest for a universal density functional, with the history of the Minnesota functionals.
Koch and Holthausen (2001), chapters 6–7: GGAs and hybrids explained for chemists.
Becke (2014): Becke’s personal perspective on fifty years of DFT, from the man behind B88 and B3LYP.

title: Lecture 8 · Dispersion and noncovalent interactions
Lecture 8 · Dispersion and noncovalent interactions
text:
1.1 The “easy” reactions really were easy
In Experiment 3 you computed four small energy differences: two rotational barriers (3a ethane, 2.73 kcal/mol; 3b methanol, 1.01 kcal/mol), a conformational change of butane-1,4-diol that breaks an intramolecular hydrogen bond (3c, 3.29 kcal/mol), and the cis→trans isomerization of pent-2-ene (3d, −1.15 kcal/mol). The 16 methods range from LSDA to hybrid meta-GGAs, plus Hartree–Fock.
What you probably saw on the signed error chart is a sea of very short bars. For 3a, 3b and 3d, nearly every method lands within a few tenths of a kcal/mol of the reference, whatever its rung. The ranking among the best methods changes from reaction to reaction, and the differences between them are often smaller than 0.1–0.2 kcal/mol. Differences that small are close to the uncertainty of the reference values and of your own numerical settings, so they should not be over-interpreted.

1.1.1 Why: error cancellation
The explanation is the one we anticipated in Lecture 7. Each reaction compares two forms of the same molecule. The number of electrons, the bonds, the lone pairs and the core orbitals are identical on both sides. An approximate functional makes errors in describing each of these features, but it makes nearly the same errors in the reactant and in the product. When you compute ΔE = E(product) − E(reactant), those errors cancel. What remains is the error in describing the small change in the density, and that change is small and local.
This is the most powerful idea in practical quantum chemistry. It is also fragile, because it depends on the reaction, not on the method. Nobody can tell in advance, from the reaction type alone, whether a conformational change will be easy. That is why we benchmark.


1.1.2 The usual outliers: butane-1,4-diol, LSDA and HF
Reaction 3c is the one where the sea of short bars breaks up. In conformer B1 the two OH groups form an intramolecular hydrogen bond; in B43 they do not. So 3c measures, roughly, the energy of one hydrogen bond plus some conformational strain. A change in a noncovalent interaction does not cancel.
The two methods that most often stand out are at the two ends of the ladder:

LSDA (SPW92) is known to overbind hydrogen bonds and, more generally, to give too much attraction wherever two densities overlap weakly. The uniform-electron-gas model has no way to tell a weak, stretched interaction from a real bond. For 3c this makes the hydrogen-bonded conformer too stable, so the energy to break the H-bond comes out too large.
Hartree–Fock has no correlation. A hydrogen bond is mostly electrostatics, which HF describes reasonably, but the correlation and dispersion parts are missing, so HF tends to underbind. Its error on 3c has the opposite sign to LSDA’s.

The modern hybrid and meta-GGA functionals usually describe the hydrogen bond well. You may also have noticed that -D4 changed the numbers in Experiment 3 very little. The dispersion energy depends on interatomic distances, and the distances barely change in a rotation or in a cis–trans isomerization, so the -D4 contribution nearly cancels too. In 3c, where the molecule changes shape more, -D4 makes a slightly larger difference.

title: Lecture 8 · Dispersion and noncovalent interactions
text:
1.2 Cost vs accuracy
The cost vs accuracy chart plots the MAE against the time per SCF cycle on a log axis. You probably saw something like this:

SPW92 and the GGAs are the cheapest per cycle. They need only the density and its gradient on the integration grid.
Meta-GGAs cost slightly more: they need τ on the grid too, and are often run on finer grids (Lecture 11).
Hybrids are clearly more expensive per cycle. They need the HF exchange matrix K, built from the four-index two-electron integrals, and that step dominates.
Range-separated hybrids (ωB97M-V, M11) need extra integrals for the long-range exchange, and VV10 (B97M-V, ωB97M-V) adds a double integral over grid points. These are usually the most expensive per cycle.
HF needs K but no grid at all, so it costs about the same as a hybrid.
B3LYP is not special. It costs about the same as B3PW91 and PBE0, because cost is set by the rung (and by the HF exchange), not by the name.

The ideal method sits bottom-left. For Experiment 3, cheap methods are almost as accurate as expensive ones, because error cancellation does most of the work. The ranking will look very different in Experiments 4 and 5. Keep your chart: comparing it with the next two is the real lesson.






WarningCommon mistake: generalizing from easy reactions



“SPW92 was fine for the ethane barrier, so LSDA is good enough” is wrong. Experiment 3 tells you that conformational energies with similar bonding are easy. It says almost nothing about reactions where bonds or noncovalent contacts change.

title: Lecture 8 · Dispersion and noncovalent interactions
Lecture 8 · Dispersion and noncovalent interactions
text:
2.2 The physics of London dispersion

2.2.1 Fluctuating dipoles
Even a perfectly spherical atom, like argon, has an instantaneous dipole moment at every moment, because its electrons move. On average the dipole is zero. But an instantaneous dipole on atom A creates an electric field at atom B, which induces a dipole on B. The two dipoles are aligned so that they attract. The motions of the electrons on A and B become correlated, and the correlation lowers the energy. This is the picture Fritz London gave in 1930 (London 1930): dispersion is an electron correlation effect between two distant regions of space.


2.2.2 A model: two coupled oscillators
The simplest model that captures the physics is the Drude model. Represent each atom by a charge −q bound to a nucleus by a spring of force constant k = mω₀², so that it oscillates with frequency ω₀. The static polarizability of such an oscillator is α = q²/k. Put two of these oscillators a distance R apart, and let the charges move only along the line that joins them (a one-dimensional model). The dipole–dipole interaction between the displacements x₁ and x₂ is
\[
V = -\frac{2q^2 x_1 x_2}{R^3}.
\tag{1}\]
The Hamiltonian of the two coupled oscillators can be separated into two normal modes, x₁ ± x₂, with frequencies
\[
\omega_\pm = \omega_0\sqrt{1 \mp \frac{2\alpha}{R^3}} .
\tag{2}\]
Quantum mechanics says each oscillator keeps a zero-point energy ħω/2 even in its ground state. The total zero-point energy of the pair is (ħ/2)(ω₊ + ω₋). Expanding the square roots for large R with √(1 + x) ≈ 1 + x/2 − x²/8, the first-order terms cancel and the second-order terms do not:
\[
\frac{\hbar}{2}(\omega_+ + \omega_-) \approx \hbar\omega_0 - \frac{\hbar\omega_0}{2}\,\frac{\alpha^2}{R^6}.
\tag{3}\]
The first term is just the energy of two separate oscillators. The second is the interaction:
\[
E_\text{disp} = -\frac{\hbar\omega_0\,\alpha^2}{2R^6} \quad\text{(1D model)}, \qquad
E_\text{disp} = -\frac{3\hbar\omega_0\,\alpha^2}{4R^6} \quad\text{(3D model)}.
\tag{4}\]
Three lessons come out of this simple calculation.

Dispersion is always attractive.
It decays as R⁻⁶. We write Edisp = −C₆/R⁶, with a dispersion coefficient C₆.
It is a quantum effect: it comes from the change in zero-point energy. Classical static charge distributions with no dipole would not interact at all.

The model also tells us what C₆ depends on: the polarizability α (how easily the electron cloud is distorted) and a characteristic excitation energy ħω₀. London approximated ħω₀ by the ionization energy I, which gives the famous London formula for two different atoms:
\[
C_6^{AB} \approx \frac{3}{2}\,\frac{I_A I_B}{I_A + I_B}\,\alpha_A\alpha_B .
\tag{5}\]
The exact expression, due to Casimir and Polder (Casimir and Polder 1948), integrates the frequency-dependent polarizabilities at imaginary frequency:
\[
C_6^{AB} = \frac{3}{\pi}\int_0^\infty \alpha_A(i\omega)\,\alpha_B(i\omega)\,d\omega .
\tag{6}\]
Large, soft, polarizable atoms (Xe, I, S) have large C₆; small, hard ones (He, Ne, H) have small C₆. That is why boiling points rise down a group, and why long alkanes are liquids or solids while methane is a gas.






TipWorked example: the size of dispersion between two argon atoms



The C₆ coefficient of the argon dimer is about 64.3 Eh a₀⁶. Convert it to kcal/mol Å⁶ using 1 Eh = 627.5095 kcal/mol and 1 a₀ = 0.529177 Å, so 1 a₀⁶ = 0.529177⁶ Å⁶ = 0.021958 Å⁶:
\[
C_6 = 64.3 \times 627.5095 \times 0.021958\ \text{kcal mol}^{-1}\,\text{Å}^6 = 886\ \text{kcal mol}^{-1}\,\text{Å}^6 .
\]
At the equilibrium distance of Ar₂, R ≈ 3.76 Å, R⁶ = 3.76⁶ = 2.83 × 10³ Å⁶, and
\[
-\frac{C_6}{R^6} = -\frac{886}{2.83\times 10^{3}} = -0.31\ \text{kcal/mol}.
\]
The full well depth of Ar₂ is about 0.28 kcal/mol (Experiment 7 studies this curve). The dispersion attraction is slightly larger than the well depth, because Pauli repulsion already cancels part of it at that distance.


Figure 1 (a) shows a Lennard-Jones model of a rare-gas dimer. The minimum arises from the balance of a steep repulsion and the R⁻⁶ attraction. Without the attraction there is no minimum at all: the curve is purely repulsive.






Figure 1: (a) Lennard-Jones model of Ar₂ (ε = 0.285 kcal/mol, σ = 3.35 Å), split into its repulsive R⁻¹² and attractive R⁻⁶ terms. (b) The dispersion energy −C₆/R⁶ for Ar–Ar (C₆ = 64.3 Eh a₀⁶) without damping, with rational (Becke–Johnson-type) damping and with zero (Fermi-type) damping. The damping radius is illustrative, not the -D4 value. All curves are analytic models.

title: Lecture 8 · Dispersion and noncovalent interactions
section: 2.3 Why semilocal DFT and Hartree–Fock miss dispersion
text:
2.3 Why semilocal DFT and Hartree–Fock miss dispersion

2.3.1 Semilocal functionals
A GGA writes the exchange–correlation energy as a single integral over space:
\[
E_\text{xc}^\text{GGA}[\rho] = \int f\big(\rho(\mathbf r), \nabla\rho(\mathbf r)\big)\,d\mathbf r .
\tag{7}\]
The energy density at each point depends only on the density and its gradient at that point. A meta-GGA adds τ(r), still at the same point. Now consider two argon atoms far apart, so that their densities do not overlap. At every point in space, the density is either that of atom A or that of atom B (or zero). The integral splits into a sum of two atomic integrals, and the interaction energy is exactly zero. As the atoms approach and the densities start to overlap, the semilocal functional “sees” the overlap, but this effect decays exponentially with distance, like the density tails, not as R⁻⁶.
Dispersion is a correlation between fluctuations at r in atom A and at r′ in atom B, which may be far apart. A functional that looks only at one point at a time cannot know about it. This is a limitation of the form of the functional, not of its parameters.
Different semilocal functionals fail in different ways in the overlap region, where they can produce spurious binding or spurious repulsion. LSDA tends to overbind weakly interacting systems. PBE gives a little binding for some dispersion-bound complexes. B88 exchange (in BLYP, B3LYP) is quite repulsive, so BLYP and B3LYP often predict little or no binding for rare-gas and alkane dimers. None of these behaviors comes from real dispersion: they are side effects of how the exchange functional behaves where the density is small and varies quickly. Getting binding from LSDA is “right for the wrong reason”.


2.3.2 Hybrids
Hybrid functionals add a fraction of HF exchange, which is nonlocal. But dispersion is a correlation effect, and the correlation part of a hybrid is still semilocal. Hybrids miss dispersion just as GGAs do.


2.3.3 Hartree–Fock
Hartree–Fock describes each electron in the average field of the others. Instantaneous, correlated fluctuations are exactly what the mean field leaves out, so HF has no dispersion at all. HF describes electrostatics, induction and Pauli repulsion, so it binds hydrogen-bonded or ionic complexes partially, but rare-gas and alkane dimers come out unbound. Experiment 1 already showed this for (HCl)₂.


2.3.4 Wave-function methods
Correlated wave-function methods include dispersion naturally, because they include excitations on both monomers at once. MP2 includes it at second order (and tends to overestimate it for π stacks). CCSD(T) describes it accurately, which is why it provides the reference values for noncovalent databases such as S66 (Řezáč et al. 2011; Řezáč and Hobza 2016).

title: Lecture 8 · Dispersion and noncovalent interactions
section: 2.4 How to put dispersion back into DFT
text:
2.4 How to put dispersion back into DFT
Three strategies are in use (Grimme et al. 2016, 2011). Experiment 4 compares all three.

2.4.1 Strategy 1: pairwise corrections (-D)
The simplest idea is to add the London formula, atom pair by atom pair, to the DFT energy:
\[
E_\text{tot} = E_\text{DFT} + E_\text{disp}, \qquad
E_\text{disp} = -\sum_{A<B}\sum_{n=6,8} s_n\,\frac{C_n^{AB}}{R_{AB}^n}\,f_{\text{damp},n}(R_{AB}) .
\tag{8}\]
Here RAB is the distance between atoms A and B, C₆AB and C₈AB are dispersion coefficients (the C₈/R⁸ term describes dipole–quadrupole fluctuations and matters at medium range), sn are scaling factors fitted for each functional, and fdamp is a damping function. The correction depends only on the geometry, so it costs almost nothing and does not change the density or the orbitals. It adds energy (and forces, for geometry optimizations).
Why damping? The bare −C₆/R⁶ diverges at short distance (Figure 1 b). It would make molecules collapse. Moreover, at short and medium range the functional already describes some correlation; adding the full −C₆/R⁶ there would count it twice. The damping function switches the correction off where the functional is already doing the job. Two forms are common:

zero damping sends the correction to zero at short range. D2 used a Fermi-type function of R/R₀, and the original D3 a similar “zero-damping” function.
rational (Becke–Johnson, BJ) damping replaces R⁶ by R⁶ + R₀⁶, so the correction tends to a finite constant at short range (Grimme et al. 2011):

\[
f_\text{damp,n}^\text{BJ}(R) = \frac{R^n}{R^n + (a_1 R_0^{AB} + a_2)^n}, \qquad R_0^{AB} = \sqrt{C_8^{AB}/C_6^{AB}} .
\tag{9}\]
The parameters a₁, a₂ and s₈ are fitted for each functional, because each functional has its own amount of spurious short-range binding or repulsion. That is why the same -D4 correction gives different numbers on PBE and on B3LYP.
A short history. Grimme’s first corrections (D, 2004, and D2, 2006 (Grimme 2006a)) used fixed C₆ for each element. But the C₆ of carbon depends on its environment: an sp³ carbon in an alkane is less polarizable than an sp² carbon in benzene. D3 (2010) made C₆ depend on the coordination number of each atom, computed from the geometry (Grimme et al. 2010). D3(BJ) added rational damping (Grimme et al. 2011).
-D4, the version used in this course (Caldeweyher et al. 2017, 2019), goes one step further. Its main ingredients are:

reference polarizabilities. For each element, D4 stores frequency-dependent polarizabilities α(iω) of reference systems with different coordination numbers.
coordination and charge. For each atom in your molecule, D4 interpolates between these references using the atom’s coordination number and its partial charge. The charges come from a fast electronegativity-equilibration model that uses only the geometry. An anion-like atom is more polarizable (larger C₆) than a cation-like one, which D3 could not capture.
Casimir–Polder integration. The atom-in-molecule α(iω) are combined with Equation 6 to give C₆AB for every pair.
a three-body term. The Axilrod–Teller–Muto term describes the dispersion among three atoms at once. It is usually repulsive for compact arrangements and matters for large molecules and molecular crystals.

In Q-Chem, -D4 is requested with DFT_D = D4 on top of the functional (e.g., METHOD = B3LYP). The site’s input generator does it for you.


2.4.2 Strategy 2: nonlocal correlation functionals (VV10, rVV10)
The second strategy is to fix the functional itself, by adding a correlation term that couples two points of space:
\[
E_\text{c}^\text{nl} = \frac{1}{2}\iint \rho(\mathbf r)\,\Phi(\mathbf r, \mathbf r')\,\rho(\mathbf r')\,d\mathbf r\,d\mathbf r' + \beta N .
\tag{10}\]
The kernel Φ depends on the distance |r − r′| and on the local density and its gradient at both points. The first functional of this kind was vdW-DF by Dion, Lundqvist and co-workers (Dion et al. 2004; Lee et al. 2010). Vydrov and Van Voorhis built the simpler and more accurate VV10 (Vydrov and Van Voorhis 2010). Its kernel has the form
\[
\Phi^\text{VV10} = -\frac{3}{2\,g\,g'\,(g+g')}, \qquad g = \omega_0(\mathbf r)\,R^2 + \kappa(\mathbf r), \quad R = |\mathbf r - \mathbf r'|,
\tag{11}\]
where ω₀(r) is a local excitation frequency built from the density and its gradient, and κ(r) controls the short-range behavior. For large R, g ≈ ω₀R², and Φ ≈ −3/(2ω₀ω₀′(ω₀+ω₀′)R⁶): the R⁻⁶ law is recovered, with C₆ coefficients that come from the density itself, not from a table. The kernel has two parameters, b and C; b in particular is adjusted for each host functional. The constant β is chosen so that the term vanishes for the uniform electron gas.
rVV10 (Sabatini et al. 2013) is a revised form of the kernel that can be evaluated much faster (via a Fourier-space interpolation), with nearly the same accuracy. B97M-rV (Mardirossian et al. 2017) is B97M-V with rVV10 in place of VV10.
Compared with -D4, nonlocal functionals respond to the actual electron density (they “know” about charge transfer or unusual bonding), at the price of an extra double integral over the grid. This is why B97M-V and ωB97M-V cost more per SCF cycle.


2.4.3 Strategy 3: fitted functionals
The third strategy is to include noncovalent complexes in the training set of a highly flexible functional, and let the fit find parameters that reproduce their binding energies. Many Minnesota functionals (M06-2X, M11, MN15) work this way (Zhao and Truhlar 2008; Peverati and Truhlar 2011; Yu et al. 2016). They describe medium-range dispersion (the region around the equilibrium distance of most complexes) surprisingly well. But they are still semilocal (plus HF exchange) in their correlation, so they have no true R⁻⁶ tail at long range. Dispersion corrections for some Minnesota functionals have been proposed (Goerigk and Grimme 2011; Goerigk 2015), but they are small by design.

WarningCommon mistakes about dispersion corrections




“-D4 changes the orbitals.” It does not. It adds an energy computed from the geometry (it does change optimized geometries, through the forces).
“Adding -D4 always helps.” It fixes missing dispersion. It cannot fix other errors of the functional, and if the functional already has spurious binding (or the basis has BSSE), adding -D4 can overbind.
“The V in ωB97M-V means it is a meta-GGA.” V stands for VV10, a correlation term. The rung is set by the exchange and by the ingredients.

title: Lecture 8 · Dispersion and noncovalent interactions
text:
2.5 Intramolecular dispersion: branched alkanes
Dispersion does not act only between molecules. Any two atoms that are a few ångström apart in the same molecule also attract each other. In a long, extended chain most atom pairs are far apart. In a compact, branched molecule, more atoms are at medium distance (1,3- and 1,4-contacts between C and H atoms), so the total intramolecular dispersion is larger.
This is part of the reason why branched alkanes are more stable than their linear isomers: for example, neohexane (2,2-dimethylbutane) lies below n-hexane. Schleyer and co-workers called the stabilizing 1,3-interactions in alkanes protobranching. The effect is small, a few kcal/mol, but it is a classic difficulty for DFT. In 2006 Grimme (Grimme 2006b) and Wodrich, Corminboeuf and Schleyer (Wodrich et al. 2006) showed that popular functionals such as B3LYP make systematic errors for the relative stability of alkane isomers, and that the errors grow with the size of the molecule. Missing medium-range correlation (dispersion) is one of the causes. Karton, Gruzman and Martin computed benchmark values for all the alkane isomers up to octane (Karton et al. 2009); reaction 4b comes from that work, via the AlkIsomer11 subset of MGCDB84.
Notice how different this is from Experiment 3. There, the molecule changed shape but kept the same set of close contacts, so dispersion nearly cancelled. Here, the number of medium-range contacts changes.

title: Lecture 8 · Dispersion and noncovalent interactions
text:
2.6 A reminder about BSSE
When you compute the binding energy of a dimer, E(dimer) − E(monomer A) − E(monomer B), BSSE makes the dimer artificially too stable (Lecture 7). With def2-TZVP the BSSE is much smaller than with double-ζ sets, but it is not zero, and for a dimer bound by 1–2 kcal/mol even a few tenths matter. We do not correct for it in Experiment 4. Lecture 10 defines the counterpoise correction that removes most of it.

What each reaction tests:

4a, Diels–Alder. Two π bonds become two new C–C σ bonds and one π bond moves. The bonding changes substantially between reactants and product. This is a test of how well a functional describes bond formation, not dispersion.
4b, alkane isomerization. Same atoms, same bond types (all C–C and C–H single bonds), but a different number of medium-range contacts. A test of intramolecular dispersion and of subtle electronic effects in alkanes.
4c, ethane dimer. Almost pure dispersion. A direct test of how each method treats dispersion.
4d, methanol dimer. A hydrogen bond. Mostly electrostatics and induction, with a smaller dispersion part.

title: Lecture 8 · Dispersion and noncovalent interactions
text:
3.2 Methods and jobs
The same 16 methods as Experiment 3, all with def2-TZVP. Ten molecules × 16 methods = 160 jobs.

title: Lecture 8 · Dispersion and noncovalent interactions
text:
3.3 What to watch out for

Directions and signs. 4c and 4d are written as monomers → dimer, so the reference values are negative: a negative ΔE means the dimer is bound. A positive signed error for a dimer means it is bound too weakly.
Coefficients. In 4c the ethane monomer counts twice: ν = −2. In 4a and 4d three species are involved.
Two different methanol monomers. In 4d the monomers are cut from the dimer and have slightly different geometries, so compute both (A and B). Do not use one monomer twice.
Pairs of methods. PBE/PBE-D4 and B3LYP/B3LYP-D4 differ only by the dispersion correction. The Does -D4 help? chart compares each pair directly.
The dimer chart. The binding of the two dimers chart groups the methods by how they treat dispersion (none, D4, VV10, fitted). Before you look, write down what you expect for each group on 4c and on 4d, and why the two dimers might behave differently.
Lock in your predictions on the experiment page before you run anything.

title: Lecture 8 · Dispersion and noncovalent interactions
text:
3.4 Key points

Conformational and cis–trans reactions are easy because errors cancel between two forms of the same molecule; noncovalent changes (like the H-bond in 3c) cancel less.
LSDA overbinds weak interactions, HF underbinds them; neither is reliable for noncovalent chemistry.
Hybrids cost more per SCF cycle than (meta-)GGAs because of the exchange matrix K; range separation and VV10 add more. B3LYP is not special in cost.
London dispersion is an attractive correlation between fluctuating dipoles. It decays as −C₆/R⁶, with C₆ set by polarizabilities.
Semilocal functionals and Hartree–Fock cannot describe dispersion: semilocal ones see one point at a time, HF has no correlation.
-D4 adds damped pairwise −C₆/R⁶ and −C₈/R⁸ terms with coordination- and charge-dependent C₆, plus a three-body term. VV10/rVV10 add a nonlocal correlation functional of the density. Minnesota functionals capture medium-range dispersion by fitting.
Damping prevents the divergence of −C₆/R⁶ at short range and avoids double counting with the functional.
Intramolecular dispersion helps make branched alkanes more stable than linear ones, and is a known difficulty for popular functionals.

title: Lecture 8 · Dispersion and noncovalent interactions
text:
3.5 Study questions

Why does adding -D4 change the reaction energies of Experiment 3 so little?
Explain, with the signs, why LSDA and HF tend to err in opposite directions on the hydrogen-bond-breaking reaction 3c.
Starting from Equation 2, carry out the expansion and verify Equation 3. Why do the first-order terms cancel?
Use Equation 5 to explain why C₆ for two xenon atoms is much larger than for two neon atoms.
Two argon atoms are 5.0 Å apart. Using C₆ = 886 kcal mol⁻¹ Å⁶, compute the undamped dispersion energy. Is damping important at this distance? (Look at Figure 1.)
Explain in your own words why a GGA gives zero interaction energy for two atoms whose densities do not overlap.
What is the role of the damping function in -D4? What would happen in a geometry optimization without it?
What does -D4 add over D3? Give one chemical situation where the difference should matter.
Compare -D4 and VV10: which one depends on the electron density, which is cheaper, and which one has an R⁻⁶ tail with coefficients computed from the density?
Why is a branched alkane stabilized more by dispersion than its linear isomer?

title: Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
text:
1.1 The errors exploded
The first thing you probably noticed in Experiment 5 is the scale of the signed error chart. In Experiment 3 the bars were measured in tenths of a kcal/mol; in Experiment 4 in kcal/mol; here many are measured in tens of kcal/mol, and a few in hundreds. No method was accurate for all four reactions. Most methods had at least one error well above chemical accuracy.
What you probably saw, reaction by reaction, and why:

Hartree–Fock is catastrophic for the two dissociations, 5b (CaO) and especially 5c (H₂SO₄ atomization). It badly underestimates both, because the molecule has much more correlation energy than the separated atoms, and HF has none (Lecture 9). Its error on 5c is so large that it dominates the chart.
LSDA (SPW92) errs the other way: it overbinds molecules, so its atomization energies are far too large. This is the classic failure of LSDA that motivated GGAs in the first place.
GGAs (BP86, BLYP, PBE) still make large errors, typically overbinding CaO by many kcal/mol. Their delocalization error and the difficulty of open-shell atoms add up, with no cancellation.
Hybrids and hybrid meta-GGAs usually reduce the errors, but none of them is uniformly good. The sign of the error changes from reaction to reaction and from functional to functional.
The two ozone reactions (5a and 5d) are hard for almost everyone. Ozone’s multireference character is not described well by any single-determinant functional, and different functionals miss it in different directions.

title: Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
text:
1.2 -D4 is not a universal fix
Compare B3LYP with B3LYP-D4 and PBE with PBE-D4. What you probably saw is that -D4 changes these reaction energies only a little, and not always in the right direction. That is exactly what the theory predicts. -D4 adds the dispersion energy between atom pairs. In an atomization or a dissociation, the dispersion energy of the molecule is a tiny fraction of the bond energies, and the errors in Experiment 5 come from somewhere else: self-interaction, static correlation, the description of open-shell atoms. A correction designed for one physical effect cannot repair another.

title: Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
text:
1.3 Absolute and relative errors
The relative-error chart shows the same errors as a percentage of each reference value. Reaction 5c has the largest reference (602.18 kcal/mol), so its percentage errors look modest even when the absolute errors are the largest of the experiment. For example, a 12 kcal/mol error on 5c is only 2%, but it is twelve times chemical accuracy. A rotational barrier of 1 kcal/mol computed with a 0.3 kcal/mol error looks bad at 30%, but it is chemically harmless. The lesson of Lecture 9 stands: chemistry is decided by absolute energies; relative errors only help compare quantities of very different size.

title: Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
text:
1.4 The CaO spotlight
The spotlight chart for 5b highlights MN15. You probably saw that MN15 has one of the smallest errors on CaO, while most other functionals miss it by many kcal/mol. This is not proof that MN15 understands CaO better. CaO is part of the database MN15 was fitted to (Yu et al. 2016; Yu and Truhlar 2015), so reproducing it well is what the fit was designed to do. On the other reactions of Experiment 5, MN15 is not exceptional. A functional must be judged on data it was not trained on. This is true of every fitted functional, Minnesota or not.

title: Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
text:
1.5 From easy to hard
The easy → hard chart puts your Experiments 3, 4 and 5 side by side, with the MAE of each method on a log scale. Three trends usually appear:

Everything gets worse from left to right. The MAE of a typical method grows by one to two orders of magnitude from Experiment 3 to Experiment 5. Error cancellation does the work in the easy reactions; in the hard ones, the functional is on its own.
The ranking changes. Methods that look equivalent in Experiment 3 separate in Experiment 4 (dispersion) and again in Experiment 5 (self-interaction and static correlation). LSDA and HF, which hid among the others in Experiment 3, become the worst.
Modern functionals win on average. The best overall performers are usually among the modern meta-GGAs and hybrid meta-GGAs with good dispersion treatment, such as ωB97M-V, B97M-V or the Minnesota hybrids. But no method wins every reaction, and the margin between the best few is smaller than the spread of errors within each experiment.

Look at the thick line on the chart: your Experiment 3 “draft pick”. Was it still a good choice by Experiment 5? If not, what would you have needed to know in advance? This is the question every computational chemist faces when choosing a method, and it is why we read benchmarks on the subsets closest to our problem (Lecture 14).






WarningCommon mistake: “Functional X is the best”



There is no best functional, only functionals that are better on average or better for a class of problems. Experiment 5 shows that a functional can be excellent on one reaction and poor on the next, even among reactions with five heavy atoms. As Hopmann put it, “Do not use DFT for mechanisms it cannot handle” (Hopmann 2019).

title: Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
text:
2.1 Two approximations, two errors
Every calculation makes the two approximations of Lecture 1: a finite basis set (approximating Ψ, or the Kohn–Sham orbitals) and an approximate method (approximating Ĥ, here the exchange–correlation functional). Each introduces an error. To separate them, imagine computing the same reaction with the same functional in a complete basis set (CBS). Then
\[
\underbrace{\Delta E^{\text{method/basis}} - \Delta E^\text{ref}}_{\varepsilon_\text{total}}
= \underbrace{\Delta E^{\text{method/CBS}} - \Delta E^\text{ref}}_{\varepsilon_\text{method}}
+ \underbrace{\Delta E^{\text{method/basis}} - \Delta E^{\text{method/CBS}}}_{\varepsilon_\text{basis}} .
\tag{1}\]
This is an identity: we have only added and subtracted ΔEmethod/CBS. But it is a useful one.

εmethod is the error of the functional itself. It does not depend on the basis. It is what benchmark papers report, using large basis sets.
εbasis is the error caused by the finite basis. It goes to zero as the basis grows, as you saw in Experiment 1.

In practice there are other terms too: the integration grid (Lecture 11), SCF convergence and stability (Lecture 12), the geometry, and the uncertainty of the reference itself. With the settings used in this lab they are usually smaller than the first two, but they are not always negligible.
The two main errors have different origins, and so they have independent signs. When they have the same sign, they add up. When they have opposite signs, they partly cancel, and the total error can be smaller than the method error alone (Figure 1). A small basis can then make a method look better than it really is. This is luck, not accuracy: change the reaction, and the two errors may no longer have opposite signs.






Figure 1: Schematic error budget. In each case the method error is the same (+4 kcal/mol). Near the CBS limit the basis error is small, and the total error is essentially the method error. With a small basis, the basis error can have the opposite sign (errors cancel, the result looks good) or the same sign (errors add up). The numbers are illustrative, not results.









TipWorked example: splitting the error



A functional gives these results for one reaction (illustrative numbers, not from any experiment in this course): ΔE = −26.00 kcal/mol with a large, nearly complete basis, and ΔE = −29.50 kcal/mol with a small basis. The reference is −30.00 kcal/mol. Treating the large-basis value as the CBS limit:

εmethod = −26.00 − (−30.00) = +4.00 kcal/mol;
εbasis = −29.50 − (−26.00) = −3.50 kcal/mol;
εtotal = −29.50 − (−30.00) = +0.50 kcal/mol = 4.00 + (−3.50).

The small-basis result is eight times closer to the reference than the large-basis one. But the functional did not get better: two errors of opposite sign cancelled. This is the situation in the middle of Figure 1.

title: Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
text:
2.3 Basis-set superposition error
The basis-set superposition error (BSSE) appears whenever two fragments come close: two molecules in a dimer, or two distant parts of one molecule. Each fragment is described by its own basis functions, but in the complex it can also use the functions centered on its partner. The isolated fragment has no such help. So the complex is described with an effectively larger basis than the separated fragments, and it comes out artificially too stable. For a dimer, BSSE always makes the binding too strong.
BSSE is not limited to dimers. In a large, compact molecule, an atom can borrow functions from other atoms that are close in space but far along the chain. This intramolecular BSSE favors compact structures over extended ones. It matters, for example, when comparing a branched alkane with a linear one, or a folded conformer with an unfolded one (Kruse and Grimme 2012).
BSSE shrinks quickly as the basis grows, because a fragment that already has a nearly complete basis gains little from its partner. It is a significant problem for double-ζ sets and much smaller for triple-ζ and quadruple-ζ sets. It is a different thing from BSIE, although both are consequences of an incomplete basis.

2.3.1 The counterpoise correction
Boys and Bernardi proposed a simple way to remove most of the BSSE of a dimer AB (Boys and Bernardi 1970): compute the monomers with the same basis they enjoy in the dimer. In practice, the monomer A is computed at its geometry in the dimer, together with the basis functions of B placed at B’s atomic positions, but without B’s nuclei and electrons. These are called ghost atoms. Writing \(E_X^{Y}\) for the energy of fragment X computed in the basis of Y, all at the dimer geometry, the counterpoise-corrected interaction energy is
\[
\Delta E_\text{int}^\text{CP} = E_{AB}^{AB} - E_{A}^{AB} - E_{B}^{AB} .
\tag{2}\]
The uncorrected interaction energy uses \(E_A^{A}\) and \(E_B^{B}\) instead. The difference between the two is the counterpoise estimate of the BSSE:
\[
\delta_\text{BSSE} = \big(E_A^{AB} - E_A^{A}\big) + \big(E_B^{AB} - E_B^{B}\big) \le 0 .
\tag{3}\]
Each term is negative (or zero), because a larger basis can only lower the energy variationally. If the monomers relax their geometry in the dimer, a small deformation term is added, but the idea is the same. Q-Chem and most other programs can do counterpoise calculations with ghost atoms.
The counterpoise correction is the standard tool for dimers, but it has limits. It is defined for well-separated fragments, not for intramolecular BSSE. And it removes the BSSE but not the BSIE, so a counterpoise-corrected double-ζ result is still far from the CBS limit. For large systems, Kruse and Grimme proposed a geometric counterpoise correction (gCP) that estimates the inter- and intramolecular BSSE from the geometry alone (Kruse and Grimme 2012).

title: Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
text:
2.4 Why B3LYP/6-31G* became so popular

2.4.1 A brief history
In the 1990s two things happened at once. Becke introduced hybrid functionals (Becke 1993), and in 1994 Stephens, Frisch and co-workers defined B3LYP (Stephens et al. 1994), which quickly became available in the most widely used quantum chemistry program of the time (Gaussian). The 6-31G* basis set of Pople and co-workers (Hariharan and Pople 1973; Francl et al. 1982) was already one of the most used basis sets, in that program and in the textbooks. Computers were slow: a double-ζ basis was what you could afford for a molecule with ten or twenty heavy atoms.
B3LYP/6-31G* was a huge improvement over what organic chemists used before (Hartree–Fock, semi-empirical methods). Geometries were good, reaction energies were often within a few kcal/mol, and calculations finished overnight. Papers that used it worked, so the next papers used it too. B3LYP’s original papers became some of the most cited in all of chemistry, and the combination B3LYP/6-31G* became a de facto standard, often chosen because “everybody uses it” rather than because it was tested for the problem at hand.


2.4.2 Right for the wrong reasons
B3LYP has no dispersion (Lecture 8). With a complete basis, it underbinds dimers and gives too little stability to compact molecules. 6-31G* is a small, unbalanced basis with a large BSSE, which artificially stabilizes compact structures and complexes. The two errors have opposite signs. In many organic systems, the BSSE of 6-31G* partly compensates the missing dispersion of B3LYP, and the combination looks better than B3LYP with a large basis.
Kruse, Goerigk and Grimme analyzed this in detail in 2012 (Kruse et al. 2012). They showed that much of the apparent success of B3LYP/6-31G* comes from this fortuitous cancellation, that it fails badly when the cancellation does not happen, and that adding dispersion and BSSE corrections (or simply using a better basis and a modern functional) removes the problem. Their title says it plainly: the standard B3LYP/6-31G* model chemistry should not be used for molecular thermochemistry. A broader analysis of small basis sets and their error sources was given by Sure, Brandenburg and Grimme (Sure et al. 2016).
The worrying part is not that B3LYP/6-31G* is sometimes accurate. It is that we cannot predict when. Lucky cancellations depend on the reaction. Experiment 6 lets you see this for yourself.






WarningCommon mistakes with small basis sets




Concluding that a small basis is “more accurate” because it gave a smaller error once.
Adding -D4 to a functional used with a small basis without thinking: if BSSE is already mimicking dispersion, adding -D4 counts the attraction twice and can overbind.
Comparing two functionals with a small basis and drawing conclusions about the functionals. Compare methods at a (nearly) converged basis first.
Assuming all double-ζ sets are equivalent because they share the label “DZ”.

title: Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
section: 2.5 Not all double-ζ sets are equal
text:
2.5 Not all double-ζ sets are equal

2.5.1 Four polarized double-ζ sets
All four basis sets of Experiment 6 are “polarized double-ζ”: two functions per valence atomic orbital, plus polarization functions. But they were built differently:

6-31G* (Pople) (Hariharan and Pople 1973; Francl et al. 1982): a split-valence set from the 1970s. The star adds one set of d functions on non-hydrogen atoms only. Hydrogen has no polarization functions (that would be 6-31G**). The s and p functions of each valence shell share exponents (“sp shells”), which was a trick to speed up integral evaluation on old computers.
def2-SVP (Karlsruhe) (Weigend and Ahlrichs 2005): split valence plus polarization on all atoms, including p functions on hydrogen. Optimized mostly at the HF level and designed to be balanced across the periodic table.
cc-pVDZ (Dunning) (Dunning 1989): correlation consistent. The polarization functions were chosen to recover correlation energy in wave-function methods. Same composition as def2-SVP for first-row atoms, but different exponents and contractions.
pc-1 (Jensen) (Jensen 2001, 2002): polarization consistent, optimized specifically for DFT. If it is not available, the smallest Karlsruhe set, def2-SV(P), which drops the p functions on hydrogen, is a fallback.



2.5.2 How to count basis functions
The number of basis functions K (or Nbf) sets the cost of a calculation. You can find it in every Q-Chem output, but you should also be able to count it by hand. You need the contracted composition of the basis for each element, written in square brackets as the number of contracted s, p, d, … shells. Each shell contributes:

s: 1 function;
p: 3 functions;
d: 5 functions if spherical (“pure”, 5d), or 6 if Cartesian (6d);
f: 7 (spherical) or 10 (Cartesian).

The compositions you need for first-row atoms and hydrogen are:



Table 1: Contracted compositions of the four polarized double-ζ sets for H and first-row atoms. For 6-31G*, the core 1s is one contracted s function, and the inner and outer valence shells each contribute one s and one p shell.

Two details matter:

Spherical or Cartesian d. The Pople sets were defined with six Cartesian d functions; the def2, cc and pc sets use five spherical d functions. Many programs follow these conventions by default, but they can be changed. Always check the number your output reports.
Same count, different quality. Two sets with the same number of contracted functions can differ in the number of primitive Gaussians in each contraction and in the exponents. That affects both the accuracy and the cost of computing the integrals.







TipWorked example: water and ethene



Water, H₂O. One O and two H.

6-31G*: O = 3 s + 2 × 3 p + 1 × 6 d (Cartesian) = 3 + 6 + 6 = 15; each H = 2. Total = 15 + 2 × 2 = 19 (or 18 with spherical d).
def2-SVP, cc-pVDZ, pc-1: O = 3 + 6 + 5 = 14; each H = 2 + 3 = 5. Total = 14 + 2 × 5 = 24.

Ethene, C₂H₄. Two C and four H.

6-31G*: 2 × 15 + 4 × 2 = 38 (or 36 with spherical d).
def2-SVP, cc-pVDZ, pc-1: 2 × 14 + 4 × 5 = 28 + 20 = 48.

The difference comes almost entirely from hydrogen. In 6-31G* each H has 2 functions; in the other three it has 5, because of the p polarization functions. The more hydrogen atoms a molecule has, the bigger the gap. In Experiment 6 you will do the same count for cyclohexene and compare it with your outputs.


Since cost grows as a power of K (Experiment 1), a basis with 25% more functions can cost roughly twice as much. That was a real advantage of 6-31G* in the 1990s. Today it is rarely a good reason.

title: Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
text:
3.2 Methods and jobs

Functionals: B3LYP and B3LYP-D4.
Basis sets: 6-31G*, def2-SVP, cc-pVDZ and pc-1, plus def2-TZVP as the comparison.
Eight molecules × 2 functionals × 4 small basis sets = 64 new jobs. They are all small; running one basis set at a time works well.
The def2-TZVP energies are not recomputed: the Import button on the results form copies your B3LYP and B3LYP-D4/def2-TZVP energies from Experiments 4 and 5 (from this browser). If you worked on another computer, load your saved files on those pages first.
For every job, record the total energy and the number of basis functions. The basis-size table uses them to compare the four sets for cyclohexene.

title: Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
text:
3.3 What to watch out for

Think in terms of Equation 1. For each reaction, the def2-TZVP result is your best estimate of the B3LYP method error. The difference between a small-basis result and the def2-TZVP result estimates the basis-set error. Ask whether the two have the same or opposite signs.
The anomaly spotter. The spot the anomaly chart asks you to flag cells where a small basis does better than def2-TZVP. Flag them before you explain them, then ask, for each one: is this a better description, or a cancellation of errors?
-D4 with small basis sets. Ask whether BSSE and -D4 describe the same attraction or different ones, and what that implies when both are present.
CaO. Ca is a period-4 element with a large, polarizable electron cloud. Think about how well each double-ζ set might describe it, and remember that the products are atoms.
pc-1. If BASIS = pc-1 is not available on the server, use def2-SV(P) and say so in your report.
Optional. Run the three reactions with ωB97M-V/6-31G* and compare with your ωB97M-V/def2-TZVP results. Does a modern functional benefit from the small basis the same way?
Lock in your predictions on the experiment page before you run anything.

title: Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
text:
3.4 Key points

In Experiment 5, errors grew to tens of kcal/mol for hard reactions; HF and LSDA failed in opposite directions on dissociations, and ozone was hard for nearly everyone.
-D4 corrects dispersion only; it does not fix self-interaction, static correlation or open-shell atoms.
MN15’s good result on CaO comes from its training set. Judge a functional on data it was not fitted to.
Total error = method error + basis-set error (+ smaller terms). The two have independent signs and can cancel.
BSIE is the error from a finite basis; BSSE is the artificial stabilization of a complex (or a compact molecule) that borrows its partner’s basis functions. Both shrink as the basis grows.
The counterpoise correction computes the monomers in the full dimer basis using ghost atoms: \(\Delta E^\text{CP}_\text{int} = E_{AB}^{AB} - E_A^{AB} - E_B^{AB}\).
B3LYP/6-31G* became popular for historical and practical reasons. Its successes often come from BSSE compensating missing dispersion, a cancellation that is unpredictable.
To count basis functions, add up the contracted shells of each atom: s = 1, p = 3, d = 5 (spherical) or 6 (Cartesian). 6-31G* has no polarization on H, so it is smaller than def2-SVP, cc-pVDZ and pc-1.

title: Lecture 10 · Basis-set error vs functional error
text:
3.5 Study questions

Why does -D4 barely change the error of B3LYP on the atomization of H₂SO₄?
A functional has errors of +0.3, +2.5 and +25 kcal/mol in Experiments 3, 4 and 5. Another has +0.5, +1.5 and +8. Which would you choose for a new organic reaction, and what else would you want to know?
Using Equation 1, a method gives ΔE = 10.0 kcal/mol at the CBS limit and 12.5 kcal/mol with a small basis; the reference is 12.0 kcal/mol. Compute εmethod, εbasis and εtotal. Is the small-basis result trustworthy?
Explain the difference between BSIE and BSSE. Which one can be corrected with the counterpoise method?
Write the counterpoise-corrected interaction energy for a water dimer. Which calculations do you need, and which use ghost atoms?
Why is the counterpoise estimate of the BSSE (Equation 3) always negative or zero?
Explain how the BSSE of 6-31G* and the missing dispersion of B3LYP can cancel. Give an example of a reaction where you would expect them not to cancel.
Count the basis functions of methanol (CH₃OH) in 6-31G* (Cartesian d) and in def2-SVP.
Why does the difference in size between 6-31G* and def2-SVP grow with the number of hydrogen atoms?
A colleague reports a reaction energy with B3LYP-D4/6-31G* that agrees with experiment within 0.5 kcal/mol. What would you ask before believing that the method is reliable for this reaction?

title: Lecture 12 · SCF stability, open shells and transition metals
Lecture 12 · SCF stability, open shells and transition metals
section: 1.1 Wiggles are grid noise, not physics
text:
1.1 Wiggles are grid noise, not physics
The reference Ar₂ curve has one minimum. Most of you probably found curves with two, three or more minima, especially on SG-1. Those extra minima are not chemistry. Argon atoms do not have several preferred distances. As Lecture 11 explained, the grid moves with the atoms, so the integration error changes erratically from one distance to the next. The binding energy is only 0.28 kcal/mol, or 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ \(E_h\), so an integration error of a few 10⁻⁵ \(E_h\) is enough to draw a new minimum.
Two simple tests separate noise from physics:

Does the feature survive a finer grid? A physical minimum stays where it is when you go from SG-2 to SG-3. A grid artifact moves, shrinks or disappears.
Does it make physical sense? A real potential between two closed-shell atoms has one well. Several minima a few tenths of an ångström apart are a red flag.

The max Δ vs SG-3 column of the wiggle report measures the first test. It compares each curve with the same functional on the finest grid, without using the reference, so it measures grid convergence alone.

title: Lecture 12 · SCF stability, open shells and transition metals
section: 1.2 Which functionals needed the finest grid?
text:
1.2 Which functionals needed the finest grid?
The typical pattern, which you probably reproduced:

SG-1 is too coarse for this problem for almost everyone. Even B3LYP may show small ripples at SG-1 on a scale of 0.1 kcal/mol, invisible in ordinary reaction energies but obvious here.
The meta-GGAs M06-L and M11-L and the hybrid meta-GGA M11 were usually the most sensitive. Their curves often still had spurious minima at SG-2, and sometimes small irregularities even at SG-3. This matches what Wheeler and Houk (Wheeler and Houk 2010) and Mardirossian and Head-Gordon (Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2016b) reported for Minnesota functionals.
ωB97M-V is also a meta-GGA, but it was designed with smoothness in mind (Mardirossian and Head-Gordon 2016a). It usually converges by SG-2.
B3LYP converges quickly with the grid, because a GGA hybrid has a smooth integrand.

title: Lecture 12 · SCF stability, open shells and transition metals
text:
1.3 Grid convergence is not accuracy
Now look at the shape of the converged curves. B3LYP has no dispersion, and argon is held together only by dispersion. On a converged grid, B3LYP’s curve is probably repulsive at every distance, or nearly so. Any “well” it showed on SG-1 was made by the grid. Some Minnesota functionals bind Ar₂ only weakly on a converged grid. ωB97M-V includes VV10 nonlocal correlation and usually has a well of about the right depth. A smooth curve tells you the grid is good enough. It does not tell you the functional is right.

title: Lecture 12 · SCF stability, open shells and transition metals
text:
1.5 Recommendations

Use at least SG-2 for meta-GGAs, and SG-3 or (99,590) for Minnesota functionals and other heavily parametrized ones. SG-1 is acceptable for GGAs and GGA hybrids in ordinary reaction energies, but not for weak interactions or frequencies.
Use the same grid for every species in a reaction.
Report the grid in every methods section, by name or as \((n_r, n_\Omega)\).
Hartree–Fock has no grid problem. If you answered question 7 with “no, because HF exchange is computed analytically”, you were right.

title: Lecture 12 · SCF stability, open shells and transition metals
text:
2.1 The SCF finds stationary points
In Lecture 4 you saw the SCF loop: guess orbitals, build the Fock (or Kohn–Sham) matrix, diagonalize, repeat until nothing changes (see Lecture 4). When it stops, the energy no longer changes to first order when you mix occupied and virtual orbitals. That is a statement about the gradient. It says nothing about the curvature.
To make this precise, write any small change of the occupied orbitals as a rotation that mixes occupied orbital \(i\) with virtual orbital \(a\) by an amount \(\kappa_{ai}\):
\[
\phi_i \;\rightarrow\; \phi_i + \sum_a \kappa_{ai}\,\phi_a + \dots
\]
The energy is a function of all the rotation parameters \(\boldsymbol{\kappa}\). Expanded around the converged solution,
\[
E(\boldsymbol{\kappa}) = E_0 + \mathbf{g}^{\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{\kappa} + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\boldsymbol{\kappa}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{H}\,\boldsymbol{\kappa} + \dots
\]
The SCF convergence criterion is \(\mathbf{g} = 0\) (the off-diagonal occupied–virtual block of the Fock matrix vanishes; this is Brillouin’s theorem). A point with zero gradient is a stationary point. It can be

a minimum: all eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{H}\) positive;
a saddle point: some eigenvalues negative;
a maximum: all eigenvalues negative (rare in practice).

The matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) of second derivatives of the energy with respect to orbital rotations is the electronic Hessian (or orbital Hessian). Note what is being differentiated: the energy, with respect to orbital rotations. This is not the nuclear Hessian you use for vibrational frequencies.

title: Lecture 12 · SCF stability, open shells and transition metals
section: 2.2 A picture of an unstable solution
text:
2.2 A picture of an unstable solution
Figure 1 shows the toy model used by the stability-landscape widget of Experiment 8. One angle \(\theta\) mixes two orbitals, and the energy is
\[
E(\theta) = \Delta\,\sin^2\theta - \sin^2 2\theta.
\]
At \(\theta = 0\) the gradient is zero for every value of \(\Delta\), so an SCF can converge there. The curvature is \(E''(0) = 2\Delta - 8\). For a large gap (\(\Delta > 4\)) the curvature is positive and \(\theta = 0\) is a minimum. For a small gap (\(\Delta < 4\)) it is negative: \(\theta = 0\) is a maximum along this direction, and lower solutions exist at \(\cos 2\theta^{*} = \Delta/4\).






Figure 1: Toy model of SCF (in)stability (schematic; the same function as the Experiment 8 widget). With a large gap Δ between two low-lying states (blue), the converged point θ = 0 is a minimum. With a small gap (red), the same point still has zero gradient but negative curvature, and two lower solutions exist.









TipWorked example: when does the toy model become unstable?



For \(\Delta = 2\), \(E''(0) = 2(2) - 8 = -4 < 0\), so the converged point is unstable. The lower solutions satisfy \(\cos 2\theta^{*} = 2/4 = 0.5\), so \(2\theta^{*} = 60^\circ\) and \(\theta^{*} = 30^\circ\). Their energy is
\[
E(30^\circ) = 2\sin^2 30^\circ - \sin^2 60^\circ = 2(0.25) - 0.75 = -0.25,
\]
below the converged value \(E(0) = 0\). For \(\Delta = 6\), \(E''(0) = +4\) and there is nothing to fix. The crossover is at \(\Delta = 4\), where the curvature changes sign. Small gaps between states make instabilities likely.

title: Lecture 12 · SCF stability, open shells and transition metals
text:
2.3 The electronic Hessian
For a real, closed-shell Hartree–Fock determinant, the Hessian has a simple block structure built from two matrices (Čı́žek and Paldus 1967; Seeger and Pople 1977):
\[
A_{ia,jb} = (\varepsilon_a - \varepsilon_i)\,\delta_{ij}\,\delta_{ab} + \langle aj \| ib \rangle, \qquad
B_{ia,jb} = \langle ab \| ij \rangle,
\]
where \(i, j\) label occupied orbitals, \(a, b\) virtual orbitals, \(\varepsilon\) orbital energies and \(\langle pq\|rs\rangle\) antisymmetrized two-electron integrals. The solution is stable with respect to real rotations if \(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}\) has no negative eigenvalues, and with respect to complex rotations if \(\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}\) has none. In Kohn–Sham DFT the same structure holds, with the exchange–correlation kernel (the second derivative of \(E_\mathrm{xc}\)) added to the two-electron terms.
Two remarks help the intuition:

The first term is the orbital-energy gap \(\varepsilon_a - \varepsilon_i\). A large HOMO–LUMO gap makes the diagonal large and positive, and the solution is almost certainly stable. Small gaps are where trouble lives.
\(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are the same matrices that appear in time-dependent HF and DFT for excitation energies. A negative eigenvalue of the Hessian corresponds to a “negative excitation energy”: there is a state of the same kind below the one you converged to.

title: Lecture 12 · SCF stability, open shells and transition metals
text:
2.4 Internal and external instabilities
Every SCF calculation works within constraints: restricted or unrestricted spin orbitals, real or complex coefficients. These form a hierarchy (Seeger and Pople 1977; Fukutome 1981):
\[
\text{RHF} \subset \text{UHF} \subset \text{GHF}, \qquad \text{real} \subset \text{complex}.
\]

An internal instability means a lower solution exists within the same constraints: for example, a UHF (or UKS) solution that can lower its energy by rotating to a different UHF solution. This is the typical case for open-shell atoms that converged to the wrong occupation of their d orbitals.
An external instability means a lower solution exists only if you relax a constraint. The classic example is a restricted solution with a lower unrestricted solution (an RHF → UHF, or triplet, instability). Stretch H₂ and the RHF solution, stable near equilibrium, becomes externally unstable past the Coulson–Fischer point (roughly 1.2 Å for HF). From there on, UHF lets the two electrons localize on separate atoms and gives a lower energy.

A stability analysis computes the lowest eigenvalues of the Hessian. If one is negative, the program rotates the orbitals along the corresponding eigenvector, which is downhill by construction, converges the SCF again from there, and checks the new solution. It repeats until all eigenvalues are non-negative (Bauernschmitt and Ahlrichs 1996).

title: Lecture 12 · SCF stability, open shells and transition metals
text:
2.5 Stability analysis in Q-Chem
In Q-Chem, add one line to the $rem section:
INTERNAL_STABILITY  TRUE
After the SCF converges, Q-Chem checks for internal instabilities. If it finds one, it follows it, reconverges and checks again, and the output reports what it found and the new energy. The energy after a successful stability analysis can only be equal to or lower than the energy without it. Q-Chem (Epifanovsky et al. 2021) has separate options for external (restricted → unrestricted) checks; the manual describes them. In this course the open-shell atoms already use unrestricted orbitals, so internal stability is what matters.
A stability analysis costs extra time, usually a few times the cost of the SCF itself, because finding the lowest Hessian eigenvalues requires work similar to a few excited-state calculations. For a small molecule that is nothing. For a large one, run the analysis on the final geometry at least.






WarningCommon mistakes with SCF solutions




“It converged, so it’s right.” Convergence means \(\mathbf{g} = 0\), nothing more.
Comparing energies from different solutions. If one state of a reaction was stabilized and the other wasn’t, the reaction energy mixes two different kinds of solution.
Ignoring an energy that goes up. A stable solution can never be higher than the unstable one it came from. If the “with stability” energy is higher, the two jobs did not use the same settings.

text:
3.1 Spin and ⟨S²⟩
A state with total spin quantum number \(S\) is an eigenfunction of \(\hat S^2\) with eigenvalue \(S(S+1)\) (in units of \(\hbar^2\)), and has multiplicity \(2S + 1\). For \(N_\alpha\) α electrons and \(N_\beta\) β electrons in the high-spin component, \(S = M_S = (N_\alpha - N_\beta)/2\):

A restricted open-shell (ROHF/ROKS) determinant uses the same spatial orbitals for α and β electrons and is a proper spin eigenfunction. An unrestricted (UHF/UKS) determinant lets α and β orbitals differ. That gives more variational freedom and a lower energy, but the determinant is no longer an eigenfunction of \(\hat S^2\). For UHF,
\[
\langle S^2 \rangle_\mathrm{UHF} = S(S+1) + N_\beta - \sum_{i}^{N_\alpha}\sum_{j}^{N_\beta} \big|\langle \phi_i^\alpha | \phi_j^\beta \rangle\big|^2 ,
\]
which is always at least \(S(S+1)\). The excess is spin contamination: the determinant contains some admixture of higher spin states. Q-Chem prints ⟨S²⟩ after every unrestricted SCF.






TipWorked example: is this triplet contaminated?



A UKS calculation on a triplet (\(S = 1\)) prints ⟨S²⟩ = 2.03. The exact value is \(S(S+1) = 2\), so the excess is 0.03, or 1.5%. That is small; the state is essentially a triplet. If it printed 2.60, the excess would be 0.60 (30%), a sign that the determinant is far from a pure triplet, for example a broken-symmetry mixture with a quintet (\(\langle S^2\rangle = 6\)).


In Kohn–Sham DFT, ⟨S²⟩ of the determinant is not strictly the ⟨S²⟩ of the real system: the KS determinant describes a fictitious non-interacting system. It is still a useful diagnostic. A value far from \(S(S+1)\) means the calculation has a problem worth looking at. Note that following an instability can increase spin contamination: the lower solution may break spin symmetry to gain energy.

title: Lecture 12 · SCF stability, open shells and transition metals
text:
3.2 Why transition metals are hard
In main-group chemistry, a closed-shell molecule usually has one dominant electron configuration with a large HOMO–LUMO gap, and the SCF converges to it easily. Transition metals break both assumptions.
Near-degenerate configurations. The 3d and 4s orbitals (4d and 5s in the second row) have similar energies. The iron atom has the ground configuration [Ar]3d⁶4s² (a quintet, ⁵D), but states of the 3d⁷4s¹ configuration lie only about 1–2 eV higher. Each configuration also has many ways to place the d electrons in five d orbitals, so there are many low-lying states and many SCF solutions close in energy. In the language of Figure 1, the gap Δ is small, and instabilities are common.
Symmetry breaking. An open-shell atom with a partially filled d shell has a spherically symmetric density only on average over all the degenerate components. A single KS determinant picks one component and has a non-spherical density. Different starting guesses can land on different components, which in an approximate functional need not have exactly the same energy.
Spin-state energetics. The energy difference between spin states of the same metal depends strongly on the functional. Exact (HF) exchange stabilizes parallel spins, so functionals with more HF exchange tend to favor high-spin states, and semilocal functionals tend to favor low-spin states. No single functional is reliable for all transition-metal spin-state gaps, which is why they are a demanding benchmark (Cao and Ryde 2019).
SCF convergence. With many nearly degenerate orbitals, the SCF can oscillate between occupations from one cycle to the next and never converge. Remedies exist (better guesses, damping, level shifting, direct-minimization algorithms), but some functionals fail more often than others. Experiment 8 keeps only the functional/atom pairs that converged reliably on the IQmol server; the ones that were removed are a lesson in themselves.

title: Lecture 12 · SCF stability, open shells and transition metals
text:
3.3 Effective core potentials and relativity
Ruthenium has 44 electrons and palladium 46. Their core electrons are chemically inert, but they cost basis functions and they move fast. Near a nucleus with charge \(Z\), an inner electron’s speed is a sizable fraction of the speed of light (roughly \(Z/137\) in atomic units). Scalar relativistic effects contract and stabilize s and p orbitals, and through better screening expand and destabilize d and f orbitals. For 4d metals they shift orbital energies and excitation energies by amounts that matter chemically.
An effective core potential (ECP) solves both problems at once. It replaces the core electrons with a potential fitted to accurate relativistic atomic calculations, so the scalar relativistic effects of the core are built in (Andrae et al. 1990). Only the valence electrons are treated explicitly, with a basis set designed for that ECP. The def2 basis sets use small-core ECPs for elements beyond krypton (Weigend and Ahlrichs 2005): for the 4d metals, 28 core electrons (the shells 1s through 3d) are replaced.






TipWorked example: how many electrons does Q-Chem see for Ru⁺?



Ruthenium has \(Z = 44\). Ru⁺ has 43 electrons. The def2 ECP replaces 28 core electrons, so the calculation treats \(43 - 28 = 15\) electrons explicitly, moving in the field of an effective core of charge \(44 - 28 = +16\). For the sextet, \(N_\alpha - N_\beta = 5\) and \(N_\alpha + N_\beta = 15\), so \(N_\alpha = 10\) and \(N_\beta = 5\). For the quartet, \(N_\alpha = 9\) and \(N_\beta = 6\).


In Q-Chem, ECPs are requested with ECP = def2-ECP; the website’s input generator adds it for Ru and Pd. Iron (a 3d metal) is treated with all its electrons in def2 basis sets. Its relativistic effects are smaller, and in this course we ignore them. Spin–orbit coupling, the other relativistic effect, is not included in standard ECPs or in standard DFT. It returns in Lecture 13.
